## PART I : ALGEBRA

## Foundations of Algebra

### Theory

<a href="articles_maths/sets-functions-and-relations.html">Sets, Functions and Relations</a>
<!-- sets and the membership relation; subsets, the power set and the algebra of subsets; ordered pairs and the Cartesian product; relations and their properties; equivalence relations, partitions and quotients; order relations, partial and total; functions as a special kind of relation, injective, surjective and bijective maps, composition and inverse; families and indexed sets; the algebra of subsets as the first example of a Boolean algebra, forward-referenced to Part VI. -->

<a href="articles_maths/logic-and-proof.html">Logic and Proof</a>
<!-- propositional logic: the connectives, truth tables and tautologies; the laws of the algebra of propositions and their identity with the algebra of subsets, forward-referenced to the Boolean algebras of Part VI; predicate logic: variables, quantifiers, free and bound occurrences; the rules of inference and the structure of a formal proof; direct, contrapositive and contradiction arguments; induction and recursion as proof principles; consistency and completeness in outline; the notational conventions used throughout this corpus. -->

<a href="articles_maths/order-theory-and-lattices.html">Order Theory and Lattices</a>
<!-- partial orders, total orders and well-orders; lattices, complete, distributive and modular lattices; Galois connections; the Knaster–Tarski theorem; the lattice of subsets, forward-referenced to the Boolean algebras of Part VI. -->

<a href="articles_maths/mereology-and-collective-set-theory.html">Mereology and Collective Set Theory</a>
<!-- the whole as primitive and the parts as the divisions of the whole, against the element-first construction of Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory; the division relation and its postulates, a pre-order that is not antisymmetric, with the divisibility of $\mathbb{Z}$ as the standard model and the passage to $\mathbb{N}$ as the antisymmetrisation; the observation that the postulates constrain the relation and not the quotient, so a unit-quotient rule is a physical hypothesis rather than a theorem; the quotient by mutual division; parthood and the two definitions of a proper part, which agree exactly when the relation is antisymmetric; mutual parts; overlap and disjointness; the strong and the weak supplementation principle, the non-part and the disjoint forms of the first, and the two-element order that separates them, together with the recovery of the classical implication under the second definition of a proper part when antisymmetry fails; extensionality as a postulate independent of antisymmetry under the first definition and equivalent to it under the second; the correspondence of classical mereology with a Boolean algebra without a least element, forward-referenced to Part VI. -->

<a href="articles_maths/cardinality-and-the-axiom-of-choice.html">Cardinality and the Axiom of Choice</a>
<!-- finite and infinite sets; equipotence and cardinality; countable and uncountable sets, the countability of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ and of $\mathbb{Z}$, the uncountability of the power set of $\mathbb{N}$; Cantor's theorem and the cardinality of the power set; the continuum hypothesis; the axiom of choice, Zorn's lemma and the well-ordering theorem, and their equivalence; the uses of Zorn's lemma in this corpus: maximal ideals, bases of a vector space, algebraic closure, maximal filters; cardinal arithmetic. -->

<a href="articles_maths/set-theoretic-foundations.html">Set-Theoretic Foundations</a>
<!-- the Zermelo–Fraenkel axioms and the axiom of choice; ordinals and cardinals; transfinite induction and recursion; the cumulative hierarchy; the independence of the continuum hypothesis; large cardinals in outline. -->

<a href="articles_maths/formal-logic-and-computability.html">Formal Logic and Computability</a>
<!-- first-order logic, formal systems and derivations; soundness and completeness; compactness and the Löwenheim–Skolem theorem; Turing machines and recursive functions; decidability and undecidability; Gödel's incompleteness theorems; the halting problem. -->

<a href="articles_maths/model-theory.html">Model Theory</a>
<!-- structures and languages; satisfaction and elementary equivalence; compactness; quantifier elimination; ultraproducts; the model theory of algebraically closed, real-closed and valued fields. -->

<a href="articles_maths/proof-theory-and-type-theory.html">Proof Theory and Type Theory</a>
<!-- natural deduction and the sequent calculus; cut elimination; normalisation; intuitionistic logic; the Curry–Howard correspondence; the lambda calculus; the categorical reading of proofs. -->

<a href="articles_maths/universal-properties-and-categories.html">Universal Properties and Categories</a>
<!-- objects and morphisms; the categories of sets, of groups, of rings and of modules over a fixed ring; functors, natural transformations and equivalence of categories; initial and terminal objects; universal properties and universal objects, with existence and uniqueness formulated as a single statement; products, coproducts, free objects, quotients and localisations as universal constructions; the universal properties this corpus relies on: the free group, the tensor product, the symmetric and exterior algebras, the fraction field, the completion; adjunction in outline. -->

### Operator Theory

<a href="articles_maths/operators-on-a-lattice.html">Operators on a Lattice</a>
<!-- the lattice endomorphisms and the maps preserving the meet and the join; the congruences read as kernels and the quotient as an operator; the lattice of congruences and the operator view of a lattice. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-converse-relation-as-an-operator.html">The Converse Relation as an Operator</a>
<!-- the passage $R\mapsto R^{-1}$ as an operator on relations; its behaviour under composition, inclusion and iteration; the pairs of mutually converse relations and the symmetrisation. -->

<a href="articles_maths/endomorphisms-of-a-relational-structure.html">Endomorphisms of a Relational Structure</a>
<!-- the maps preserving a relation; the endomorphism monoid and its group of units, the automorphism group of the structure; the embeddings and the strong endomorphisms. -->

<a href="articles_maths/closure-operators-and-the-consequence-operator.html">Closure Operators and the Consequence Operator</a>
<!-- closure as extensive, idempotent and monotone; the Galois connection to the family of closed sets; the consequence operator of a logic, its finitary part and the compactness of the closure. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-order-automorphism-group.html">The Order Automorphism Group</a>
<!-- $\operatorname{Aut}(P)$ of a poset and its action on the elements and on the ideals; the fixed-point structure; the group as a subgroup of $\operatorname{Sym}(P)$, with the linear and the affine orders as the extreme cases. -->

<a href="articles_maths/operators-on-a-poset.html">Operators on a Poset</a>
<!-- monotone, antitone and residuated maps; the monoid of monotone maps with the constant maps and the identity; the Galois connections as pairs of residuated maps. -->

### * Theory

<a href="articles_maths/orthocomplemented-lattices-and-the-involution.html">Orthocomplemented Lattices and the Involution</a>
<!-- the complement as an order-reversing involution; the De Morgan laws; the failure of the complement in a general lattice and the passage to a semiorthocomplement. -->

<a href="articles_maths/orthomodular-lattices.html">Orthomodular Lattices</a>
<!-- orthomodularity as the weak modular law; the failure of distributivity; the projection lattice of a Hilbert space, forward-referenced to Part II. -->

<a href="articles_maths/relation-algebras-and-the-converse.html">Relation Algebras and the Converse</a>
<!-- the relation algebra axioms; the converse as the involution and composition as the product; the residuals and the Peircean law. -->

<a href="articles_maths/involutive-categories-and-the-dagger-functor.html">Involutive Categories and the Dagger Functor</a>
<!-- the dagger as a contravariant involution on the morphisms; dagger categories, dagger functors and unitary morphisms; the self-adjoint morphisms and the dagger-theoretic analogues of the algebraic notions. -->

<a href="articles_maths/boolean-algebras-with-an-involution.html">Boolean Algebras with an Involution</a>
<!-- the complement as the involution; involutive Boolean algebras and their homomorphisms; the representation and the fixed part. -->

<a href="articles_maths/groupoids-with-an-involution.html">Groupoids with an Involution</a>
<!-- inversion on a groupoid as the canonical instance; the involutive structure, its orbits and its fixed elements; the non-abelian case and what the involution does not fix. -->

<a href="articles_maths/involutive-set-theory-and-the-symmetric-difference.html">Involutive Set Theory and the Symmetric Difference</a>
<!-- symmetric difference as the product and the complement as the involution; the Boolean ring of sets and its self-adjoint part; the identification with the Boolean algebras of this category. -->

### * Operator Theory

<a href="articles_maths/the-converse-as-an-adjoint.html">The Converse as an Adjoint</a>
<!-- the converse $R^{-1}$ as the adjoint of $R$ under the pairing of relations; the Galois reading and the associated unit and counit. -->

<a href="articles_maths/involutions-of-the-operator-layer.html">Involutions of the Operator Layer</a>
<!-- the involution acting on the operators themselves; the adjoint operation, its fixed elements and its behaviour with respect to composition and order. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-converse-relation-as-an-adjoint.html">The Converse Relation as an Adjoint</a>

## Groups

### Theory

<a href="articles_maths/groups.html">Groups</a>
<!-- definition (associativity, unit, inverses), elementary properties, order and powers, cyclic subgroups, subgroups, homomorphisms, cosets and Lagrange's theorem, normal subgroups and quotient groups, the isomorphism theorems, the centre, the commutator subgroup and abelianization, group actions, orbits and the orbit–stabiliser theorem, conjugacy and the class equation, $p$-groups, the Sylow theorems, symmetric, alternating and dihedral groups. -->

<a href="articles_maths/infinite-abelian-groups.html">Infinite Abelian Groups</a>
<!-- abelian groups as modules over $\mathbb{Z}$; free abelian groups and rank; torsion and torsion-free groups; divisible groups and their classification; the structure of infinite abelian groups, the finitely generated case being treated separately. -->

<a href="articles_maths/transformation-groups.html">Transformation Groups</a>
<!-- a transformation of a set; composition and invertibility; the symmetric group $\operatorname{Sym}(X)$ and $\operatorname{Aut}(X)$ for a structure $X$; a group acting on a set as a homomorphism $G\to\operatorname{Sym}(X)$; faithful and effective actions; Cayley's theorem; the permutation representation; the automorphism group of a structure and its monotonicity in the structure. -->

<a href="articles_maths/group-actions-and-structure.html">Group Actions and Structure</a>
<!-- group actions, orbits, stabilisers, the orbit–stabiliser theorem, Burnside's lemma, the centre, the commutator subgroup and abelianization, composition series, the Sylow theorems. -->

<a href="articles_maths/solvable-and-nilpotent-groups.html">Solvable and Nilpotent Groups</a>
<!-- solvable groups, the derived series and the commutator subgroup; nilpotent groups and the lower central series; Hall subgroups; the Fitting and Frattini subgroups; examples from matrix groups. -->

<a href="articles_maths/generators-presentations-and-free-products.html">Generators, Presentations and Free Products</a>
<!-- generating sets, presentations, free groups, free products, direct and semidirect products. -->

<a href="articles_maths/combinatorial-group-theory.html">Combinatorial Group Theory</a>
<!-- free groups, presentations and the word problem; the Nielsen–Schreier theorem; the Kurosh subgroup theorem; HNN extensions and amalgamated products; the accessibility of finitely presented groups. -->

<a href="articles_maths/infinite-groups.html">Infinite Groups</a>
<!-- infinite groups and their properties; finitely generated infinite groups, torsion groups and the Burnside problem; the Tits alternative; the algebraic theory only, the geometric theory of Cayley graphs and growth belonging to Part II. -->

<a href="articles_maths/coxeter-groups.html">Coxeter Groups</a>
<!-- Coxeter systems and diagrams; the presentation of a Coxeter group; finite and affine Coxeter groups and the classification of the finite ones; the word problem; reflection groups and Weyl groups require a form and belong to Part II. -->

<a href="articles_maths/braid-groups.html">Braid Groups</a>
<!-- the braid group on $n$ strands and its presentation; the pure braid group; the relation to the symmetric group; the algebraic properties of the braid groups. -->

<a href="articles_maths/group-cohomology.html">Group Cohomology</a>
<!-- the cohomology of a group, the standard resolution and the low-dimensional interpretations; $H^1$ and $H^2$ as derivations and as extensions; the Schur multiplier; the cohomology of finite groups. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-classification-of-finite-simple-groups.html">The Classification of Finite Simple Groups</a>
<!-- the statement of the classification; the alternating groups; the groups of Lie type; the sporadic groups; the Feit–Thompson theorem; the classification of groups of small order. -->

<a href="articles_maths/finite-simple-groups-of-lie-type.html">Finite Simple Groups of Lie Type</a>
<!-- the Chevalley, Steinberg, Suzuki–Ree and twisted groups as abstract finite groups; the classification of the finite simple groups of Lie type; the orders of the groups; the algebraic-group structure, the Zariski topology and the building-theoretic constructions belong to Part II. -->

### Operator Theory

<a href="articles_maths/inner-conjugation-and-the-class-operator.html">Inner Conjugation and the Class Operator</a>
<!-- inner conjugation $x\mapsto gxg^{-1}$ as an operator on a group; the orbits, which are the conjugacy classes, the class operator and the class equation; the action on the subgroups and on the normal subgroups. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-action-of-a-group-on-itself.html">The Action of a Group on Itself</a>
<!-- the regular action of a group on itself by left translation; the two-sided action by left and right translation and the associated permutation representation; the kernel and its triviality, Cayley's theorem. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-conjugation-representation.html">The Conjugation Representation</a>
<!-- conjugation as a homomorphism $G\to\operatorname{Aut}(G)$; the inner automorphisms and the outer automorphisms as the quotient; the action of the group on its own conjugacy classes. -->

<a href="articles_maths/left-and-right-multiplication-in-a-group.html">Left and Right Multiplication in a Group</a>
<!-- the one-sided actions $x\mapsto ax$ and $x\mapsto xa$; their commutation and the generation of the two-sided action; the regular representation they define. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-cayley-action.html">The Cayley Action</a>
<!-- the action of a group on itself by left translation read as a faithful permutation action; the embedding $G\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Sym}(G)$ and the regular representation as its linearisation. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-signed-sandwich-on-a-group.html">The Signed Sandwich on a Group</a>
<!-- the two-sided sandwich $x\mapsto axb$ twisted by the grade involution, $x\mapsto a\,\alpha(x)\,b$, on a group; the reflections it realises and its relation to the unsigned sandwich. -->

<a href="articles_maths/reflections-as-signed-two-sided-operators-on-a-group.html">Reflections as Signed Two-Sided Operators on a Group</a>
<!-- the reflections of a group read as signed two-sided operators; the correspondence between reflections and the elements acting by an involution, and its failure in the degenerate cases. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-signed-left-multiplication-on-a-group.html">The Signed Left Multiplication on a Group</a>
<!-- the signed one-sided action $x\mapsto a\,\alpha(x)$ on a group; its relation to the unsigned left multiplication and the elements it fixes. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-graded-action-on-a-module-over-a-group.html">The Graded Action on a Module over a Group</a>
<!-- the action of a graded module over a group; the compatibility of the action with the grading and the sign rule it imposes. -->

### * Theory

<a href="articles_maths/involutive-groups.html">Involutive Groups</a>
<!-- an involutive group, that is a group with an involution, an anti-automorphism of order two; the notion presupposes no commutativity, and unlike a ring a group always carries one, the inversion, which is the canonical isomorphism with the opposite group, so the informative object is the set of involutions, in bijection with the involutive automorphisms through $\sigma \mapsto \sigma\iota$ and with the split extensions by $C_2$, while an anti-automorphism is an automorphism exactly when the group is abelian. The general structure: the fixed set $A^\sigma$, a subgroup exactly when its elements commute pairwise, and the inverted set $I(\sigma) = G^{\sigma\iota}$, which always is one; the conjugate products $g\sigma(g)$ and $\sigma(g)g$, which are only conjugate and need not be fixed; real, strongly real and ambivalent elements, with $S_n$ and $D_n$ ambivalent and strongly real, $Q_8$ ambivalent with only $\pm 1$ as products of two elements of order two, and $A_4$ not ambivalent; $\sigma$-stable subgroups and the induced involution on a quotient, with the image of the fixed set possibly strict; products, the swap with fixed set the diagonal, and the graph of an anti-isomorphism as the fixed set of a twisted involution; the semidirect product by an involutive automorphism, the split and non-split extensions, with the dihedral and dicyclic examples and the groups of order $2p$; and the involutions read off a presentation, the inversion and the word reversal in a free group, the Coxeter inversion together with the diagram automorphisms, and the inversion and reversal automorphisms of the braid groups, which are torsion-free and have no elements of order two. **An additional structure on the group, not a rung of any chain; it stands in the Theory list immediately after *Group Cohomology*, the last article it draws on, and before *The Classification of Finite Simple Groups*, so that every article it uses precedes it and the classification still closes the category.** The geometry of the spaces built from a fixed subgroup is Part IV, and the representation-theoretic treatment of the real elements is later still. -->

<a href="articles_maths/involutions-and-the-fixed-point-subgroup.html">Involutions and the Fixed-Point Subgroup</a>
<!-- the fixed-point set of an involution of a group and when it is a subgroup; the inversion as the canonical involution, whose fixed set is central and generally not a subgroup. -->

<a href="articles_maths/involutive-group-actions.html">Involutive Group Actions</a>
<!-- a group acting on an involutive structure and preserving the involution; the induced involution on the fixed points and on the quotients. -->

<a href="articles_maths/free-involutions-and-the-quotient.html">Free Involutions and the Quotient</a>
<!-- a fixed-point-free involution of a group; the quotient and the double cover it defines, with the antipodal and the dihedral examples. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-commuting-algebra-of-an-involution.html">The Commuting Algebra of an Involution</a>
<!-- the elements commuting with an involutive automorphism; the centraliser, its relation to the fixed subgroup and its place in the semidirect product. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-centre-of-an-involutive-group.html">The Centre of an Involutive Group</a>
<!-- the centre of a group with an involution and the involution it inherits; the compatibility of the involution with centrality and with the commutator subgroup. -->

<a href="articles_maths/involutions-and-the-word-problem.html">Involutions and the Word Problem</a>
<!-- the word problem for a group presented with an involution; the effect of the involution on the presentation and the decidability of the word problem. -->

<!-- the adjoint of a reflection read as a signed operator on a group; the self-adjointness of the reflections and its failure in the degenerate case. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-signed-adjoint-of-the-left-multiplication-on-a-group.html">The Signed Adjoint of the Left Multiplication on a Group</a>
<!-- the adjoint of the signed left multiplication on a group; its explicit expression and its relation to the signed sandwich. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-graded-adjoint-action-on-a-module-over-a-group.html">The Graded Adjoint Action on a Module over a Group</a>

## Rings and Fields

### Theory

<a href="articles_maths/rings.html">Rings</a>
<!-- definition of an associative ring with $1 \neq 0$, elementary properties, subrings, ring homomorphisms and quotients of rings; ideals, left, right and two-sided, generated ideals, the correspondence theorem, quotient rings; units, zero divisors, nilpotents and idempotents as vocabulary; prime and maximal ideals with their quotient characterisations. **This is the Ring rung of the chain that follows.** The former multi-rung article has been apportioned: the commutative law to *Commutative Rings*, nilpotent structure to *Reduced Rings and the Nilradical*, the domain to *Integral Domains*, fields to *Fields*, division rings to *Division Rings*, the factorisation rungs to *Unique Factorisation Domains*, *Principal Ideal Domains* and *Euclidean Domains*, and modules and algebras to *Modules* and *Algebras*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/commutative-rings.html">Commutative Rings</a>
<!-- the commutative law and what it adds: the binomial and multinomial theorems, the commutativity of the product of ideals, sums, products and intersections of ideals and the radical of an ideal; coprime ideals and the Chinese remainder theorem; the commutative theory of prime and maximal ideals — a quotient by a prime ideal is a domain and a quotient by a maximal ideal is a field; $\operatorname{Spec} R$ as a poset; the failure of each statement without commutativity. Ideals and quotient rings themselves are owned by *Rings*, §§6–7. -->

<a href="articles_maths/reduced-rings-and-the-nilradical.html">Reduced Rings and the Nilradical</a>
<!-- nilpotents as a class; a ring is reduced when it has no nonzero nilpotent, equivalently when its nilradical vanishes; the nilradical as the intersection of the prime ideals and as the radical of the zero ideal; reduced rings as subrings of products of domains; $\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$ as the counterexamples that fix the rung. -->

<a href="articles_maths/integral-domains.html">Integral Domains</a>
<!-- a commutative ring with $1 \neq 0$ and no zero divisors; cancellation; associates and divisibility; irreducibles and primes; the characteristic and the embedding of the prime field; the root theorem, that a polynomial over a domain of degree $< m$ with $m$ roots is zero; $\mathbb{Z}$ and $K[x]$ as the standard examples; the fraction field once localization is available; the domain that is not a unique factorisation domain is deferred to the rung below. -->

<a href="articles_maths/gcd-domains.html">GCD Domains</a>
<!-- the greatest common divisor and the least common multiple in a domain; the gcd of two elements always existing; a GCD domain as the most general rung at which divisibility is governed by a gcd; the ideal-theoretic characterisation; UFD and Bézout domains as the two incomparable strengthenings, forward-referenced. -->

<a href="articles_maths/bezout-domains.html">Bézout Domains</a>
<!-- Bézout's identity promoted to a definition: every finitely generated ideal is principal; the relation to the gcd; a Bézout domain is a GCD domain, and the converse fails; the principal ideal domains as the Noetherian Bézout domains, forward-referenced; the ring of all algebraic integers as the standard non-Noetherian example. -->

<a href="articles_maths/unique-factorisation-domains.html">Unique Factorisation Domains</a>
<!-- irreducibles and primes; existence and uniqueness of factorisation into irreducibles; a domain is a unique factorisation domain exactly when every irreducible is prime; Euclid's lemma; the failure of unique factorisation in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$; content and Gauss's lemma; Eisenstein's criterion; the transfer of unique factorisation to the polynomial ring and the factorisation of polynomials over a field; $c(f)$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/principal-ideal-domains.html">Principal Ideal Domains</a>
<!-- every ideal principal; a principal ideal domain is a unique factorisation domain; the ideal structure of the quotient by a prime ideal; the maximal ideals; $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ as the unique factorisation domain that is not principal. -->

<a href="articles_maths/euclidean-domains.html">Euclidean Domains</a>
<!-- the Euclidean degree function $N$, division with remainder, the Euclidean algorithm and the extended form giving Bézout coefficients; a Euclidean domain is a principal ideal domain and hence a unique factorisation domain, giving the chain Euclidean $\Rightarrow$ principal $\Rightarrow$ unique factorisation; norm-Euclidean domains; $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ and the Gaussian primes as the standard worked example; $\mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{-19})/2]$ as the principal ideal domain that is not Euclidean. -->

<a href="articles_maths/localization-and-the-fraction-field.html">Localization and the Fraction Field</a>
<!-- multiplicative sets, localization, $\operatorname{Frac}(R)$, local rings, the universal property. -->

<a href="articles_maths/noetherian-and-artinian-rings.html">Noetherian and Artinian Rings</a>
<!-- the ascending and descending chain conditions; the Hilbert basis theorem; the Akizuki–Hopkins theorem; the relation to the finitely generated modules of Part I. -->

<a href="articles_maths/primary-decomposition.html">Primary Decomposition</a>
<!-- primary ideals and primary decomposition; the uniqueness of the associated primes; the relation to the Nullstellensatz and to the ideals of this part. -->

<a href="articles_maths/integral-extensions-and-krull-dimension.html">Integral Extensions and Krull Dimension</a>
<!-- integral extensions; the lying-over, going-up and going-down theorems; the Krull dimension; the dimension of a polynomial ring. -->

<a href="articles_maths/dedekind-domains-and-ideal-class-groups.html">Dedekind Domains and Ideal Class Groups</a>
<!-- Dedekind domains and the unique factorisation of ideals; fractional ideals; the ideal class group and the finiteness of the class number. -->

<a href="articles_maths/valuation-theory-and-henselian-rings.html">Valuation Theory and Henselian Rings</a>

<!-- the non-commutative analogue of a reduced ring: a ring with no nonzero nilpotent ideal; the lower nilradical as the intersection of the prime ideals; a semiprime ring as a subdirect product of prime rings; the commutative case is *Reduced Rings and the Nilradical*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/prime-rings.html">Prime Rings</a>
<!-- a ring in which a product of two nonzero ideals is nonzero; prime ideals in the non-commutative sense and the failure of the commutative correspondence with quotients; every prime ring is semiprime and the converse fails; every domain is prime and the converse fails. -->

<a href="articles_maths/non-commutative-domains.html">Non-Commutative Domains</a>
<!-- a ring with $1 \neq 0$ and no zero divisors, without the commutative hypothesis; cancellation on both sides; the asymmetry of the left and the right ideals; $\mathbb{H}$, the free algebra, the Weyl algebra and the group ring of a torsion-free group; the intersection with the commutative rung is exactly the integral domains. -->

<a href="articles_maths/ore-domains-and-division-rings-of-fractions.html">Ore Domains and Division Rings of Fractions</a>
<!-- the Ore condition and the Ore domain; the division ring of fractions of an Ore domain, the non-commutative analogue of the fraction field; Malcev–Neumann series over an ordered group; the division ring of fractions of the Weyl algebra; the free algebra as the standard non-Ore domain; no completion and no adic topology are used. -->

<a href="articles_maths/division-rings.html">Division Rings</a>
<!-- a ring with $1 \neq 0$ in which every nonzero element is a unit, without the commutative hypothesis; a skew field; the centre is a field and the division ring is an algebra over it, possibly of infinite dimension there; a commutative division ring is a field; Wedderburn's little theorem, that every finite division ring is a field; $\mathbb{H}$ and the division ring of fractions of the Weyl algebra as the two kinds of example. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-column-ideals-of-a-matrix-ring.html">The Column Ideals of a Matrix Ring: One Idempotent and $n-1$ Nilpotents</a>
<!-- the column ideal $L_j=AE_{jj}$ of the matrix ring $M_n(D)$ over a division ring $D$, the matrices supported in one column, a minimal left ideal of dimension $n$; the Peirce decomposition of the algebra by the matrix units into the corners $E_{ii}AE_{kk}=DE_{ik}$, one-dimensional over $D$; the cut of the column into one diagonal corner $E_{jj}AE_{jj}=DE_{jj}$, a division ring isomorphic to $D$ whose identity $E_{jj}$ is an idempotent, and $n-1$ off-diagonal corners $E_{ii}AE_{jj}=DE_{ij}$, each square-zero, so that an off-diagonal corner has no nonzero idempotent and its nonzero elements are nilpotents; the theorem that a corner-adapted basis, one element per corner, has exactly one idempotent, $E_{jj}$, and $n-1$ nilpotents, the off-diagonal matrix units, the off-diagonal nilpotency being insensitive to the normalisation of the corner element while the diagonal idempotency requires that element to be the identity of its corner; the count $1+(n-1)=n=\dim_D L_j$ as the arithmetic of the corners, $n-1$ being the number of off-diagonal corners of a column; the nilpotents of the column as exactly the off-diagonal part $N_j$, each square-zero, $N_j$ being the kernel of the surjective ring homomorphism $\pi(x)=x_{jj}$ to $D$, so that $L_j/N_j\cong D$, that $N_j^2=0$ and that the column is a ring with right identity $E_{jj}$ but no two-sided identity for $n\geq2$; the idempotents of the column as the affine family $E_{jj}+N_j$ of dimension $n-1$, so that the count is a count of basis elements and not of idempotents, and a basis of the column can consist entirely of idempotents; the counts per column and per algebra, the $n$ diagonal corners giving the complete orthogonal family $E_{11},\dots,E_{nn}$ and the $n(n-1)$ off-diagonal corners the nilpotents $E_{ik}$; the boundary, that over a ring with a proper nonzero ideal the column is not minimal, with $M_n(I)E_{jj}$ the counterexample, so that the coefficient ring must be a division ring; the scalar-side trap for $D$ noncommutative, where $dE_{ik}\neq E_{ik}d$ and the corners are read as left multiples; and the biquaternion instance $n=2$, $D=\mathbb{C}$, where the first column is the spinor space $\mathbb{B}\tilde\Pi_1=\mathbb{C}\{\tilde\Pi_1,\hat\Upsilon_2\}$ with one idempotent and one nilpotent and with $\tilde\Pi_1+c\hat\Upsilon_2$ the affine family. The matrix units and the left ideals are *Matrix Algebras*; the Peirce decomposition is *Unital Algebras*, §*Idempotents and the Peirce Decomposition*; the rank and the length are *Direct Sums, Free Modules and Rank*; and the biquaternion instance is *Ideals and Peirce Decomposition of the General Plain Algebra*, with the physical reading in *The Spinor Space as a Module and as a Hilbert Space*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/von-neumann-regular-rings.html">Von Neumann Regular Rings</a>
<!-- a ring in which every principal left ideal is generated by an idempotent, equivalently every finitely generated left ideal is idempotent-generated; the commutative von Neumann regular rings as exactly the reduced rings of Krull dimension zero, equivalently those whose localization at every maximal ideal is a field; reduced von Neumann regular rings as the strongly regular rings; Boolean rings as the examples of characteristic two, and $\mathbb{Z}$, $k[x]$, $\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ and the local rings as the non-examples; the failure of the class to be closed under quotients, and the place of the class among the rings of *Reduced Rings and the Nilradical*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/real-algebraic-geometry.html">Real Algebraic Geometry</a>
<!-- real algebraic sets and semialgebraic sets; the Tarski–Seidenberg theorem; the relation to the real-closed fields of this part. -->

### * Theory

<a href="articles_maths/involutive-rings.html">Involutive Rings</a>
<!-- an involutive ring, that is a ring with an involution, an anti-automorphism of order two; the notion presupposes no commutativity, and it is the same datum as an order-two isomorphism $A \to A^{\mathrm{op}}$, so every ring with an involution is isomorphic to its opposite ring, while in the commutative case the opposite ring is the ring itself and the notion degenerates to an automorphism of order dividing two. The general structure: the fixed set $A^\sigma$ and the symmetric and skew elements, with $A = \mathrm{Sym} \oplus \mathrm{Skew}$ as abelian groups when $2$ is invertible, and the failure without commutativity of the multiplicative grading and of the closedness of $A^\sigma$ under multiplication; $\sigma$-ideals, the induced involution on a quotient and on a product, and $\sigma$-prime ideals and $\sigma$-prime rings, with the sufficient elementwise condition $aAb^{*} \neq 0$, with prime implying $\sigma$-prime and with the converse failing. The commutative case: $\sigma$ an automorphism of order two, $R = R^\sigma \oplus R^-$ with the characteristic-two failure, the conjugate product $x\sigma(x)$ and the conjugate sum $x+\sigma(x)$, the monic quadratic and the integrality of $R$ over $R^\sigma$, the affine involutions of $R[x]$ and their fixed subrings, localization and $\operatorname{Frac}(R)^\sigma = \operatorname{Frac}(R^\sigma)$, fields with involution as quadratic Galois extensions, quadratic in one characteristic and Artin–Schreier in the other, the exclusion of nontrivial order-preserving involutions of an ordered field, a table of examples, and the fixed ring $k[x^2,xy,y^2]$ of $k[x,y]$ as a ring that is not a unique factorisation domain. **An additional structure on the ring, not a rung of either chain; it stands at the seam between the commutative half and the non-commutative chain, after *Algebraically Closed Fields* and before *Semiprime Rings*.** The classification of the involutions of a central simple algebra is *Involutions of a Central Simple Algebra*, in *Algebras*; the forms attached to an involution, and everything a form or a pairing defines, are *Hilbert Algebras*, in Part II. -->

<a href="articles_maths/matrix-rings-with-an-involution.html">Matrix Rings with an Involution</a>
<!-- the transpose, the conjugate transpose and the symplectic involution on a matrix ring; the classification of the involutions of $M_n(R)$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/rings-with-a-semilinear-involution.html">Rings with a Semilinear Involution</a>
<!-- a semilinear involution with respect to a ring automorphism; the $\sigma$-semilinear case and the failure of the naive identities. -->

<a href="articles_maths/involutions-of-a-group-ring.html">Involutions of a Group Ring</a>
<!-- the involutions of a group ring induced by the inversion and by an involution of the group; the twisted group ring and the compatibility with the coefficients. -->

<a href="articles_maths/involutive-local-rings.html">Involutive Local Rings</a>
<!-- local rings with an involution; the involution on the maximal ideal and on the residue field, and the lifting of the residue involution. -->

<a href="articles_maths/involutions-of-a-polynomial-ring-and-the-symmetric-part.html">Involutions of a Polynomial Ring and the Symmetric Part</a>
<!-- the involutions of $R[x]$, chiefly $x\mapsto -x$; the symmetric part and the graded decomposition it induces. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-skew-field-of-a-ring-with-involution.html">The Skew Field of a Ring with Involution</a>
<!-- the skew elements $\{x : x^* = -x\}$ against the symmetric elements; their interaction with the product and with the trace. -->

## Algebras

### Theory

<a href="articles_maths/algebras-a-general-introduction.html">Algebras</a>
<!-- modules over a commutative ring; what an algebra is (an $R$-module with a bilinear product); the relation to modules; associativity, unit and commutativity; ideals and quotients; constructions, including the tensor and free algebras. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-symmetric-and-antisymmetric-parts-of-an-algebra-product.html">The Symmetric and Antisymmetric Parts of an Algebra Product</a>
<!-- the splitting of a bilinear product into its commutative and its anticommutative half, $xy=x\bullet y+x\wedge y$ with $x\bullet y=\tfrac12(xy+yx)$ and $x\wedge y=\tfrac12(xy-yx)$, unique over a field of characteristic not $2$; the split as the exchange $x\otimes y\mapsto y\otimes x$ on the tensor square and as the direct sum of the symmetric products and the antisymmetric products, with the structure constants splitting as $\binom{n+1}{2}n$ and $\binom{n}{2}n$; the symmetrisation as the polarisation of the square, $(x+y)^2-x^2-y^2=2(x\bullet y)$; the Lie-admissible algebras, whose antisymmetrisation satisfies the Jacobi identity, with the associator criterion that decides it; the Jordan-admissible algebras, whose symmetrisation satisfies the Jordan identity; the independence of the two conditions, with a Lie-admissible algebra that is not Jordan-admissible and a Jordan-admissible algebra that is not Lie-admissible; the opposite algebra, and the relatives $x\bullet y+\lambda(x\wedge y)$ with the same symmetric half; the collapse of the split in characteristic $2$; and the uses in the operator layer, in the ternary product, in the biquaternion products and in deformation quantisation. -->

<a href="articles_maths/associative-algebras.html">Associative Algebras</a>
<!-- the associative algebras; associativity as a polynomial identity; the associator, and the power-associativity that outlives it; the free associative algebra and the tensor algebra; the universal enveloping algebra of a Lie algebra as the associative algebra attached to a non-associative one; the algebras that fail associativity. -->

<a href="articles_maths/unital-algebras.html">Unital Algebras</a>
<!-- the algebras with an identity, and the rings with identity read as algebras; the unit group and the invertible elements; the unitisation of a non-unital algebra by adjoining a unit; the homomorphisms that preserve the identity and those that do not; the idempotents, the Peirce decomposition $A=eAe\oplus eAf\oplus fAe\oplus fAf$ and the central idempotents that split the algebra as a product; the non-unital algebras of the corpus. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-algebra-generated-by-an-element-and-the-chinese-remainder-decomposition.html">The Algebra Generated by an Element and the Chinese Remainder Decomposition</a>
<!-- the evaluation map $f\mapsto f(a)$ and the subalgebra $k[a]$; the minimal polynomial $m_a$ and the isomorphism $k[a]\cong k[x]/(m_a)$; the dimension $\deg m_a$ and the power basis $1,a,\dots,a^{d-1}$; the Chinese remainder decomposition for $m_a=m_1\cdots m_r$ with the factors pairwise coprime, the canonical idempotents $\varepsilon_i=g_i(a)$, and the components $a_i=a\varepsilon_i$ with minimal polynomial $m_i$; the primary decomposition $m_a=\prod_i f_i^{e_i}$ and the two extreme cases of an irreducible polynomial and a power of a linear one; the distinction between the decomposition of $k[a]$ and the Peirce decomposition of $A$ when the idempotents are not central; the companion matrix of $x^3-x$ with its three rational idempotents, the split-complex and dual numbers, and the complex numbers as a real algebra; the commutative-ring caveat on the minimal polynomial and on the units $\lambda_i-\lambda_j$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/separable-elements-and-split-minimal-polynomials.html">Separable Elements and Split Minimal Polynomials</a>
<!-- the separable polynomials and the criterion $\gcd(f,f')=1$; the discriminant, the resultant and the Vandermonde determinant; characteristic $p$, the polynomial $x^p-t$ and perfect fields; separable elements, split elements and the split squarefree form $m_a=\prod_i(x-\lambda_i)$; the trace form $\tau(x,y)=\operatorname{Tr}(L_{xy})$ on $k[a]$, the theorem that its nondegeneracy is the separability of $a$, and the identity $\det T=\Delta(m_a)$ in the power basis; the distinction between separable elements and separable algebras, with $M_p(k)$ over an imperfect field as the warning; the independence table for the split and the separable conditions; and the roles of the two conditions in the eigenvalue and Jordan–Chevalley decompositions. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-eigenvalue-decomposition-of-an-element.html">The Eigenvalue Decomposition of an Element</a>
<!-- the eigenvalues as the roots of $m_a$, the criterion that $a-\lambda$ is not invertible, and the left and right eigenvalue equations; the multiplicity in $m_a$ against the algebraic multiplicity; the decomposition $a=\sum_i\lambda_i e_i$ with distinct $\lambda_i$, orthogonal idempotents $e_i$ and $\sum_i e_i=1$; the equivalence with $m_a$ split with distinct roots, with $L_a$ diagonalisable and with $R_a$ diagonalisable; uniqueness and the Lagrange idempotents; the eigenspaces $\ker(L_a-\lambda_i)=e_iA$ and $\ker(R_a-\lambda_i)=Ae_i$, the simultaneous eigenspaces $e_iAe_j$ and the two-sided Peirce decomposition; the matrix case and the distinction between the matrix eigenspace $e_iV$ and the algebra eigenspace $e_iA$; the generalized eigenvalue decomposition $a=\sum_i(\lambda_i\varepsilon_i+n_i)$ for a split polynomial with repeated roots; and the Jordan block and biquaternion examples. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-lagrange-sylvester-eigenprojector-formula.html">The Lagrange–Sylvester Eigenprojector Formula</a>
<!-- Lagrange interpolation at distinct eigenvalues and the eigenprojector formula $e_i=\prod_{j\ne i}(a-\lambda_j 1_A)/(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)$; the minimal-polynomial form $e_i=m_i(a)/m_i(\lambda_i)=m_i(a)/m_a'(\lambda_i)$; Sylvester's formula $f(a)=\sum_i f(\lambda_i)e_i$ for polynomials and holomorphic functions; the resolvent identity $(z-a)^{-1}=\sum_i e_i/(z-\lambda_i)$ and the contour formula $e_i=(2\pi i)^{-1}\oint(z-a)^{-1}\,dz$; Hermite interpolation in the repeated-root case, the generalized eigenprojectors $\varepsilon_i=q_i(a)u_i(a)$ with $q_i=m_a/(x-\lambda_i)^{e_i}$ and $u_i q_i\equiv1$ modulo $(x-\lambda_i)^{e_i}$, the generalized Sylvester formula, and the higher-order poles of the resolvent; and the two-by-two, companion, Jordan-block and block-with-two-eigenvalues examples. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-centraliser-and-the-diagonal-peirce-part.html">The Centraliser and the Diagonal Peirce Part</a>
<!-- the centraliser $C(a)=\{x:ax=xa\}=\ker\operatorname{ad}_a=C(k[a])$; the theorem $C(a)=\bigoplus_i e_iAe_i$ for a split separable element, with the proof from the two-sided Peirce decomposition and the distinct eigenvalues; the dimension $\sum_i\dim e_iAe_i$, and $\sum_i m_i^2\ge n$ in $M_n$; the double centraliser $C(C(a))=k[a]$ in a full matrix algebra and its failure in a general algebra; the diagonal part $D=\bigoplus_i e_iAe_i$ and the off-diagonal part $N=\bigoplus_{i\ne j}e_iAe_j$; the diagonal projection $\pi$, its multiplicativity criterion, and the contrast between $N=0$ and the vanishing of the diagonal part of $N^2$; the identity $C(a)=\bigcap_i C(e_i)$; and the scalar, distinct-eigenvalue, multiplicity, upper-triangular and central examples. -->

<a href="articles_maths/off-diagonal-peirce-components-and-noncentral-idempotents.html">Off-Diagonal Peirce Components and Noncentral Idempotents</a>
<!-- the Peirce decomposition $A=eAe\oplus eAf\oplus fAe\oplus fAf$ for one idempotent and the multiplication table of the four corners; the diagonal part $D=eAe\oplus fAf$ and the off-diagonal part $N=eAf\oplus fAe$, with $N^2\subseteq D$; the commutator interpretation $N=[e,A]$, the kernel $C(e)=D$, the eigenspaces of $\operatorname{ad}_e$ for $0,\pm1$ and the $\mathbb{Z}$-grading; the equivalence of centrality with $N=0$ and with $A\cong Ae\times Af$; the noncentral case, the ideal $AeA=eAe\oplus eAf\oplus fAe$ and the corner quotient $A/AeA\cong fAf$; the warning that $N$ measures noncentrality, not noncommutativity; the rank-$k$ matrix case with $\dim N=2k(n-k)$, $N^2=D$ and the quotient $M_{n-k}(k)$; and the biquaternion rank-one example. -->

<a href="articles_maths/nilpotent-elements-and-the-jordan-chevalley-decomposition.html">Nilpotent Elements and the Jordan–Chevalley Decomposition</a>
<!-- nilpotent elements, their index, the failure of the sum of nilpotents to be nilpotent and the closure under commuting sums and products; the radical and the nilradical; the semisimple elements as those with squarefree minimal polynomial, against the separable elements; the additive decomposition $a=s+n$ with $sn=ns$, $s$ semisimple and $n$ nilpotent, and its uniqueness; the theorem over a perfect field via the Chinese remainder decomposition and the lifting of the roots, with $s,n\in k[a]$, $m_s$ the squarefree part of $m_a$ and the index of $n$ the largest exponent; the general-field criterion and the failure of $x^p-t$ squared over $\mathbb{F}_p(t)$ and of its companion matrix; the multiplicative decomposition $a=su$ for units, with $u$ unipotent; the generalized eigenvalue decomposition $s=\sum_i\lambda_i\varepsilon_i$ and $n=\sum_i n_i$; the matrix case and the Jordan form; and the Jordan block, the block with two eigenvalues and the unipotent biquaternion examples. -->

<a href="articles_maths/idempotents-and-involutions-of-an-algebra.html">Idempotents and Involutions of an Algebra</a>
<!-- the idempotents $e^2=e$ and the involution $\sigma$ acting on them by $e\mapsto e^*$; the Klein four action generated by $\sigma$ and the complement $e\mapsto1-e$, with orbit contained in $\{e,e^*,1-e,1-e^*\}$; the Hermitian idempotents $e^*=e$ and the $*$-stable Peirce corners with the diagonal corners as $*$-subalgebras; the complementary idempotents $e^*=1-e$, equivalently $e+e^*=1$ and $e^*e=ee^*=0$, in bijection with the skew roots $u=2e-1$ of the identity when $2$ is invertible; the left isotropic idempotents $e^*e=0$, the right isotropic $ee^*=0$ and the two-sided condition $e^*e=ee^*=0$, equivalent to $e+e^*$ being idempotent when $2$ is invertible; the matrix algebras with the transpose, the conjugate transpose, the hyperbolic and the symplectic involutions, and the split algebra with the exchange involution; and the characteristic-two collapse of the halving. -->

<a href="articles_maths/complementary-idempotents-and-the-peirce-decomposition.html">Complementary Idempotents and the Peirce Decomposition</a>
<!-- the complement $1-e$, the fixed-point-free involution of the set of idempotents and the order it reverses, and the relative complement $g-e$ in a corner; the Boolean algebra $B(A)$ of central idempotents; the Peirce decomposition $A=\bigoplus_{i,j}A_{ij}$ of a complete orthogonal family with $A_{ij}=e_iAe_j$, the multiplication table $A_{ij}A_{kl}\subseteq\delta_{jk}A_{il}$, the diagonal part $D$, the off-diagonal bimodule $N$ and the diagonal projection, with its multiplicativity criterion; the generalised matrix algebra of the corners; the refinement obtained by splitting a member and the coarsening obtained by a partition, and the primitive families and local corners; the central families, the product decomposition $A\cong\prod_iA_{ii}$ and the atoms of $B(A)$; and the split-complex, upper triangular, matrix, biquaternion and noncentral $M_3$ examples. -->

### * Theory

<a href="articles_maths/involutive-algebras.html">Involutive Algebras</a>
<!-- an involution of an algebra, that is an anti-automorphism of order two, form-free, together with the involutive automorphism that preserves the product: the definition, the opposite algebra with the coset $\operatorname{Anti}(A)=\sigma\operatorname{Aut}(A)$, the centre, the group of units and the two conjugate elements $a+\sigma(a)$ and $a\sigma(a)$; the decomposition $A=A^+\oplus A^-$ when $2\neq0$ and its collapse in characteristic two, where the symmetric and the skew elements coincide; the skew elements as a Lie algebra under the commutator, so that $A^-\oplus A^+$ is a $\mathbb{Z}/2$-graded Lie algebra, and the symmetric elements as a Jordan algebra under $x\circ y=\tfrac12(xy+yx)$, a subalgebra exactly when its elements commute pairwise, so that the fixed set of an anti-automorphism is a Jordan algebra and may still be an algebra (the diagonal matrices inside the upper triangular ones) while the fixed set of an involutive automorphism is always a subalgebra and the algebra is $\mathbb{Z}/2$-graded; the induced involution on a quotient by a $\sigma$-stable ideal, the exchange involution on $A\times A^{\mathrm{op}}$ whose fixed set is the diagonal, whose swap on $A\times A$ is instead an involutive automorphism, and the tensor product $\sigma\otimes\tau$ with its symmetric and skew parts; and the scalars, that is the $\varsigma$-semilinear involutions, the restriction to $F\cdot1$, the first and the second kind by the centre, and the descent $(B\otimes_FK)^{\mathrm{id}\otimes\varsigma}=B\otimes1$ for a quadratic extension. No form, no norm, no distance: the adjoint involutions, the orthogonal and the symplectic type and the trace and the reduced norm belong to *Hilbert Algebras*, and the graded algebra to *Superalgebras and Graded Structures*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/opposite-algebras-and-anti-isomorphisms.html">Opposite Algebras and Anti-Isomorphisms</a>
<!-- the opposite algebra and the anti-isomorphisms onto it; an involution as an isomorphism $A\to A^{\mathrm{op}}$. -->

<!-- the involutions of the tensor algebra and of its quotients; the extension of an involution of the space and the sign rules. -->

<a href="articles_maths/involutions-of-a-free-algebra.html">Involutions of a Free Algebra</a>
<!-- the involutions of a free algebra; the reversal of words as the canonical anti-involution and the involutions of its quotients. -->

<a href="articles_maths/involutive-graded-algebras.html">Involutive Graded Algebras</a>
<!-- algebras with a grading and an involution compatible with it; the graded involution and the super-involution. -->

<a href="articles_maths/unitary-elements-of-an-involutive-algebra.html">Unitary Elements of an Involutive Algebra</a>
<!-- the elements with $u^*u = uu^* = 1$; the group of unitary elements, its Lie algebra of skew elements and their relation to the self-adjoint part. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-self-adjoint-part-of-an-algebra.html">The Self-Adjoint Part of an Algebra</a>
<!-- the self-adjoint elements $H(A)$ and their Jordan structure under the symmetrised product; the symmetric and the skew parts. -->

<!-- the self-adjoint element $h^*=h$ and its eigenvalue decomposition $h=\sum_i\lambda_i e_i$; the permutation law $e_i^*=e_{\pi(i)}$, $\lambda_{\pi(i)}=\varsigma(\lambda_i)$; the equivalence of Hermitian $e_i$ and fixed $\lambda_i$; the first kind, where every eigenprojector of a self-adjoint element is Hermitian, and the second kind, where the non-fixed eigenvalues occur in conjugate pairs and the projectors are exchanged; the orbit idempotents $g_J=\sum_{i\in J}e_i$ and the decomposition over the fixed field, with the two-element orbit $\frac{s}{2}g_J+btv_J$ where $v_J$ is skew and $v_J^2=g_J$; the Peirce corners $A_{ij}^*=A_{ji}$; and the conjugate transpose, transpose, entrywise-conjugation and repeated-eigenvalue examples. -->

<a href="articles_maths/unitary-elements-and-their-algebraic-decompositions.html">Unitary Elements and Their Algebraic Decompositions</a>
<!-- the unitary elements $u^*u=uu^*=1$ and their eigenvalue decompositions; the permutation law $e_i^*=e_{\pi(i)}$, $\lambda_{\pi(i)}^{-1}=\varsigma(\lambda_i)$; the equivalence of Hermitian eigenprojectors and unimodular eigenvalues $\lambda\varsigma(\lambda)=1$; the first kind $\lambda^2=1$ and the second kind $\lambda\bar\lambda=1$; the orbit decomposition, the generalized decomposition with unipotent parts, the unitary roots and the Cayley transform; the failure without separability, with the dual-number unitary $1+\varepsilon$ of minimal polynomial $(x-1)^2$; and the conjugate transpose, transpose rotation, cyclic group algebra and exchange-involution examples. -->

<a href="articles_maths/involutions-of-a-path-algebra.html">Involutions of a Path Algebra</a>
<!-- the involutions of a path algebra; the reversal of the arrows and the compatibility with the relations of the quiver. -->

<!-- the involutions of a central simple algebra; the first and the second kind, the transpose and the symplectic types, and the classifying invariants. -->

<!-- the matrix Jordan–Chevalley decomposition $A=A_s+A_n$ with $A_s$ semisimple, $A_n$ nilpotent and commuting; existence and uniqueness over a perfect field, the Hermite interpolation polynomial $A_s=p(A)$, and the algorithm through the primary decomposition; the Jordan basis reading $A_s$ diagonal and $A_n$ strictly upper triangular; the multiplicative version $A=A_sA_u$ with $A_u=I+A_s^{-1}A_n$ unipotent, the exponential $e^A=e^{A_s}e^{A_n}$ and the logarithm; the distinction between semisimple and diagonalisable over $\mathbb{R}$, the real Jordan form, and the failure over an imperfect field with the companion matrix of $x^p-t$; the centraliser $C(A)=C(A_s)\cap C(A_n)$ and the simultaneous decomposition of a commuting family. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-number-systems-as-algebras-with-and-without-nontrivial-idempotents.html">The Number Systems as Algebras with and without Nontrivial Idempotents</a>
<!-- the number systems compared by their idempotents: $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{C}$ and $\mathbb{H}$ have only $0,1$ because they are division algebras; $\mathbb{D}'$ has only $0,1$ because it is local, although it is not a division algebra; $\mathbb{D}=\mathbb{R}[j]$ has the four idempotents $0,1,\frac12(1\pm j)$ and is $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}$; $\mathbb{H}_{\mathbb{D}}\cong\mathbb{H}\times\mathbb{H}$ has four central idempotents; $\mathbb{B}\cong M_2(\mathbb{C})$ has a two-parameter family of noncentral rank-one projections and only the central idempotents $0,1$; the halving bijection between the idempotents and the roots of $1$; and the exact criterion, the primitivity of $1$ and the locality of a finite-dimensional algebra, with the table of the division, local, simple and semisimple properties. -->
