## Sesqualgebras

### Theory

<a href="articles_maths/sesqualgebras.html">Sesqualgebras</a>
<!-- an $R$-module with a product that is $R$-linear in the first slot and $\varsigma$-semilinear in the second, $(\lambda x)y=\lambda(xy)$ and $x(\lambda y)=\varsigma(\lambda)(xy)$, where $\varsigma$ is an involution of the base ring and is part of the datum; equivalently, with the conjugate module $A^{\varsigma}$ carrying the twisted action $\lambda\cdot x=\varsigma(\lambda)x$, a product that is $R$-bilinear as a map $A\times A^{\varsigma}\to A$; the collapse to an ordinary (bilinear) algebra exactly when $\varsigma=\mathrm{id}$, so the sesquilinear kind contains the bilinear one; the relation to the algebras of *Algebras* and the reason the object is not a special case of them for $\varsigma\neq\mathrm{id}$; the derived operation $x\star y=xy^{*}$ of an algebra with a $\varsigma$-semilinear involution as the standard example, its failure of associativity, its right unit without a left one, and the ternary product it forces; the standing hypotheses of the category. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-sesquilinear-product.html">The Sesquilinear Product</a>
<!-- the two-variable product $\star:A\times A\to A$; linearity in the first slot and $\varsigma$-semilinearity in the second as the two axioms; the rule of the scalars of a combination and the structure constants; the conjugate of a product and the conjugate module; the transposed product $y\star x$, of the opposite parity and bilinear on $A^{\varsigma}\times A$, against $x\star y$; the difference, which vanishes exactly when the involution on $A$ is the identity and the algebra is commutative, and for an algebra of full type only when $\varsigma=\mathrm{id}$; the one-sided products $a\star x$ and $x\star a$, conjugate-linear and linear, the module structures they give when the product is associative, and the $\varsigma$-twisted composition of two one-sided operators. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-symmetric-and-antisymmetric-parts-of-a-sesqualgebra-product.html">The Symmetric and Antisymmetric Parts of a Sesqualgebra Product</a>
<!-- the split of a $\varsigma$-sesquilinear product $\star$ into its symmetric part $f_{+}=\tfrac12(f+E(f))$ and its antisymmetric part $f_{-}=\tfrac12(f-E(f))$ by the plain exchange $E(f)(x,y)=f(y,x)$; the reconstruction $f=f_{+}+f_{-}$, the uniqueness of the pair, the vanishing of the antisymmetric part on the diagonal, and the polarisation of the square, all four independent of the scalar rules and identical to the bilinear case; the obstruction, that the exchanged product is $\varsigma$-semilinear in the first slot and $R$-linear in the second, so its two parts are only $R^{\varsigma}$-bilinear; the two projections $p$ and $q$ of the additive maps, idempotent, orthogonal and summing to the identity, so that a symmetric and an antisymmetric map are independent data, against the failure of the projections to preserve the class; the two halves named as the symmetrised sesquilinear product $x\circ y$ and half the sesquilinear commutator $[x,y]_{\varsigma}$; the Hermitian values of the symmetric part and the skew-Hermitian values of the antisymmetric part in the derived case $x\star y=xy^{*}$, and the Hermitian square on the diagonal; the split of the constants by the transposition of the two lower indices, and the reason the bilinear counts $\binom{n+1}{2}n$ and $\binom{n}{2}n$ do not transcribe; the biquaternion instance $\mathrm{SPS}$, $\mathrm{APS}$, $\mathrm{SQS}$, $\mathrm{AQS}$ of the two sesqualgebra products, only $\mathbb{R}$-bilinear; the class-preserving alternative $c(y\star x)$ of *The Conjugate-Symmetric and Skew-Conjugate-Symmetric Parts of a Sesquilinear Product*; and the collapse when $\varsigma=\mathrm{id}$ and in characteristic two. -->

<a href="articles_maths/conjugate-linear-maps-and-the-conjugate-dual.html">Conjugate-Linear Maps and the Conjugate Dual</a>
<!-- the $\varsigma$-semilinear maps $f(\lambda x)=\varsigma(\lambda)f(x)$ and the reading $\operatorname{Hom}_{\varsigma}(M,N)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{R}(M^{\varsigma},N)$; their additive group and the scalar action that makes them a module; the parity rule, two semilinear maps composing to a linear one, and the $\mathbb{Z}/2$-graded ring of the linear and semilinear endomorphisms; the conjugate dual $M^{\varsigma*}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\varsigma}(M,R)\cong(M^{\varsigma})^{*}$, distinct from the conjugate module; the pairing linear in the first slot and $\varsigma$-semilinear in the second, which the ordinary dual cannot see; the transpose of a semilinear map, exchanging the two duals; the evaluation into the double conjugate dual as the evaluation of the conjugate module; the transport of a sesquilinear structure along a conjugate-linear map, which preserves the parity. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-sesquilinear-associator-and-the-ternary-product.html">The Sesquilinear Associator and the Ternary Product</a>
<!-- the associator $[x,y,z]=(x\star y)\star z-x\star(y\star z)$ of the sesquilinear product; the $\varsigma$-twisting it carries; the associator of the derived product $xy^{*}$, its value $x((zy)^{*}-zy^{*})$, and the criterion for the derived product to be associative; the theorem that an associative or a commutative product forces the trivial involution, so an algebra of full type with a nontrivial involution is neither; the ternary product that the failure forces, and the passage to it. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-conjugate-symmetric-and-skew-conjugate-symmetric-parts-of-a-sesquilinear-product.html">The Conjugate-Symmetric and Skew-Conjugate-Symmetric Parts of a Sesquilinear Product</a>
<!-- the split of a $\varsigma$-sesquilinear product into two halves by an exchange twisted by a conjugation $c$; the obstruction, that the plain transposition reverses the parity and is semilinear in the first slot, so the plain split into the symmetrised product and the difference is only $R^{\varsigma}$-bilinear and splits the scalar form into its $\varsigma$-even and $\varsigma$-odd parts; the adapted exchange $x\star^{c}y=c(y\star x)$ as an involution of the class of products, its uniqueness, the two projections $p$ and $q$, and the independence of the two halves; the scalar theorem, that a Hermitian scalar form lies wholly in the conjugate-symmetric half, and the diagonal of the skew half, which need not vanish in the sesquilinear case although it stays scalar-free; the constants of the exchange, conjugate-symmetry $c^{k}{}_{ij}=\varsigma(c^{k}{}_{ji})$ and the equal rank $n^{3}$ of the two halves over the fixed field; the failure of the polarisation of the square, which sees the plain symmetrisation and not the exchanged one; the standard example, the complex matrices with the entrywise conjugation, and the four general products with their two exchanges. -->

<a href="articles_maths/algebraic-j-star-algebras.html">Algebraic J*-Algebras</a>
<!-- the algebraic, norm-free $J^{*}$-algebra: an $R$-module $V$ with a ternary product that is additive in each slot, $R$-linear in the outer two and $\varsigma$-semilinear in the middle, satisfying the Jordan triple identity, and naming no binary product; the model $\{x,y,z\}=xy^{*}z$ of an associative algebra with a $\varsigma$-semilinear involution; the unital recovery of the binary product and the involution, which make the binary product the shadow of the ternary one; the witness that a $J^{*}$-algebra need not be an algebra; the outer symmetry as the axiom the $J^{*}$-algebra omits and the Jordan triple system of *The Lie–Jordan Decomposition of a Bilinear Product and the Jordan Triple System* requires. -->

<a href="articles_maths/hermitian-and-skew-hermitian-elements.html">Hermitian and Skew-Hermitian Elements</a>
<!-- the fixed and anti-fixed sets of the involution, $H(A)=\{x:x^{*}=x\}$ and $S(A)=\{x:x^{*}=-x\}$; the decomposition $A=H\oplus S$ when $2$ is invertible and its failure in characteristic two; the Hermitian part closed under the symmetrised product, hence a Jordan algebra developed in *The Hermitian Jordan Algebra*; the two halves of the sesquilinear product, with the Lie algebra formed by the skew-Hermitian part developed in *The Unitary Lie Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/hermitian-squares-and-the-algebraic-positive-cone.html">Hermitian Squares and the Algebraic Positive Cone</a>
<!-- the element $x\star x=xx^{*}$ and its Hermitian property; the sum of Hermitian squares and the positive cone $C(A)$ they generate inside the Hermitian part, the purely algebraic half of positivity; the scalar action of the square semiring and the invariance under congruence; the preorder $y-x\in C(A)$ and the properness that a genuine order requires, which the algebra alone does not supply in general; the matrix model with the conjugate transpose, which is proper, against two non-proper examples. -->

<a href="articles_maths/ideals-and-quotients-of-a-sesqualgebra.html">Ideals and Quotients of a Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the left, right and two-sided ideals, and the $R$-submodule condition that the scalar rules put on them (automatic in the unital case); closure of the ideals under intersection and sum; the conjugate image $I^{*}$, which carries a left ideal to a right ideal, and the smallest invariant ideal $I+I^{*}$ containing a two-sided ideal $I$, equal to $I$ exactly when $I$ is an invariant ideal; the quotient by a two-sided ideal, the induced sesquilinear structure over the same datum $(R,\varsigma)$, and the exact obstruction to the descent of the algebra involution when $I\neq I^{*}$; the isomorphism theorems adapted to the conjugate-linear slot; the worked quotients $\mathbb{C}$, $\mathbb{H}$ and $\mathbb{B}$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/units-and-the-unitary-elements.html">Units and the Unitary Elements</a>
<!-- the unit of a sesqualgebra and its Hermitian property, and the unit as a right unit of the derived operation only; the unitary elements $U(A)=\{u:uu^{*}=u^{*}u=1\}$ as the units with $u^{*}=u^{-1}$, and the group structure under the product; the stability of $U(A)$ under the involution and the inverse, with the involution restricting to the inversion, an anti-automorphism that is an automorphism exactly when $U(A)$ is abelian; the Hermitian unitary elements $U(A)\cap H(A)=\{u:u^{2}=1, u=u^{*}\}$; the inner $*$-automorphisms $x\mapsto uxu^{*}$ that the unitaries induce, their preservation of $H(A)$ and $S(A)$, and their restriction to the group; the worked cases $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, $\mathbb{H}$, the commutative algebras and $\mathbb{B}$; the Lie algebra of the skew-Hermitian elements is *The Unitary Lie Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/subalgebras-and-the-involution.html">Subalgebras and the Involution</a>
<!-- the subalgebras of a sesqualgebra, closed under the product and under the scalars, and the $*$-subalgebras, closed under the involution; the restriction of the sesquilinear structure to a subalgebra, which keeps the datum $(R,\varsigma)$ and makes the inclusion a morphism; the conjugate image, a subalgebra, and the $*$-stability $B^{*}=B$; the closure under intersection and the failure of the sum, against the ideals of *Ideals and Quotients of a Sesqualgebra*; the subalgebra generated by a set as the span of the words in it, and the $*$-subalgebra generated by a set as the subalgebra of the set with its conjugate image; the role of the Hermitian generators and of the Hermitian and skew-Hermitian parts; the restriction of the involution to a $*$-subalgebra, with $H(B)=B\cap H(A)$; the largest $*$-subalgebra inside a subalgebra and the smallest containing it; the reading of a $*$-subalgebra through the derived operation $x\star y=xy^{*}$; the matrix and quaternion cases; the counterexample that a subalgebra need not be $*$-stable. -->

<a href="articles_maths/derivations-of-a-sesqualgebra.html">Derivations of a Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the derivations $D(xy)=D(x)y+xD(y)$, $R$-linear and untwisted on the scalars, and the $*$-derivations with $D(x^{*})=D(x)^{*}$; the Lie algebra $\operatorname{Der}(A)$ under the commutator and its module structure; the inner derivations $D_{a}(x)=ax-xa$ and the centre as the kernel of $a\mapsto D_{a}$; the inner derivations generated by the skew-Hermitian elements and the link to *The Unitary Lie Algebra*; the failure of the Leibniz rule for the derived operation $x\star y=xy^{*}$, and the twisted derivation that it forces. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-centre-and-the-zero-divisors-of-a-sesqualgebra.html">The Centre and the Zero Divisors of a Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the centre $Z(A)=\{z: zx = xz \text{ for all } x\}$, an $R$-submodule closed under every scalar and carried to itself by the involution; the Hermitian and the skew-Hermitian parts of the centre and their decomposition when $2$ is invertible; the centre as the kernel of the inner maps; the one-sided and the two-sided zero divisors and their annihilators, which are $R$-submodules, the involution exchanging the sides; the derived operation, whose one-sided zero divisors are the same elements with the conjugate partner; the theorem that a central element lies in the annihilator over a twisted base, so a unital or annihilator-free sesqualgebra over $(\mathbb{C},\varsigma)$ has zero centre; the comparison with *Centre, Units, Zero Divisors and Division Algebras* of the bilinear layer. -->

<a href="articles_maths/hermitian-idempotents-and-the-peirce-decomposition.html">Hermitian Idempotents and the Peirce Decomposition</a>
<!-- the idempotents $e^{2}=e$ and the Hermitian ones $e=e^{*}$; the orthogonality of Hermitian idempotents, the idempotence of $e+f$ for orthogonal $e$ and $f$ when $2$ is invertible, and the partial order they carry; the Peirce spaces $eAe$, $eA(1-e)$, $(1-e)Ae$ and $(1-e)A(1-e)$, with the involution exchanging the two mixed spaces when $e$ is Hermitian; the two-sided Peirce decomposition relative to a family of orthogonal Hermitian idempotents, and the multiplication table of the spaces, transposed for the derived product; the corner algebra $eAe$ and the sesquilinear structure that it inherits; the matrix model $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, where a Hermitian idempotent is the matrix with $P^{2}=P=P^{*}$ and the four spaces are the blocks. -->

<a href="articles_maths/simple-sesqualgebras-and-minimal-ideals.html">Simple Sesqualgebras and Minimal Ideals</a>
<!-- the simple sesqualgebra, with no two-sided ideal other than $0$ and $A$ for its own product $\star$, the product being the one fixed by the two scalar rules, against the two-sided ideals of the underlying algebra for the juxtaposition product, which form a different set; the invariant-simple one, with no proper $\ast$-ideal; the theorem that in the derived model with a unit the two notions coincide, since $1\star i=i^{*}$ forces every two-sided $\star$-ideal to be stable, so the two-sided $\star$-ideals are exactly the $\ast$-ideals, the trivial direction simple $\Rightarrow$ invariant-simple being immediate from the definition; the minimal left, right and two-sided ideals, generated by the primitive idempotents of *Ideals and Peirce Decomposition of the General Plain Algebra* and *List of Rings by Their Idempotents*, with the $\ast$-stability that the Hermitian condition of *Hermitian Idempotents and the Peirce Decomposition* adds and the primitivity that makes the ideal minimal; the centre of a simple algebra and the zero divisors that it may still have; the worked cases $M_n(\mathbb{C})$ with the conjugate transpose and $\mathbb{H}$ with the quaternion conjugation. -->

<a href="articles_maths/tensor-products-of-sesqualgebras.html">Tensor Products of Sesqualgebras</a>
<!-- the sesquilinear tensor product $A\otimes_R B$ with the involution $x\otimes y\mapsto x^{*}\otimes y^{*}$; the $\varsigma$-twisting carried through the tensor product; the commuting images of $A$ and $B$; the universal property for the pairs of maps with commuting images that are compatible with the $\varsigma$-twist, the coproduct of the noncommutative case being the free product instead, as in *Tensor Products of Algebras*; the examples $\mathbb{C}\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{H}$ and $\mathbb{H}\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{H}$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/direct-products-of-sesqualgebras.html">Direct Products of Sesqualgebras</a>
<!-- the direct product $A\times B$ with the componentwise product and involution, a sesqualgebra over the same datum $(R,\varsigma)$; the component idempotents and the central Hermitian idempotents that cut a direct product; the criterion that a decomposition $A=I\oplus J$ into two-sided ideals comes exactly from a pair of orthogonal central idempotents, the central splitting being that of *Unital Algebras*, §*Idempotents and the Peirce Decomposition*, with the Hermitian condition of *Hermitian Idempotents and the Peirce Decomposition* the extra datum that makes the two ideals $\ast$-ideals, so that the involution descends to the factors; the failure of the direct product to be a coproduct, the coproduct of noncommutative algebras being the free product and the tensor product being universal only for pairs with commuting images, as in *Tensor Products of Algebras*; the worked case $R\times R$ and the exchange involution, for which the idempotent $(1,0)$ is central but not Hermitian. -->

<a href="articles_maths/real-forms-of-a-sesqualgebra.html">Real Forms of a Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the fixed ring $R^{\varsigma}$ of the base involution and the fixed subalgebra $A^{\alpha}$ of an algebra involution $\alpha$; the descent of the sesquilinear structure to the fixed ring; the real forms of a complex sesqualgebra; the two involutions and the four subobjects they cut; the worked cases $\mathbb{C}$, $\mathbb{H}$ and $\mathbb{B}=\mathbb{C}\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{H}$, and the caution that $\mathbb{H}$ carries no $\mathbb{C}$-sesquilinear structure, because the centre of $\mathbb{H}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ and the quaternion conjugation is $\mathbb{C}$-antilinear, not $\mathbb{C}$-linear. -->

### Operator Theory

<a href="articles_maths/the-left-and-right-multiplication-operators-of-a-sesqualgebra.html">The Left and Right Multiplication Operators of a Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the operators $L_a(x)=a\star x$ and $R_a(x)=x\star a$ of the sesquilinear product; $L_a$ $\varsigma$-semilinear in $\operatorname{End}_{R^{\varsigma}}(A)$ while $R_a$ is $R$-linear in $\operatorname{End}_{R}(A)$; the parameter laws $L_{\lambda a}=\lambda L_a$ and $R_{\lambda a}=\varsigma(\lambda)R_a$; the composition in the associative case and its failure in the standard example, where the residue is the two-sided multiplication $T_{a,b^{*}}$; the two regular maps, one linear and multiplicative and one conjugate-linear and anti-multiplicative, and the failure of a single faithful linear representation to carry the whole product; the comparison with *Left and Right Multiplication* and *Associative Algebras*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-sesquilinear-sandwich-operator.html">The Sesquilinear Sandwich Operator</a>
<!-- the two-sided operator $x\mapsto ax^{*}b$ as the triple product with the middle slot variable; its conjugate-linear middle slot and its reading $S_{a,b}=T_{a,b}\circ{}^{*}$; the relation to the ordinary two-sided multiplication $T_{p,q}(x)=pxq$ and to the signed sandwich of *The Signed Adjoint Sandwich on a Bimodule over an Algebra*; the composition table and the monoid the two families form, the composite of two sandwiches being linear; the invertibility $S_{a,b}^{-1}=S_{(b^{-1})^{*},(a^{-1})^{*}}$ with the central units as the kernel of the parametrisation; the reflections $S_{u,u}$ of the unitary elements and the inner involution $S_{u,u^{*}}=\sigma_u$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-sesquilinear-adjoint-operator.html">The Sesquilinear Adjoint Operator</a>
<!-- the conjugate-transpose operator of a matrix or of an endomorphism, defined by the involution of the algebra; the anti-automorphism $T\mapsto T^{\dagger}$ of the endomorphism algebra and the involution it defines; the two adjoints that a conjugate-linear operator requires, and the relation between them. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-sesquilinear-commutator.html">The Sesquilinear Commutator</a>
<!-- the bracket $[x,y]_{\varsigma}=x\star y-y\star x$ of the sesquilinear product, the antisymmetric half of the split of the product, treated for its own sake; its antisymmetry for free and its linearity over the fixed ring $R^{\varsigma}$ alone, the correction term $(\lambda-\varsigma(\lambda))(y\star x)$ being the whole difference from the bilinear case; the failure of the Jacobi identity, with the witness $E_{11},E_{22},E_{12}$ in $M_2(\mathbb{C})$ whose Jacobi sum is $E_{21}-E_{12}$, and the observation that the failure needs the noncommutativity and not the twist, since it vanishes for the sesquilinear field; the is not a Lie bracket, its values in the skew-Hermitian part; the Lie algebra that the sesqualgebra carries instead, on the skew-Hermitian half under the commutator, being *Lie Algebras of Sesqualgebras*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-sesquilinear-symmetrised-product.html">The Sesquilinear Symmetrised Product</a>
<!-- the symmetrised product $x\circ y=\tfrac12(x\star y+y\star x)$ of a sesquilinear product, the companion of the difference bracket of *The Sesquilinear Commutator* and the symmetric half of the same split; its $R^{\varsigma}$-bilinearity, each slot taking one linear and one conjugate-linear contribution so that the two parities collapse to the fixed ring, against the $R$-bilinearity that returns only in the degenerate case; its polarisation of the square $x\star x=xx^{*}$; the Hermitian value of $x\circ y$ for arbitrary arguments in the derived case $x\star y=xy^{*}$; its agreement with the plain symmetrisation $\tfrac12(xy+yx)$ on $H(A)$ and the Jordan identity there, through the associativity of the envelope; the failure of the Jordan identity off $H(A)$, with the witness $E_{12},E_{22}$ in $M_2(\mathbb{C})$; the obstruction read as the non-associativity of the derived product against the associativity of the algebra product; the worked cases $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, the sesquilinear field, $\mathbb{H}$ and $\mathbb{B}$; the Jordan structure it generates on $H(A)$ is *Jordan Algebras of Sesqualgebras*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-ternary-product-as-an-operator.html">The Ternary Product as an Operator</a>
<!-- the operator $\Theta_{x,y}(z)=\{x,y,z\}=xy^{*}z$ attached to a pair; its linearity in $z$ and conjugate-linearity in $y$; the Lie triple system the operators form under the commutator; the quadratic representation of a Jordan algebra as the commutative case; the operators it generates in the worked algebras $M_n(\mathbb{C})$ and $\mathbb{B}$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-graded-sesquilinear-action.html">The Graded Sesquilinear Action</a>
<!-- the action of a $\mathbb{Z}/2$-graded sesqualgebra on a graded module; the degree count that forces the involution of a graded sesqualgebra to be even, so that no Koszul sign enters the scalar rules; the two classes of order-two anti-maps, the graded involution and the superinvolution, and the condition $A^{1}A^{1}=0$ under which they coincide; the ternary product of a superinvolution and its failure of the Jordan triple identity on two odd elements; the graded $\varsigma$-compatibility, holding on the even part and obstructed on the odd part; the derived action $a\star m=a\cdot\theta(m)$ and the conjugation $\theta$; the matrix superalgebra as the nondegenerate case and $k[x]/(x^{2})$ with an odd $x$ as the degenerate one; the relation to *The Graded Action on a Module over an Algebra* and the one new datum. -->

### * Theory

<a href="articles_maths/the-involutions-of-a-sesqualgebra.html">The Involutions of a Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the involutions of a sesqualgebra, the $\varsigma$-semilinear anti-automorphisms $\alpha$ with $\alpha^{2}=\mathrm{id}$, and the set they form, closed under composition and inversion; the composite $\alpha\beta$ of two involutions and the criterion for it to be an involution again; the family $x\mapsto ux^{*}u$, an involution for every unitary $u$ and the composite of the datum involution with the inner $\ast$-automorphism $x\mapsto uxu^{*}$ of *Units and the Unitary Elements*; the fixed subspaces $H(A,\alpha)$ and the Galois-type correspondence between involutions and the subspaces they fix; the partial order on the set of the involutions; the datum involution $*$ as one element of the set, and the distinction from the involutive algebras of *Algebras*, where $\varsigma=\mathrm{id}$ cuts the same construction down. -->

<a href="articles_maths/lie-algebras-of-sesqualgebras.html">Lie Algebras of Sesqualgebras</a>
<!-- the Lie structures a sesqualgebra carries, the sesquilinear counterpart of the Lie half of *The Lie–Jordan Decomposition of a Bilinear Product and the Jordan Triple System*; the antisymmetrisation $[x,y]_{\varsigma}=x\star y-y\star x$ is antisymmetric and $R^{\varsigma}$-bilinear but its Jacobi identity fails, with the witness $E_{11},E_{22},E_{12}$ in $M_2(\mathbb{C})$ whose Jacobi sum is $E_{21}-E_{12}$, and it is a Lie bracket exactly when the product being antisymmetrised is associative, which for an algebra of full type forces $\varsigma=\mathrm{id}$; the Lie structure that is available is the commutator $xy-yx$ of the associative product, making $A$ a $\mathbb{Z}/2$-graded Lie algebra with even part $S(A)$, odd part $H(A)$ and the involution reversing the bracket, $[x,y]^{*}=-[x^{*},y^{*}]$; $S(A)$ as a Lie algebra over $R^{\varsigma}$, the unitary Lie algebra, acting by the inner $*$-derivations with $[\mathrm{ad}_{s},\mathrm{ad}_{t}]=\mathrm{ad}_{[s,t]}$ and kernel the central skew-Hermitian elements, and the Hermitian half acting by the skew derivations instead; the ternary companion, the Lie triple system $[[x,y],z]$ and its three identities; the degeneration to the bilinear case, with the comparison table; the worked cases $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, $\mathbb{C}$, $\mathbb{H}$ and $\mathbb{B}$; the narrow articles feeding it are *The Sesquilinear Commutator*, *The Unitary Lie Algebra*, *Derivations of a Sesqualgebra* and *The Ternary Product as an Operator*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-unitary-lie-algebra.html">The Unitary Lie Algebra</a>
<!-- the skew-Hermitian elements $x^{*}=-x$ and the Lie algebra they form under the commutator, the concrete model of the umbrella *Lie Algebras of Sesqualgebras*; the closedness of that part under the bracket, which the Hermitian part does not have; the failure of the skew-Hermitian part to be closed under the product, where $(xy)^{*}=yx$, so $xy$ is skew-Hermitian exactly when $x$ and $y$ anticommute and Hermitian exactly when they commute, and neither in general, while $xy+yx$ is always Hermitian; the action of the unitary group on the skew-Hermitian part by the inner automorphisms; the worked cases $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, $\mathbb{H}$ and $\mathbb{B}$; the unitary group itself and its elements are *Units and the Unitary Elements*, and the exponential that carries the skew-Hermitian part into it, with its convergence and its failure of surjectivity, belongs to Part II and is *The Exponential Map on a Banach Sesqualgebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/jordan-algebras-of-sesqualgebras.html">Jordan Algebras of Sesqualgebras</a>
<!-- the Jordan structures a sesqualgebra carries, the sesquilinear counterpart of the Jordan half of *The Lie–Jordan Decomposition of a Bilinear Product and the Jordan Triple System*; the symmetrisation $x\circ y=\tfrac12(x\star y+y\star x)$ is commutative and $R^{\varsigma}$-bilinear with image in $H(A)$, and it is a Jordan product exactly on $H(A)$, where the derived operation coincides with the associative product, the Jordan identity failing off $H(A)$ with the witness $E_{12},E_{22}$ in $M_2(\mathbb{C})$, the criterion that would repair it being associativity, which for an algebra of full type forces $\varsigma=\mathrm{id}$; $J(A)=(H(A),\circ)$ as a Jordan algebra over $R^{\varsigma}$, functorial in the involutive algebra, special with envelope $A$, and its quadratic representation $U_x(y)=xyx$ against the $\mathrm{ad}$ of the Lie twin; the ternary structure $\{x,y,z\}=xy^{*}z$ of an algebraic $J^{*}$-algebra on the whole module and the recovery of the binary product at the unit, with the exceptional algebras outside the class; the degeneration to the bilinear case, with the comparison table; the worked cases $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, $\mathbb{C}$, $\mathbb{H}$ and $\mathbb{B}$; the narrow articles feeding it are *The Sesquilinear Symmetrised Product*, *The Hermitian Jordan Algebra*, *Algebraic J\*-Algebras* and *The Self-Adjoint Part of an Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-hermitian-jordan-algebra.html">The Hermitian Jordan Algebra</a>
<!-- the Hermitian elements $H(A)$ under the symmetrised product $x\circ y=\tfrac12(xy+yx)$ as a Jordan algebra over the fixed ring $R^{\varsigma}$, the sesquilinear counterpart of *The Self-Adjoint Part of an Algebra*, the invariant being the scalars rather than the axioms, and the concrete model of the umbrella *Jordan Algebras of Sesqualgebras*; the axioms and the envelope, $J$ special with the associative algebra $A$ as envelope inside $A^{+}$; the powers $x^{\circ n}=x^{n}$ and the subalgebra generated by one Hermitian element; the trace form $\tau(x\circ y)=\tau(xy)$ and its reality on the Hermitian matrices; the Hermitian idempotents, the Jordan orthogonality $e\circ f=0$ equivalent to $ef=fe=0$, and the degree, $n$ for $M_n(\mathbb{C})$; the Peirce decomposition as the Hermitian part of the associative Peirce decomposition of $e$, with the eigenvalues $1,\tfrac12,0$ on the Hermitian parts of $eAe$, of $eAf\oplus fAe$ and of $fAf$; the quadratic representation $U_x(y)=xyx$; the worked cases $M_n(\mathbb{C})$ with the conjugate transpose, $\mathbb{C}$ with conjugation, $\mathbb{H}$, where the layer degenerates to the bilinear one, and $\mathbb{B}$, of degree two. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-eigenvalue-decomposition-of-a-hermitian-element.html">The Eigenvalue Decomposition of a Hermitian Element</a>
<!-- the Hermitian spectral resolution $a=\sum_i\lambda_i e_i$ in a Hermitian Jordan algebra; the eigenspaces $J_{ij}=H(e_iAe_j\oplus e_jAe_i)$; the diagonal and mixed Peirce components; the eigenvalue decomposition of a self-adjoint element and its comparison with the associative and the Jordan cases; the existence theorem and the uniqueness of the resolution. -->

<a href="articles_maths/anti-automorphisms-twisted-by-the-base-involution.html">Anti-Automorphisms Twisted by the Base Involution</a>
<!-- the anti-automorphisms of $A$ twisted by $\varsigma$, $f(\lambda x)=\varsigma(\lambda)f(x)$ and $f(xy)=f(y)f(x)$, of any order; the linear and the conjugate-linear kinds for a central simple algebra and the constraint the $\varsigma$-twist puts on the order; the order-two case, that is the involutions of the algebra, is *The Involutions of a Sesqualgebra*; the relation to *Opposite Algebras and Anti-Isomorphisms* and to *Involutions of a Central Simple Algebra* with the extra datum the $\varsigma$-twist adds. -->

<a href="articles_maths/involutions-of-a-sesquilinear-tensor-product.html">Involutions of a Sesquilinear Tensor Product</a>
<!-- the tensor involution $x\otimes y\mapsto x^{*}\otimes y^{*}$; its composition with the flip and the two involutions of the tensor square; the $\varsigma$-compatibility of the tensor product; the analogies with *Involutions of the Tensor Algebra* and the single new datum; the worked cases $\mathbb{C}\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{H}$ and $\mathbb{B}\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{B}$. -->

### * Operator Theory

<a href="articles_maths/the-adjoint-of-the-sesquilinear-sandwich.html">The Adjoint of the Sesquilinear Sandwich</a>
<!-- the adjoint of $x\mapsto ax^{*}b$, defined by the involution; the explicit expression and its dependence on the conjugate of $b$; the unitarity condition it defines; the comparison with the adjoint of the unsigned sandwich in *Algebras* and with the signed adjoint of the graded case. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-adjoint-of-the-conjugate-left-multiplication.html">The Adjoint of the Conjugate Left Multiplication</a>
<!-- the adjoint of the conjugate-linear operator $L_a(x)=a\star x$; the adjoint that a conjugate-linear operator requires and the single-slot adjoint that it does not have; the involution that makes the adjoint exist; the products $L_a^{\dagger}L_b=R_{a^{*}b}$ and $L_bL_a^{\dagger}=T_{ba^{*},1}$; the self-adjointness of $L_a$ exactly for a central $a$; the unitary case; the degeneracies when the involution is trivial; the worked matrix case. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-unitary-operators-of-a-sesqualgebra.html">The Unitary Operators of a Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the operators preserving the sesquilinear product, $T(x\star y)=Tx\star Ty$; the conjugate-linear operators among them and the group they form; the relation to the unitary group $U(A)$ of the elements; the worked case $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, with the unitary and the antiunitary operators separated. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-adjoint-of-the-ternary-product.html">The Adjoint of the Ternary Product</a>
<!-- the adjoint of $z\mapsto\{x,y,z\}$, defined by the involution; the dependence on the two parameters and the conjugate-linearity in one of them; the adjoint $\Theta_{x,y}^{\dagger}=\Theta_{y,x}$ that swaps the parameters; the self-adjointness of the quadratic representation and the Hermitian criterion $x\star y=y\star x$ for a general pair; the relation of the three readings under the adjoint; the relation to the $J^{*}$-triples and to the Jordan triple systems of *The Lie–Jordan Decomposition of a Bilinear Product and the Jordan Triple System*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-sesquilinear-structure-of-the-endomorphism-algebra.html">The Sesquilinear Structure of the Endomorphism Algebra</a>
<!-- $\operatorname{End}_R(M)$ as a sesqualgebra under $S\star T=S T^{\dagger}$; the conjugate-linear slot carried by the involution; the involutions it admits; the worked cases $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, $M_n(\mathbb{H})$ and the biquaternion algebra, with $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{C}}(\mathbb{B})\cong M_4(\mathbb{C})$ named. -->

## Sesqualgebras with a degree-2 form

### Theory

<a href="articles_maths/the-sesquilinear-form-and-the-conjugation.html">The Sesquilinear Form and the Conjugation</a>
<!-- the correspondence between a Hermitian form and the involution of the algebra, $h(x,y)=h(x^{*}y,1)$; the two directions and the compatibility; the classification of the forms into Hermitian, skew-Hermitian and alternating; the failure over a ring where $2$ is not invertible. -->

<a href="articles_maths/hermitian-forms-on-a-sesqualgebra.html">Hermitian Forms on a Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the $A$-valued Hermitian forms carried by the involution of an associative algebra with a sesquilinear product, $\Psi(x,y)=y^{*}x$ and its companion $\Phi(x,y)=xy^{*}=x\star y$; the two slots and the Hermitian property $\Psi(y,x)=\Psi(x,y)^{*}$; the product read as the form and the form read as a product; the reduction of $\Psi$ to the compatible scalar forms $h_{\varphi}(x,y)=\varphi(y^{*}x)$ of *The Sesquilinear Form and the Conjugation*; the two radicals as the left and the right annihilators, so that non-degeneracy of $\Psi$ is the vanishing of the left annihilator, one clause of the objects of full type of *Topological Sesqualgebras*; the form descended to a quotient by an invariant ideal; and the relation to *Hermitian Forms on a Hermitian Algebra with Hermitian Adjoint* of the bilinear layer, whose form $h_c(x,y)=c(x)y$ is the companion form with the two arguments exchanged. -->

<a href="articles_maths/hermitian-algebras.html">Hermitian Algebras</a>
<!-- the base structure of the layer: an associative algebra with an involution and a Hermitian form tied to the product by the adjoint axiom $h(xy,z)=h(y,x^{\dagger}z)$; the correspondence $h(x,y)=h(x^{\dagger}y,1)$; the companion form $h_c(x,y)=c(x)y$ of an anti-involution; the trace form and the induced dagger $x^{\dagger}=\sigma(\alpha(x^r))$ from reversion and the conjugate reversion; the radical, non-degeneracy and the isometry group; the unitary slice $U=\{x:x^{\dagger}x=1\}$ on which the dagger is the inverse. Positivity, completeness and the norm are *Hilbert Algebras* and the layer of Part II; the operators built from the dagger are the four groups below. -->

<a href="articles_maths/sesqualgebras-with-a-form.html">Sesqualgebras with a Form</a>
<!-- the base object of the category: an associative algebra with a $\varsigma$-semilinear involution $*$ and a Hermitian form tied by the compatibility $h(xy,z)=h(y,x^{*}z)$; the equivalent identity $h(x,yz)=h(y^{*}x,z)$ and the caution that $h(xy,z)=h(x,zy^{*})$ is an extra hypothesis, with the counterexample $\tau(xGy^{*})$; the radical as a left ideal whose image under $*$ is a right ideal, the objects of full type, the non-degeneracy criterion and the collapse at the trivial involution; the algebraic original of *Topological Sesqualgebras with a Form*, with no continuity, no norm and no completion. -->

<a href="articles_maths/polarisation-and-the-hermitian-square.html">Polarisation and the Hermitian Square</a>
<!-- the diagonal $q(x)=h(x,x)$ and the polarisation identity $q(x+y)-q(x)-q(y)=h_{\mathrm{tr}}(x,y)$; the trace form, the skew-Hermitian part the diagonal never sees, and $h=\tfrac12h_{\mathrm{tr}}+\tfrac12h_{\mathrm{sk}}$ when $2$ is invertible; the Hermitian square $xx^{*}$ with $q(x)=\varphi(xx^{*})$ and the quadratic form of the algebra; the degeneration in characteristic two and the quadratic refinement. -->

<a href="articles_maths/orthogonality-isotropy-and-the-radical.html">Orthogonality, Isotropy and the Radical</a>
<!-- orthogonality and the two orthogonal complements, with $W\subseteq W^{\perp\perp}$ and equality exactly for a non-degenerate restriction; the decomposition $A=W\oplus W^{\perp}$; isotropy, the null set and its difference from the radical; the radical as the total orthogonal complement $A^{\perp}$, the non-degenerate descent to $A/\operatorname{rad}$ and the Witt index. -->

<a href="articles_maths/isometries-and-the-unitary-group-of-a-form.html">Isometries and the Unitary Group of a Form</a>
<!-- the isometry set and the unitary group of the form; the equation $T^{*}T=1$, the determinant condition $\det(T)\varsigma(\det T)=1$ and the inversion $T^{-1}=T^{*}$ on the group; the embedding of the unitary slice by left multiplication; the polynomial nature of the equations and the algebraic-group reading. -->

<a href="articles_maths/hermitian-forms-over-algebras-and-norms.html">Hermitian Forms over Algebras and Norms</a>
<!-- the norm map $x\mapsto xx^{*}$ and its polarisation as the trace form; the quaternion norm $a^{2}-\alpha b^{2}-\beta c^{2}+\alpha\beta d^{2}$ and its multiplicativity; the reduced norm of a central simple algebra, whose polarisation $\tau(X\operatorname{adj}(Y))$ is distinct from the Hermitian form $\tau(XY^{*})$; the blade form of a Clifford algebra and its failure of multiplicativity; the boundary between the algebraic norm and the norm that defines a distance. -->

<a href="articles_maths/hermitian-clifford-algebras.html">Hermitian Clifford Algebras</a>
<!-- the real and the imaginary parts of a Hermitian form, $h=g+\mathrm{i}\omega$, and the Clifford algebra of $g=\operatorname{Re}h$; the impossibility of a Clifford relation for the sesquilinear form itself and the symplectic role of $\omega$; the dagger and the blade form on the complexified algebra; the unitary slice and the Pin and Spin groups; the CAR algebra named for the infinite-dimensional case. -->

the graph $J_n(G)$ on the tiles of a level as the Schreier graph of the nucleus, the limit space as the rescaled limit of the graphs $J_n(G)$ in the sense of the approximation theorem, and as the Gromov boundary of the self-similarity complex; the dimension theorem, the covering dimension equal to the asymptotic dimension of the orbital graphs and equal to one exactly for the faithful quotients of the contracting self-similar virtually free groups; the examples, the circle for the adding machine with the doubling map, the segment for the Grigorchuk and the dihedral groups with the tent map, the dendrite of the Fabrykowski–Gupta group, the Sierpiński gasket and the Julia sets of the sub-hyperbolic rational maps; <!-- an involutive topological ring, that is a topological ring with a continuous involution, an anti-automorphism of order two; continuity is a genuine hypothesis, free for the discrete and the indiscrete topology, for the identity, and for an involution that preserves the ideal of a linear topology, and failing on $\mathbb{R}[x]$ with the $(x)$-adic topology for $f(x)\mapsto f(b-x)$ with $b\neq0$ and on $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$ with the topology from $\mathbb{R}$ for the conjugation; the fixed and the skew sets are closed, being equalizers, so a dense fixed set forces the trivial involution, and closedness is the whole gain, the fixed set of a continuous anti-automorphism being closed without being a subring; the averaging map is continuous when $2$ is invertible and makes the fixed set a retract, so that the additive group splits topologically into the fixed and the skew parts; the $I$-adic criterion $\sigma(I)^m\subseteq I$ gives continuity whenever the involution preserves the ideal defining the topology, and the involution then extends to a continuous involution of the $I$-adic completion, whose fixed set is the closure of the fixed set when $2$ is invertible, as in $\mathbb{Z}_p[i]=\mathbb{Z}_p[X]/(X^2+1)$ with $X\mapsto-X$ and $\mathbb{R}[[x]]$ with $f(x)\mapsto f(-x)$; a $\sigma$-stable closed ideal gives a Hausdorff quotient carrying the involution, whose fixed set can be strictly larger than the image of the fixed set, as $\mathbb{Z}[i]/(2)$ shows, while the completion introduces no such new fixed element; on a topological field the fixed field of a continuous involution is a closed subfield of index two and a topological field in the subspace topology with open unit group, on an ordered field the identity is the only monotone involution and every nontrivial one is non-monotone, and $\mathbb{C}$ with the usual topology and the conjugation is the model continuous case. **An additional structure on the topological ring, not a rung of any chain; it stands immediately after *Topological Rings and Fields*, whose $I$-adic topologies, linear topologies, neighbourhoods of zero and completions it uses, and before *Absolute Values, Valuations and Completions*, which owns the $p$-adic fields and the valuation topologies that are named here and not used.** -->

the closure of a stable set and the kernel of a continuous morphism; the product algebra with the involution $\sigma\times\tau$, and the exchange involution on $A\times A^{\mathrm{op}}$ whose symmetric part is the diagonal, a subalgebra exactly when $A$ is commutative; the $\mathrm{C}^*$-case, where the involution of a $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra is isometric and determines the norm, $\lVert a\rVert^2=\lVert a^*a\rVert=r(a^*a)$, so that a *-algebra carries at most one $\mathrm{C}^*$-norm and a unital *-homomorphism of unital $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebras is contractive; <!-- the symmetry $J$ that splits an indefinite form into its positive and its negative parts; the Gram operator; the equivalence of the indefinite and the definite pairings; the passage to the Krein space of the bilinear degree-2 form category, named and deferred. -->

### Operator Theory

<a href="articles_maths/the-adjoint-under-a-hermitian-form.html">The Adjoint under a Hermitian Form</a>
<!-- the adjoint of a bounded operator with respect to the Hermitian form $h$; the anti-automorphism $T\mapsto T^{\dagger}$; the two-slot adjoint of a conjugate-linear operator; the self-adjoint and the normal operators; the relation to *Hermitian Adjoints on a Hermitian Algebra* of the bilinear layer. -->

<a href="articles_maths/unitary-and-isometric-operators-of-the-form.html">Unitary and Isometric Operators of the Form</a>
<!-- the operators preserving the form, $h(Tx,Ty)=h(x,y)$; the unitary group and the isometry group; the indefinite case and the Krein isometries; the relation to the unitary group of the elements. -->

<a href="articles_maths/self-adjoint-and-skew-operators-of-the-form.html">Self-Adjoint and Skew Operators of the Form</a>
<!-- the splitting of the operator algebra into the self-adjoint and the skew-adjoint part of the adjoint, $T=\tfrac12(T+T^{\dagger})+\tfrac12(T-T^{\dagger})$; the sign rule and the three product relations; the skew part as the Lie algebra of the unitary group and the self-adjoint part as a special Jordan algebra; the exponential and the Cayley transform; the regular representation and the indefinite transport $T^{\dagger}=JT^{*}J$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-spectra-of-self-adjoint-operators-of-the-form.html">The Spectra of Self-Adjoint Operators of the Form</a>
<!-- the finite-dimensional spectral theorem in the definite case: the $h$-orthonormal diagonalisation, the real spectrum, the spectral decomposition and the functional calculus; the min-max principle and the Rayleigh quotient; the norm identity $\|T\|=\rho(T)$; the positivity criterion $T$ positive $\iff$ the spectrum in $[0,\infty)$ and the positive square root; the imaginary spectrum of the skew-adjoint operators and the unit circle of the unitary ones; the invariance under the unitary group; the failure in the indefinite case with the hyperbolic witness. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-polar-decomposition-of-an-operator-of-the-form.html">The Polar Decomposition of an Operator of the Form</a>
<!-- the modulus $|T|=(T^{\dagger}T)^{1/2}$ and the phase $U$ with $U(|T|x)=Tx$; the decomposition $T=U|T|$ with the partial-isometry projections, the unitary case and the uniqueness; the obstruction in the indefinite case, the hyperbolic operator whose modulus would be $\mathrm{i}$ times the identity. -->

<a href="articles_maths/unitary-equivalence-and-congruence-of-operators-of-the-form.html">Unitary Equivalence and Congruence of Operators of the Form</a>
<!-- the conjugation $T\mapsto UTU^{\dagger}$ with its invariant the spectrum and the congruence $h\mapsto h\circ(C\times C)$ with its invariant the inertia; the Gram matrix transformation $H\mapsto C^{T}H\varsigma(C)$ and Sylvester's law; the unitary group as the stabiliser of the form; the transport $T\mapsto C^{-1}TC$ of the operator theory, and the failure of compatibility under a general congruence, preserved only by a $*$-automorphism. -->

<a href="articles_maths/completely-positive-maps-of-a-sesqualgebra-with-a-form.html">Completely Positive Maps of a Sesqualgebra with a Form</a>
<!-- the positive maps of the cone of the Hermitian squares and the amplification by the form on $M_n(A)$; the Hermitian sandwich $\Theta_a(x)=axa^{*}$ as the completely positive map of Kraus rank one; Choi's theorem and the Kraus form in the matrix model; the transpose as the positive and not completely positive witness; the unital and the unitary channels as the inner automorphisms. -->

### * Theory

<a href="articles_maths/the-completion-of-a-sesqualgebra-with-a-form.html">The Completion of a Sesqualgebra with a Form</a>
<!-- the completion with respect to the norm of the form; the extension of the product, of the involution and of the form; the universal property; the recovery of the form and the collapse at $\varsigma=\mathrm{id}$. -->

<!-- the Euclidean form $(x,y)=\sum_I a_Ib_I$ with orthonormal blades; the algebra as a finite-dimensional Hilbert space over a definite real form; the completion in infinite dimension carrying the canonical anticommutation relations; the boundedness of the multiplication operators with $\|xy\|\le 2^{n/2}\|x\|\|y\|$ and the non-submultiplicativity of the norm; Cauchy-Schwarz, the compact unit ball and the positive cone; the metric layer of *The Blade Form and the Hermitian Structure with Hermitian Adjoint*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-modular-structure-of-a-hermitian-algebra.html">The Modular Structure of a Hermitian Algebra</a>

## Analysis on Algebras

### Theory

<a href="articles_maths/hypercomplex-analysis.html">Hypercomplex Analysis</a>
<!-- what becomes of analyticity when the ground algebra is no longer a field: the obstructions, non-commutativity, zero divisors, a one-sided module structure and the dimension; the ambiguity of the derivative defined by a difference quotient, and why it is over-determined; the two notions that survive, holomorphy inside a commutative subalgebra and regularity with respect to a first-order operator; the Cauchy–Riemann operator $D=\sum_i e_i\partial_i$ as the generalisation of $\bar\partial$, its square as the Laplacian, and the class of regular functions it defines; the general form of the Cauchy integral formula and the hypotheses that must replace the classical ones, with the failure of Morera, Liouville and the maximum principle in each setting; the parallel structure of the theory for $\mathbb{C}$, the split complex numbers, the dual numbers, $\mathbb{H}$ and the split biquaternions, with forward references to the per-system articles; the role of the Clifford algebra in the construction of the operator. -->

<a href="articles_maths/regularity-and-the-cauchy-riemann-operator.html">Regularity and the Cauchy–Riemann Operator</a>
<!-- the first-order operator $D$ assembled from a frame of the algebra, and the class of functions it annihilates; the classical Cauchy–Riemann equations in $\mathbb{C}$, their generalisation and the several distinct meanings the equation $Df=0$ takes once multiplication is one-sided; monogenic and regular functions; the relation between regularity and holomorphy inside a commutative subalgebra; the square of the operator as the Laplacian, and the harmonicity of regular functions; the Cauchy integral formula and the hypotheses that replace the classical ones; the mean value property, the maximum principle and Liouville's theorem, with the systems in which each fails; the Fischer and Stokes decompositions; forward references to the per-system analysis articles. -->

<a href="articles_maths/clifford-analysis.html">Clifford Analysis</a>
<!-- the analysis of functions with values in a Clifford algebra; the Dirac operator and monogenic functions; the Cauchy integral formula; the relation to the Clifford algebras of Part II; the monogenic, polymonogenic and shifted theories; the Hermitean refinement, with the four Hermitean Dirac operators, the simultaneous null solutions and the circulant matrix of Cauchy kernels; the measure-theoretic boundary theory, with the Federer normal, the Cauchy and Hilbert transforms on Ahlfors–David regular surfaces, the Plemelj calculus and the complementary projections, the removable singularities, and the $d$-summable fractal boundaries on which the transform is rebuilt from the Teodorescu transform and a Whitney extension, with the approximate dimension in the solvability condition. -->

<a href="articles_maths/geometric-calculus-and-the-vector-derivative.html">Geometric Calculus and the Vector Derivative</a>
<!-- the vector derivative $\partial=\sum_ie^i\partial_i$ and the reciprocal basis; $\partial x=n$; the split $\partial F=\partial\cdot F+\partial\wedge F$ into divergence and curl; the Leibniz rule with the bracket convention; the fundamental theorem $\int_M\underline{\partial}F\,dV=\int_{\partial M}dS\,F$ and its grades, Gauss, Stokes and the fundamental theorem of calculus; $\partial^2=\Delta$ and the monogenic functions; the Green's function and the Cauchy integral formula; the exterior derivative and the codifferential; the Dirac-type and Maxwell-type equations. -->

<a href="articles_maths/clifford-modules-and-the-twisted-cauchy-riemann-operator.html">Clifford Modules and the Twisted Cauchy–Riemann Operator</a>
<!-- Clifford modules and their structure; the spinor module; the twisted Cauchy–Riemann operator acting on a Clifford module; the resulting elliptic complex and the computation of its index. -->

<a href="articles_maths/fueter-theory.html">Fueter Theory</a>
<!-- Fueter's theory of regular functions of a quaternionic variable; the Cauchy–Fueter integral formula; the relation to the hypercomplex analysis of this part. -->

<a href="articles_maths/hypercomplex-integration.html">Hypercomplex Integration</a>
<!-- integration of functions with values in a hypercomplex algebra; the contour integral and the obstruction to a Cauchy theorem when the algebra is not a field; the splitting into idempotent or characteristic coordinates, which reduces the integral to two ordinary integrals; the residue theory that survives and the systems where it degenerates; path independence and the role of the zero divisors; the relation to the measure-theoretic integral, which supplies the underlying integration of an algebra-valued function and is treated in the general theory; the Cauchy integral formula as the boundary form of the theory; forward references to the per-system integration articles for $\mathbb{C}$, the split complex numbers, the dual numbers, $\mathbb{H}$, $\mathbb{B}$ and the split biquaternions. -->

<a href="articles_maths/riemann-boundary-value-problems-and-singular-integral-equations.html">Riemann Boundary Value Problems and Singular Integral Equations</a>
<!-- the boundary value problem with a jump that the Cauchy transform and the Plemelj formulas lead to; sectionally regular functions and the classes by order at infinity; the Riemann problem $f^+=f^-B+h$ and the Plemelj projectors $P_\pm=\tfrac12(I\pm S)$; the canonical factor for a constant coefficient, the reduction to the trivial jump and the explicit solution in the classes $\mathcal{R}_{-1}$ and $\mathcal{R}_0$; the order of the factors when the algebra is not commutative; the singular integral equation of Cauchy type, its factorisation through the projectors and its split equivalence with the Riemann problem, with the closed-form solution and the degenerate coefficients; the index of a variable coefficient, the canonical function and the counting of solutions in the classical complex case; the complex, quaternion and Clifford instances, with the conventions of the Clifford source; the corpus's boundary-value criterion as the case $B=1$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/harmonic-analysis-over-hypercomplex-systems.html">Harmonic Analysis over Hypercomplex Systems</a>
<!-- the transform theory a hypercomplex algebra supports, and why it depends on the underlying additive group rather than on the multiplication; the Fourier transform on $\mathbb{C}$, on the split complex numbers, on the dual numbers and on the quaternion groups; the discrete and continuous cases; convolution and the algebra it defines; the Plancherel and Paley–Wiener theorems; the Laplace, Hilbert, Mellin and Radon transforms; the Calderón–Zygmund theory of singular integrals; the obstruction in the non-commutative and zero-divisor cases, and the reduction to the factor algebra; forward references to the per-system harmonic analysis articles. -->

<a href="articles_maths/dirac-differential-operators.html">Dirac Differential Operators</a>
<!-- the differential theory of Dirac operators: the analysis of the family of Dirac-type operators; self-adjointness, the domain and the closure, the spectrum and the compact resolvent, and the index of the chiral part; the relation to the algebraic and topological operator of Part II and to the spin geometry and index theory of Part IV. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-dirac-kahler-equation.html">The Dirac–Kähler Equation</a>
<!-- the multivector Dirac equation $(d-\delta+m)\Phi=0$; the exterior derivative, the codifferential $\delta=-\star d\star$ and the Laplace–de Rham operator, $(d-\delta)^2=\square$; the Clifford product $dx_\mu\vee dx_\nu=dx_\mu\wedge dx_\nu+\delta_{\mu\nu}$; the decomposition into four Dirac equations through the basis change $Z$ and the internal $\mathrm{SO}(2,4)$ symmetry; minimal coupling; the simplicial discretization and the equivalence to staggered fermions; the harmonic-form zero modes; the curved-spacetime failure of the fourfold split; the relation to the biquaternion algebra, the even part $\mathrm{Cl}_{1,3}^+=\mathbb{B}$ contained in the multivector and the oddness of $d-\delta$ that prevents a restriction to it. -->

<a href="articles_maths/holomorphic-functional-calculus.html">Holomorphic Functional Calculus</a>
<!-- the holomorphic functional calculus for a Banach algebra; the relation to the Banach algebras of Part II and to the spectral theory of operators. -->

<a href="articles_maths/cyclic-cohomology.html">Cyclic Cohomology</a>
<!-- cyclic cohomology as the dual of cyclic homology; the pairing with K-theory and the Chern character in its cyclic form; the relation to the cyclic homology of Part I and to the K-theory of Part II and the index theory of Part IV. -->

## Geometry on Groups

### Theory

<a href="articles_maths/the-three-two-dimensional-algebras-and-the-three-kinds-of-rotation.html">The Three Two-Dimensional Algebras and the Three Kinds of Rotation</a>
<!-- the same vector space $\mathbb{R}^2$ carries three distinct algebra structures, and the relation of the generator to $1$ selects the geometry: $\mathbb{C}$ with $i^2=-1$ gives the elliptic rotation and the compact group $U(1)\cong SO(2)$; the split complex numbers with $j^2=+1$ give the hyperbolic rotation and $SO(1,1)$; the dual numbers with $\epsilon^2=0$ give the parabolic rotation and the shear. For each: the units, the norm preserved, the parametrisation, the orbit of a point, and the fixed lines. Why a rotation implemented by multiplication needs exactly two dimensions and a multiplicative norm, why dimension three forces a non-commutative algebra, and how the sign of the square of the generator selects a definite, an indefinite or a degenerate geometry. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-rotation-group-and-orientation.html">The Rotation Group and Orientation</a>
<!-- the rotation group $SO(V,Q)$ as the kernel of the determinant on $O(V,Q)$; orientation of a space and of a form; rotations versus reflections and the Cartan–Dieudonné parity; the definite case and the notion of angle; the plane case $SO(2)$ as the unit circle; the rotation group of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and its axis; the normal form as a sequence of planar rotation blocks, quoted up to conjugation in $O(V,Q)$ with the finer classes in $SO(V,Q)$ named. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-unitary-and-symplectic-groups.html">The Unitary and Symplectic Groups</a>
<!-- the classical families from a form: $O(V,Q)$ from a symmetric bilinear form, $U(V,h)$ from a Hermitian form, $Sp(V,\omega)$ from an alternating form; the isometries of each type; $U(n)$ and $SU(n)$; the symplectic group $Sp(2n)$; the relation to $GL$, $SL$ and the quaternionic case; the four families $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$. -->

## Fractal Geometry

### Theory

<a href="articles_maths/fractal-geometry.html">Fractal Geometry</a>
<!-- fractals and their properties; the Hausdorff dimension; the relation to the metric geometry of this part and to the dynamical systems of Part III. -->

<a href="articles_maths/rectifiability-and-the-geometry-of-fractal-curves.html">Rectifiability and the Geometry of Fractal Curves</a>
<!-- rectifiable sets and curves; the arc length against the Hausdorff measure, and the dimension of a rectifiable set is one; the non-rectifiable curves, the variation and the finite-length case; the Koch curve and the snowflake as the computed examples; the relation to *Geometric Measure Theory* of this part. -->

<a href="articles_maths/fractal-trees-and-dendrites.html">Fractal Trees and Dendrites</a>
<!-- tree-like fractals and dendrites; the local cut points, the branching points and the ends; the self-similar trees and their tilings; the dendrite of the Fabrykowski–Gupta group and the tree-like Julia sets as the examples, with their limit spaces cited to *Limit Spaces and Schreier Graphs*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-geometry-of-the-julia-sets.html">The Geometry of the Julia Sets</a>
<!-- the Julia set and the Fatou set; the local connectivity and the case of a connected filled Julia set, with the external rays and the landing theorem; the dimension and the measure of the Julia sets, and the hyperbolic and parabolic cases; the Mandelbrot set as parameter space, its connectedness and the open local-connectivity question; the dynamics itself is Part III's and the ergodic theory of the Julia set too; the relation to the limit space of the iterated monodromy group of Part II. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-dimension-of-the-boundary-of-a-hyperbolic-group.html">The Dimension of the Boundary of a Hyperbolic Group</a>
<!-- the Gromov boundary of a hyperbolic group as a fractal, with the visual metric and the Hausdorff dimension of the boundary; the Patterson–Sullivan measure and the critical exponent, their equality in the cocompact case; the dimension as a quasi-isometry invariant and its behaviour under the Kleinian and the free case; the boundary of a surface group and of a free group; the group theory is Part II's, cited to *Hyperbolic Groups* and *Geometric Group Theory*. -->

### Operator Theory

<a href="articles_maths/projections-of-a-fractal-and-the-dimension.html">Projections of a Fractal and the Dimension</a>
<!-- the orthogonal projection of a fractal onto a line as an operator and the Marstrand–Mattila theorem, that for almost every direction the dimension of the projection is the minimum of the dimension and one; the exceptional set of directions, of dimension zero, and the sharpness; the slicing theorem for the section of the set by a line; the application to the distance set below. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-distance-set-of-a-fractal.html">The Distance Set of a Fractal</a>
<!-- the set of distances realised by the pairs of a fractal; the Falconer distance problem, that a set of dimension exceeding one half has a distance set of positive measure, with the dimension thresholds and the partial resolutions; the arithmetic nature of the distance set; the relation to the projection theorem above. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-hutchinson-operator-and-its-adjoint.html">The Hutchinson Operator and Its Adjoint</a>
<!-- the Hutchinson operator on the complete metric space of compact sets, its contraction and its unique fixed point, the attractor; the adjoint action on the space of probability measures, the pushforward under the contractions, and the fixed point as the self-similar measure; the duality between the attractor and the measure; the operator form of the iterated function systems of *Fractal Analysis*. -->

### * Theory

<a href="articles_maths/symmetric-fractals-and-the-involution.html">Symmetric Fractals and the Involution</a>
<!-- a fractal carrying an involutive isometry; the fixed set, which is again a fractal, and the exchanged pairs of points; the quotient by the involution and its dimension; the symmetric self-similar sets, the segment, the symmetric Cantor set and the symmetric gasket, and their tilings; the comparison with the reversible iterated function systems of *Fractal Analysis*. -->

### * Operator Theory

<a href="articles_maths/the-involution-on-the-space-of-compact-sets-and-the-symmetric-attractor.html">The Involution on the Space of Compact Sets and the Symmetric Attractor</a>
<!-- the space of nonempty compact sets with the Hausdorff metric, and the involutive isometry it acquires from a symmetry of the ambient space; the fixed compact sets and the symmetric attractor as a fixed point of the involution; the commutation of the involution with the Hutchinson operator and the existence of a symmetric fixed point; the adjoint action on the measures and the symmetric self-similar measure. -->

## Complexoid Algebraic Structures

<!-- the structures the complex algebra carries beside the field; the field itself stays in Complex Numbers. -->

<a href="articles_maths/introduction-to-the-complexoid-algebraic-structures.html">Introduction to the Complexoid Algebraic Structures</a>
<!-- what the complex space carries beside the field: the two products, the two forms and their algebraic norms, the ternary product, the subspace lattice and the two matrix models; the entry point of this category. -->

### Generalities

<a href="articles_maths/the-complexoid-as-a-vector-space-over-r.html">The Complexoid as a Vector Space over $\mathbb{R}$</a>
<!-- the complex numbers read as a one- and a two-dimensional space: over $\mathbb{R}$, the underlying $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the basis $1,i$, the doubling of the dimension, the complex structure $J$, which is multiplication by $i$, with $J^2=-\mathrm{id}$, and the contrast with complexification, which is not the space but its sum with its conjugate; over $\mathbb{C}$, the one-dimensional space over itself, with the self-duality of the one-dimensional space and the absence of a proper complex subspace against the two real subspaces the underlying real space retains; and the real-linear maps that are complex-linear, satisfying $TJ=JT$, against those that are conjugate-linear, satisfying $SJ=-JS$, with the two block shapes they give. The two products are *The Two Products of the Complexoid Space*; the general construction is *The Realification and the Effect of the Change of Scalars on the Complexoid*, below this article in this category. -->

<a href="articles_maths/remarkable-subspaces-of-the-complexoid-and-the-two-forms.html">Remarkable Subspaces of the Complexoid and the Two Forms</a>
<!-- the two involutions, the identity and complex conjugation, and the two decompositions they produce, the degenerate $\mathbb{C}=\mathbb{C}\oplus\{0\}$ of the identity and the content-bearing $\mathbb{C}=\mathbb{R}_{\mathbb{C}}\oplus i\mathbb{R}_{\mathbb{C}}$ of conjugation, with the projections $A\mapsto\frac12(A+\bar A)$ and $A\mapsto\frac12(A-\bar A)$; the real subspace $\mathbb{R}_{\mathbb{C}}$ and the imaginary subspace $i\mathbb{R}_{\mathbb{C}}$, their bases and dimensions, the subalgebra and field structure of the real subspace and the failure of the imaginary subspace to be closed under multiplication; the two products read on the four pairs of subspaces, with the same closure table, the sign the bar gives the second slot on the imaginary line, and the commutator that vanishes identically; and the units, idempotents and isotropic elements each subspace holds. The subspaces are owned here; the algebra is *Complex Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-matrix-element-representations-of-the-complexoid.html">The Matrix Element Representations of the Complexoid</a>
<!-- the complex numbers in the real matrix algebras: the regular representation in $M_2(\mathbb{R})$, its determinant $a^2+a'^2$ and trace $2a$ identifying the two algebraic norms, the invertible elements with the invertible matrices of this shape and the unit circle with the rotation group; and the $4\times4$ model, its commutant, the determinant and trace again as the two norms, and its extension of the $2\times2$ model by two nothing-adding dimensions. The two algebraic norms are *The Two Forms and the Two Algebraic Norms of the Complexoid Space*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-two-products-of-the-complexoid-space.html">The Two Products of the Complexoid Space</a>
<!-- the two products the complex space carries: the general plain bilinear product $AC$, the multiplication of the field, and the general plain sesquilinear product $A\overline{C}$, the derived operation of the algebra with its conjugate-linear involution; the collapse of the general settings to these two, the first slot carrying the identity on the commutative base; the two products on the coordinates, with their scalar parts and their vanishing vector parts; the relations between the two, $A\overline{C}=\overline{C\overline{A}}$ and the exchange of the two slots; the comparison, $\mathbb{C}$-linear in the first slot for both, $\mathbb{C}$-linear in the second for the bilinear product against conjugate-linear for the sesquilinear one, associativity and commutativity and the two-sided unit $1$ for $AC$ against non-associativity, conjugate-commutativity and the right-sided unit alone for $A\overline{C}$; the two products read on one and the same pair and set against each other, the conjugate of a product, the identities that hold for one and fail for the other, the property table of the two, the slots of the construction with the first empty and the second deciding the composition and the symmetry of the form, and the two pairings $B(A,C)=AC$ and $H(A,C)=A\overline{C}$ with the two adjoints of the ordinary and of the sesquilinear right multiplication, the transpose keeping the parameter against the adjoint conjugating it; and the two structures the two products define, the field under $AC$ and the sesqualgebra over $(\mathbb{C},\overline{\cdot})$ under $A\overline{C}$, with the antisymmetrised products collapsing to zero because the algebra is commutative. The multiplication of the field is *Complex Algebra*, which owns it; and the two forms carried by the two products are *The Two Forms and the Two Algebraic Norms of the Complexoid Space*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-two-forms-and-the-two-algebraic-norms-of-the-complexoid-space.html">The Two Forms and the Two Algebraic Norms of the Complexoid Space</a>
<!-- the two forms the products of *The Two Products of the Complexoid Space* carry, and their diagonals: the general plain bilinear form $B(A,C)=AC$, anisotropic with the realified signature $(1,1)$, and the general plain sesquilinear or Hermitian form $H(A,C)=A\overline{C}$, positive definite with the realified signature $(2,0)$; the two forms separated by their symmetry alone, $AC$ symmetric and $A\overline{C}$ conjugate-symmetric, both of Gram matrix $[1]$ over $\mathbb{C}$; the two algebraic norms, the diagonals $B(A)=A^{2}$, complex and anisotropic, and $H(A)=\lvert A\rvert^{2}$, real, positive definite and multiplicative; the two forms read on the two subspaces $\mathbb{R}_{\mathbb{C}}$ and $i\mathbb{R}_{\mathbb{C}}$, coinciding on the real line and opposite on the imaginary one, $B=H$ and $B=-H$, with the rank and the null set of each restriction; and the remark that one and the same function $H$ is both definite and multiplicative. The definite norm, its multiplicativity, the criterion of invertibility and the group of units are *Complex Norm and Invertibility*, below this article in this category. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-realification-and-the-effect-of-the-change-of-scalars-on-the-complexoid.html">The Realification and the Effect of the Change of Scalars on the Complexoid</a>
<!-- the realification of the complex numbers as the prototype of the general construction: the two scalar readings of the one algebra, over $\mathbb{C}$ and over $\mathbb{R}$, the doubling of the dimension, the complex structure $J$, which is multiplication by $i$, with $J^2=-\mathrm{id}$, and the criteria $TJ=JT$ and $SJ=-JS$ for the two kinds of real-linear map and the two block shapes they give; the two rules by which a symmetric bilinear form realifies to the split signature $(n,n)$ and a Hermitian form doubles its inertia, read on the two forms of the complex space and giving the signatures $(1,1)$ and $(2,0)$; the dictionary of the complex statements against the real ones, the trap of the count of operations on the realification, and the passage from the complex space to the two-dimensional real plane. The general construction is *The Realification and the Effect of the Change of Scalars*, below this chapter, of which this article is the two-dimensional case. -->

### The General Plain Sesqualgebra (GPS) over $\mathbb{C}$

<a href="articles_maths/the-sesquilinear-product-of-the-complexoid-space.html">The Sesquilinear Product of the Complexoid Space</a>
<!-- the sesquilinear product of the complex space, the second of the two products, with its conjugate-linear second slot: the class of the product, the absence of a two-sided unit and the two one-sided actions; the associator, which does not vanish but is confined to the sesquilinear shape, and the ternary product $\{A,B,C\}=A\overline{B}C$ it defines, with its outer and Hermitian symmetries, its contractions to the two binary products, the Jordan triple identity, the $J^{*}$-algebra structure and the flatness on the commutative base; the left and right multiplications, $L_A$ and $R_A$, which fail to coincide and generate an opposite monoid; the sesquilinear sandwich $A\mapsto BA\overline{C}$, its decomposition into a pair of one-sided multiplications and its adjoint with respect to the Hermitian form $H$; and the commutator $A\overline{C}-C\overline{A}$, which is the imaginary part of $H$, with its symmetrisation recovering the real part and its Jacobi identity holding because the space is two-dimensional. The product is *The Two Products of the Complexoid Space*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-hermitian-form-and-the-positivity-of-the-complexoid-algebra.html">The Hermitian Form and the Positivity of the Complexoid Algebra</a>
<!-- the Hermitian side of the second product: the canonical Hermitian form on the regular module, $H(A,C)=A\overline{C}$, its conjugate symmetry, its linearity in the first slot and conjugate-linearity in the second, its Gram matrix, and the Cauchy-Schwarz and triangle inequalities as statements of the form; the positivity, the Hermitian cone, which is the ray of the non-negative reals, the order it defines and its completeness, which makes the algebra the Hilbert algebra of rank one; the Hermitian modules, free and definite, classified by rank alone, with the group of linear maps preserving the form as their unitary group; the classification of Hermitian forms by rank and signature over the reals and the Witt group of the definite forms; and the comparison with the indefinite case, where the cone is not a ray. -->

The norm criterion is a form and a distance and belongs to *Split-Complex Norm and Invertibility*. -->

#### Properties of Split-Complex Algebra over $\mathbb{R}$

<a href="articles_maths/split-complex-norm-and-invertibility.html">Split-Complex Norm and Invertibility</a>
<!-- the norm $N(q+jq')=q^2-q'^2$ and its multiplicativity; the isotropic cone as the zero divisors, so the form is not definite; the invertibility criterion $N\neq0$; the group of units, its four components and its non-compactness; the three-way classification; the modulus $\sqrt{|N|}$ and its two regimes. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-classes-of-element-of-the-split-complex-algebra.html">The Classes of Element of the Split-Complex Algebra</a>
<!-- the hub of the classes of element of the split-complex ring: the classes owned elsewhere, named with their pointers, the zero divisors of *Split-Complex Zero Divisors*, the idempotents and projections of *Split-Complex Idempotents and Projections*, and the ideals and the Peirce decomposition of *Split-Complex Ideals and Peirce Decomposition*; and the classes this article owns: the nilpotents, of which $0$ is the only one, the ring being reduced although not a field; the square roots of minus one, zero and plus one, the two of minus one being $\pm j$ in the non-scalar position with no central root; the square roots of a general element, which exist for an element whose two idempotent coordinates are non-negative and fail off that cone; the square-zero elements, the zero element alone; and the order cone of squares and its relation to the null cone. The ring property behind all of them is *The Specificities of the Split-Complex Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/split-complex-zero-divisors.html">Split-Complex Zero Divisors</a>
<!-- definition and criterion; the zero divisor set as the null cone $\{q^2=q'^2\}$ and the two null lines $\mathbb{R}(1\pm j)$; the structure of the two families; the relation to the idempotents and to the isotropic cone; the distribution of the zero divisors. The criterion by the vanishing of the norm needs a distance and is in *Split-Complex Norm and Invertibility*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/split-complex-idempotents-and-projections.html">Split-Complex Idempotents and Projections</a>
<!-- the two nontrivial idempotents $\Pi_\pm=\tfrac{1}{2}(1\pm j)$ and the complementary pair; orthogonality, completeness and primitivity; the direct sum decomposition $\mathbb{D}=\mathbb{R}\Pi_+\oplus\mathbb{R}\Pi_-$ and the algebra isomorphism $\mathbb{D}\cong\mathbb{R}\oplus\mathbb{R}$; the zero divisors as the off-diagonal elements in the idempotent basis; the idempotents as projections. -->

<a href="articles_maths/split-complex-ideals-and-peirce-decomposition.html">Split-Complex Ideals and Peirce Decomposition</a>
<!-- ideals in a commutative algebra; the two-sided ideals and the two minimal ideals $\mathbb{R}\Pi_\pm$; the Peirce decomposition of $\mathbb{D}$; the idempotents as matrix units in the idempotent basis; the lattice of ideals; the failure of simplicity and the reason, against the simplicity of the complex field. -->

<a href="articles_maths/eigenvalue-decomposition-of-a-split-complex-number.html">Eigenvalue Decomposition of a Split-Complex Number</a>
<!-- the eigenvalue decomposition of a split-complex number: the spectrum $\{\lambda_+,\lambda_-\}=\{q+q',q-q'\}$ from the invertibility criterion; the characteristic polynomial $p_Q(X)=X^2-2qX+\langle Q\rangle_{*}=(X-\lambda_+)(X-\lambda_-)$ and the discriminant $4q'^2$; the eigenprojections $\Pi_\pm=\tfrac12(1\pm j)$ with $Q\Pi_\pm=\lambda_\pm\Pi_\pm=(q\pm q')\Pi_\pm$ and the Lagrange–Sylvester formulas; the decomposition $Q=\lambda_+\Pi_++\lambda_-\Pi_-=(q+q')\Pi_++(q-q')\Pi_-$, its uniqueness up to the exchange of labels and its semisimplicity for $q'\neq0$; the Peirce decomposition relative to $\Pi_+$, with vanishing off-diagonal corners, diagonal part the whole algebra and centraliser all of $\mathbb{D}$; the polynomial calculus, the powers, the inverse and the group isomorphism $\mathbb{D}^\times\cong\mathbb{R}^\times\times\mathbb{R}^\times$; the algebraic fibre and the coordinate change, with the integral eigenvalue lattice and its parity-matched image in the coefficient coordinates; the hyperbolic polar form $Q=r(\cosh t+j\sinh t)$, with $\lambda_\pm=re^{\pm t}$ on the identity component and $\lambda_\pm=-r e^{\pm t}$ on the opposite timelike component, and the spacelike values $\lambda_+=\varepsilon re^{\varepsilon s}$, $\lambda_-=-\varepsilon re^{-\varepsilon s}$; and the degenerate regimes, the scalar case with its one-term eigenprojection and unique two-term refinement, the zero-divisor case $Q=2q\Pi_\pm$ with eigenvalues $2q$ and $0$, and the absence of nonzero nilpotents, the algebra being reduced. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-specificities-of-the-split-complex-algebra.html">The Specificities of the Split-Complex Algebra</a>
<!-- the properties that single out the split-complex ring: it is commutative and associative, of dimension two over $\mathbb{R}$, reduced, so that its only nilpotent is $0$, but not a field, with exactly two nontrivial idempotents $\Pi_\pm$ and a null cone of zero divisors; it is isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}\oplus\mathbb{R}$, hence semisimple and not simple, its only ideals being the two idempotent lines, and it is the split analogue of the complex field, obtained by changing the sign of the square; the consequences for the classes of element, the non-emptiness of the zero-divisor and idempotent classes that are empty on the complex field, and the degeneracy of the matrix models; and the comparison with the complex case, a field and simple. The classes are *The Classes of Element of the Split-Complex Algebra*; the complex specificities are *The Specificities of the Complex Algebra*, in the category *Complex Numbers*. -->
