#### Properties of Quaternion Algebra over $\mathbb{R}$

##### Basic Properties

<a href="articles_maths/introduction-to-the-quaternion-algebra.html">Introduction to the Quaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the general plain bilinear product read as a multiplication and the algebra it defines: the rule on the four real coordinates and its well-definedness; the sixteen products of the basis; bilinearity and the determination by the values on the basis pairs; associativity; the two-sided unit $e_0$; the division property, every nonzero element invertible, hence no zero divisor and no nonzero nilpotent and no idempotent but $0$ and $e_0$; the centre as the scalar line; simplicity; the generators $e_1,e_2$ and the presentation; the subalgebra generated by one element; and the reading of the other five products as *The Algebraic Structures over the Quaternioid $\mathbb{R}$ Space*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/norm-and-invertibility-in-the-quaternion-algebra.html">Norm and Invertibility in the Quaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the quaternion norm $N(\tilde q)=\tilde q\,\tilde q^{\natural}$ and its multiplicativity; the positive definiteness and the absence of zero divisors; the invertibility criterion $q\neq0$, the division property; the group of units, a positive scale and a unit sphere; the three-way classification. -->

<a href="articles_maths/zero-divisors-of-the-quaternion-algebra.html">Zero Divisors of the Quaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the zero divisors of the general plain product over $\mathbb{R}$, which are the empty set: the criterion $\tilde q\tilde q^{\natural}=0$ and its collapse under the positive definite quaternion norm; the three-way classification, whose zero-divisor slot is empty and whose unit slot is the whole punctured algebra; the division property of $\mathbb{H}$; the two families of the complexified block, the pure nilpotents and the non-pure multiples of the idempotents, both empty over $\mathbb{R}$; and the reading on the centre and the vector subspace. The sibling classes are *Idempotents of the Quaternion Algebra* and *Nilpotents of the Quaternion Algebra*; the complexified counterpart is *Zero Divisors of the Quaternion Algebra*, and the annihilators are *Annihilators of the Quaternion Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/annihilators-of-the-quaternion-algebra.html">Annihilators of the Quaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the annihilators of the general plain product over $\mathbb{R}$: the left and the right multiplication $L_{\tilde p}\tilde x=\tilde p\tilde x$ and $R_{\tilde p}\tilde x=\tilde x\tilde p$, of trace $4p_0$, determinant $N(\tilde p)^2$ and characteristic polynomial $(t^2-2p_0t+N(\tilde p))^2$; the annihilator $\{0\}$ at every nonzero element and the whole space at the origin, the plain product being a division algebra over $\mathbb{R}$; the two sides coinciding trivially; the dichotomy that carries no more than the division property, against the biquaternion block's pair of annihilator planes on the cone; and the reading on the remarkable subspaces. The zero divisors are the empty set (*Zero Divisors*); the sibling annihilators are *Annihilators of the General Quaternionic Algebra*, *Annihilators of the Symmetric Plain Algebra* and *Annihilators of the Antisymmetric Plain Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/square-roots-of-one-and-the-idempotents-of-the-quaternion-algebra.html">Square Roots of One and the Idempotents of the Quaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the roots of $+1$ of the general plain product over $\mathbb{R}$ described by the scalar and vector split, the vector equation $2\xi_0\boldsymbol\xi=0$ leaving only the scalar equation on each branch, the two-point class $\pm e_0$ stated as such and no empty class occurring; the roots of $-1$ as a closing remark, the pure elements of the level set $\{N=1\}$ of the vector subspace, read from the same reduction because over $\mathbb{R}$ the centre has no element of square $-e_0$, so the sign cannot be flipped and the roots of $-1$ are not the image of the roots of $+1$, and used nowhere; the relation to the idempotents; the idempotents of the general plain product over $\mathbb{R}$, the equation $\tilde\pi(\tilde\pi-e_0)=0$ and the absence of zero divisors leaving exactly $0$ and $e_0$; the absence of nontrivial, orthogonal, complete and primitive families beyond the degenerate ones; the trivial Peirce decomposition, with Peirce spaces $\mathbb{H}$ and $\{0\}$ and no off-diagonal unit; the affine correspondence $\tilde\pi\mapsto2\tilde\pi-e_0$ with the two roots of $+e_0$, namely $\pm e_0$; the complementary idempotent $e_0-\tilde\pi$ with the orthogonality $0\cdot e_0=0$; no idempotent being a zero divisor and every idempotent being the origin or a unit; and the reading on the centre and the vector subspace, the two idempotents central and the vector subspace carrying the origin alone. The siblings are *Zero Divisors of the Quaternion Algebra* and *Square Roots of Zero and the Nilpotents of the Quaternion Algebra*; the roots of $0$ are the latter, the roots of $-1$ are the closing remark of this article, and the complexified counterpart is *Square Roots of One and the Idempotents of the Quaternion Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/square-roots-of-zero-and-the-nilpotents-of-the-quaternion-algebra.html">Square Roots of Zero and the Nilpotents of the Quaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the roots of $0$ of the general plain product over $\mathbb{R}$ described by the scalar and vector split, the scalar branch and the pure branch both returning the origin, the one-point class $\{0\}$ stated as such and no empty class occurring; the nilpotents of the general plain product over $\mathbb{R}$, the non-zero elements of square zero, of which there are none: the square $\tilde q^2=[q_0^2-|\mathbf q|^2]e_0+2q_0\mathbf q$ vanishes only at the origin, so the nilpotent class is empty and the nilpotent cone is the empty set, and there is no element of nilpotency index two or more; the criterion $q_0=0$ and $\mathbf q=0$; the index-two theorem, a vanishing power vanishing at the first step, with the square and the cube of a general element; the relation to the zero divisors, a non-zero nilpotent being a zero divisor with itself while the zero-divisor set is empty; the relation to the idempotents, the two classes meeting only at $0$; and the reading on the centre and the vector subspace, both carrying the origin alone. The sibling classes are *Zero Divisors of the Quaternion Algebra* and *Square Roots of One and the Idempotents of the Quaternion Algebra*; the complexified counterpart is *Square Roots of Zero and the Nilpotents of the Quaternion Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/square-roots-of-a-general-element-in-the-quaternion-algebra.html">Square Roots of a General Element in the Quaternion Algebra</a>

<a href="articles_maths/the-specificities-of-the-quaternion-algebra.html">The Specificities of the Quaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the properties that single out $\mathbb{H}$ among the six structures: associativity, the two-sided unit, the division property, so that the classes of the zero divisors, of the nonzero nilpotents and of the nontrivial idempotents are empty or two-point and have their own articles (*Zero Divisors*, *Idempotents* and *Nilpotents of the Quaternion Algebra*), their summaries folded here; the centre, the tensor decomposition, the Frobenius theorem; the real division algebras; and the isolation of this block among the six by the three generating operations. -->

### Comparisons with $\mathbb{H}$

<a href="articles_maths/zero-divisors-in-the-algebraic-structures-over-the-quaternioid-r-space.html">Zero Divisors in the Algebraic Structures over the Quaternioid $\mathbb{R}$ Space</a>

The cone of the biquaternion comparison group has no twin here, the quaternion norm being definite over $\mathbb{R}$; the annihilators read from the same products are *Annihilators in the Algebraic Structures over the Quaternioid $\mathbb{R}$ Space*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/annihilators-in-the-algebraic-structures-over-the-quaternioid-r-space.html">Annihilators in the Algebraic Structures over the Quaternioid $\mathbb{R}$ Space</a>
<!-- the annihilating elements of the three companion structures of the quaternion real space: the elements that kill every partner for a fixed product, the left, the right and the two-sided set of an element, the common kernel of the one-sided multiplications, which is the radical of the product and is distinguished from the radical of the associated form; the diagonal criterion, an element annihilating the space exactly when it annihilates the four units; the value $\{0\}$ for the general quaternionic product and the symmetric plain product; the scalar line $\mathbb{R}_{\mathbb{H}}$ for the plain cross product, the centre of the algebra and not the centre of the bracket, which is $\{0\}$; the three-row table, one row to a structure, each cell a sentence that gives the set and its reason; the coincidence of the two one-sided sets in all three, against the two exceptions of the biquaternion space, which appear only at an element of vanishing norm; and the comparison with the zero divisors, every element of the annihilating set other than the origin being a zero divisor of the same product. The zero divisors are *Zero Divisors in the Algebraic Structures over the Quaternioid $\mathbb{R}$ Space*; the radical of the forms is *The 2 Forms over the Quaternioid $\mathbb{R}$ Space*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/square-roots-of-one-and-the-idempotents-in-the-algebraic-structures-over-the-quaternioid-r-space.html">Square Roots of One and the Idempotents in the Algebraic Structures over the Quaternioid $\mathbb{R}$ Space</a>
<!-- the root of $+1$ read structure by structure in the three companion structures of the quaternion real space, with the roots of $-1$ in a closing remark, in the order and the section shape of *Square Roots of Minus One, Zero and Plus One* of the biquaternion comparison group: the root set of a central value as the solution of $\tilde\xi\star\tilde\xi=\lambda e_0$ with $\lambda$ real; the theorem that a root of $+1$ has $N=1$, hence is a unit with the two-sided inverse $\tilde\xi^{\natural}/N(\tilde\xi)$, with the decomposition $\mathbb{H}=\{0\}\cup\mathbb{H}^{\times}$ of the division algebra; the three structures one by one, product, square and root set of $+1$, each cited from its owner, the pair $\pm e_0$ for SPA, the sphere $S^3$ of the unit quaternions for GQA and no root of $+1$ for APA; the roots of $-1$, read against the roots of $+1$, the sphere $S^2$ of the pure unit quaternions for the plain square and the empty set for GQA and APA, no central imaginary existing over $\mathbb{R}$ to flip the sign; the three-row table of the root set of $+1$; the theorem that the algebra product and the general quaternionic product differ at $+1$ as they do at $-1$, with the remark that the word there is *differ* and not *coincide*, against the empty zero-divisor set they share; the value in coordinates; the two families of the plain reduction, the pair $\pm e_0$ in the centre; then the idempotents read across the three structures: the two-point set $\{0,e_0\}$ for SPA and GQA, the single origin for APA, the square operator, the halving map from the roots of $+1$ to the idempotents, the classification theorem and the collapse against the biquaternion case. The other values are *Square Roots of Zero and the Nilpotents in the Algebraic Structures over the Quaternioid $\mathbb{R}$ Space*; the general value is *Square Roots of a General Element in the Algebraic Structures over the Quaternioid $\mathbb{R}$ Space*; the empty zero-divisor set is *Zero Divisors in the Algebraic Structures over the Quaternioid $\mathbb{R}$ Space*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/square-roots-of-zero-and-the-nilpotents-in-the-algebraic-structures-over-the-quaternioid-r-space.html">Square Roots of Zero and the Nilpotents in the Algebraic Structures over the Quaternioid $\mathbb{R}$ Space</a>
<!-- the root of $0$ read structure by structure in the three companion structures of the quaternion real space, in the order and the section shape of *Square Roots of Minus One, Zero and Plus One* of the biquaternion comparison group: the root set of a central value as the solution of $\tilde\xi\star\tilde\xi=\lambda e_0$ with $\lambda$ real; the cone reading, the root set of $0$ a cone with the origin as its apex while the two signed values carry no apex; the theorem that a non-zero root of $0$ is a square-zero element and its own annihilator, with the decomposition $\mathbb{H}=\{0\}\cup\mathbb{H}^{\times}$ of the division algebra; the three structures one by one, product, square and root set of $0$, each cited from its owner, the whole space at $0$ for APA and the origin alone for SPA and GQA; the three-row table of the root sets; the theorem that the algebra product and the general quaternionic product agree at $0$, against the word *differ* at the two signed values, and the value in coordinates; the square-zero elements read across the three structures: the square-zero set as a solution set, $0$ allowed, and the nilpotent as a nonzero member; the origin alone for SPA, by the division property and the absence of a real isotropic direction, and for GQA, by the definiteness of the norm; the whole space for APA, by alternation; the three-row table; the classification theorem; and the comparison of the square-zero elements, the zero divisors and the roots of $0$, the three classes coinciding away from the origin only for the antisymmetric plain structure. The two signed values and the idempotents are *Square Roots of One and the Idempotents in the Algebraic Structures over the Quaternioid $\mathbb{R}$ Space*; the general value is *Square Roots of a General Element in the Algebraic Structures over the Quaternioid $\mathbb{R}$ Space*; the empty zero-divisor set is *Zero Divisors in the Algebraic Structures over the Quaternioid $\mathbb{R}$ Space*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/square-roots-of-a-general-element-in-the-algebraic-structures-over-the-quaternioid-r-space.html">Square Roots of a General Element in the Algebraic Structures over the Quaternioid $\mathbb{R}$ Space</a>
<!-- the root equation $\tilde\xi\star\tilde\xi=\lambda e_0$ at a general central value for the three companion structures: the two squares that group them, the plain square and the quaternion square; the sphere of radius $\sqrt{-\lambda}$ in the vector subspace, the origin and the two points $\pm\sqrt{\lambda}\,e_0$ for the plain square of SPA (and of the algebra product); the empty set at the negative values, the origin, and the sphere of radius $\sqrt{\lambda}$ of real dimension three for GQA; the whole space at $0$ and nothing elsewhere for APA; the three-row table of general $\lambda$; the root sets of $0$, the origin alone for SPA and GQA and the whole space for APA, the plain form being isotropic over $\mathbb{R}$ only at the origin; and the three existence classes, a root of every real value for SPA, of every non-negative value for GQA and of $0$ alone for APA, with the scaling that carries the root set of $\lambda$ to the root set of $\mu^{2}\lambda$. The named values and the idempotents are *Square Roots of One and the Idempotents in the Algebraic Structures over the Quaternioid $\mathbb{R}$ Space*, and the value $0$ and the nilpotents are *Square Roots of Zero and the Nilpotents in the Algebraic Structures over the Quaternioid $\mathbb{R}$ Space*. -->

#### Properties of the Biquaternion Algebra over $\mathbb{C}$

##### Basic Properties

<a href="articles_maths/norm-and-invertibility-in-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">Norm and Invertibility in the Biquaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the norm $N(\tilde{Q})=\tilde{Q}\bar{\tilde{Q}}=\sum_\mu Q_\mu^2$ and its multiplicativity; the polarisation $B(\tilde{P},\tilde{Q})=\sum_\mu P_\mu Q_\mu$ and the complex quadratic space it defines; the norm as the semi-norm and the audit of the norm axioms, of which only the sign axiom survives; the unique multiplicative real norm $r=\sqrt{|N|}=\sqrt{|\det\mathsf{M}_2|}$; the norm from the halves; the Euclidean norm read from the Hermitian form defined in *The 4 Forms over the Biquaternion $\mathbb{C}$ Space*; the real forms and their signatures $(4,4)$, $(1,1)$, $(3,3)$, $(4,0)$, $(0,4)$, $(1,3)$, $(3,1)$; the associated Clifford algebra; the invertibility criterion $N(\tilde{Q})\neq0$; left and right inverses and the inverse formula; the group of units; the three-way classification by the sign of the norm; the distribution of the invertible elements over the remarkable subspaces. This article absorbs the polarisation, the real forms and the Clifford algebra that formerly opened *Biquaternion Null Quadric and Projective Geometry*, since merged into *Biquaternion Topology*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/norm-and-invertibility-in-the-general-quaternionic-algebra.html">Norm and Invertibility in the General Quaternionic Algebra</a>
<!-- The general quaternionic bilinear product $\tilde P\star\tilde Q=\tilde P^{\natural}\tilde Q$ has a central square, $\tilde Q\star\tilde Q=N(\tilde Q)e_0$ with $N(\tilde Q)=\sum_\mu Q_\mu^2=Q_0^2+(\mathbf Q,\mathbf Q)$, and this scalar is the norm of the product: the same quadratic form as the norm of the plain algebra, with polar form the scalar coefficient $N(\tilde P,\tilde Q)=P_0Q_0+(\mathbf P,\mathbf Q)$ of the symmetrised product and with the multiplicative law $N(\tilde P\star\tilde Q)=N(\tilde P)N(\tilde Q)$. The product has the left unit $e_0$ and no right one, hence no two-sided unit, and the definition of the inverse, which requires one, applies to no element: there is no invertible element and no group of units of the quaternionic product. What survives is the pair of one-sided equations relative to $e_0$: both have the same unique solution, $(\tilde P^{-1})^{\natural}=\tilde P/N(\tilde P)$, exactly when $N(\tilde P)\neq0$, and neither has a solution when $N(\tilde P)=0$. The criterion is thus the norm, as for the plain product, and the elements of non-vanishing norm form the plain group of units $\mathbb{B}^{\times}$, closed under $\star$ and carrying the invertible left multiplications, without being a group of the product. On the quaternion and the anti-quaternion subspaces the norm is definite and every nonzero element is a unit of the plain product; on the centre, the vector, the Hermitian and the anti-Hermitian subspaces it is indefinite and they carry the zero divisors; the mixed real form $W=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{e_0,e_1,ie_2,ie_3\}$ of signature $(2,2)$, with $N|_W=a^{2}+b^{2}-c^{2}-d^{2}$ and projective quadric the doubly ruled surface $S^{1}\times S^{1}$. The article also carries the norm read as a norm of the algebra: the naming of $N$ as the **semi-norm** of the literature together with the audit of the norm axioms, of which only the sign axiom survives, the triangle inequality being inapplicable to a complex value and the scaling axiom failing for a complex scalar, since $\sqrt{\lambda^{2}}$ lies in the right half-plane and not at $\lvert\lambda\rvert$; the **unique** multiplicative real norm on the units normalised by $r(\lambda e_0)=\lvert\lambda\rvert$ for real $\lambda$, namely $r(\tilde Q)=\sqrt{\lvert N(\tilde Q)\rvert}=\sqrt{\lvert\det\mathsf M_2(\tilde Q)\rvert}$, which is the polar scale, the $4\times4$ regular representation carrying $\det=N^{2}$; the splitting of the norm on the halves $\tilde Q=q_r+iq_i$ into $\Re N=N(q_r)-N(q_i)$ and $\Im N=2\langle q_r,q_i\rangle$, so that $N=0$ reads as equal norms and vanishing scalar product of the two halves; and the relation to the Hermitian form $\tilde Q\tilde Q^{*}$, whose scalar part $\sum_\mu\lvert Q_\mu\rvert^{2}$ is definite, gives the Euclidean norm and detects no zero divisor, the two forms coinciding exactly on the quaternion subspace and differing by a sign on the imaginary sector. -->

<a href="articles_maths/zero-divisors-of-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">Zero Divisors of the Biquaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the zero divisors of the general plain bilinear product: the definition of a left, a right and a two-sided zero divisor of a general product $\star$, stated for $\star$ and then read on the products of the space, the product entering the equation and the equation being the whole definition, so that a zero divisor is always a zero divisor of a named product; the plain-product reading $\tilde Q\tilde R=0$ or $\tilde R\tilde Q=0$; the criterion for the plain product, $\tilde Q\tilde Q^{\natural}=0$, with the proof that uses the plain-product inverse and the reason the other three general products have no criterion of that form; the three-way classification by $\tilde Q\tilde Q^{\natural}$, invertible, zero, zero divisor; the two families, pure and non-pure; the square of a pure and of a non-pure biquaternion; the criterion in terms of the scalar part, which needs no norm; the bivector (real two-vector) form of the pure zero divisors, with the orthogonality and equal-length conditions and the dimension count; the associated idempotent; the structure of each family and the comparison table; the union; the zero divisor set. The criterion by the vanishing of the norm needs a distance and is in *Norm and Invertibility in the General Quaternionic Algebra*; the four general products and their common zero-divisor set are in the zero-divisor article of the derived-structures category. -->

<a href="articles_maths/annihilators-of-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">Annihilators of the Biquaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the annihilators of the general plain bilinear product, the left and the right multiplication being the operators $L_{\tilde P}\tilde X=\tilde P\tilde X$ and $R_{\tilde P}\tilde X=\tilde X\tilde P$ of determinant $C(\tilde P)^2$ and trace $4P_0$: both vanish off the zero-divisor cone and are complex planes on it, of complex dimension two, the reading through the matrix model $M_2(\mathbb{C})$, in which a nonzero element of the cone is a rank-one matrix and the two annihilators are the kernels of its left and right multiplication; the two planes distinct, sharing the line $\mathbb{C}\tilde Q^{\natural}$; and the examples at $e_0+ie_1$ and $e_1+ie_2$. The parent of the four general products, and the one for which the two sides are genuinely two; the zero-divisor set is *Zero Divisors of the Biquaternion Algebra*, and the siblings are *Annihilators of the General Quaternionic Algebra*, *Annihilators of the General Plain Sesqualgebra* and *Annihilators of the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/square-roots-of-one-and-the-idempotents-of-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">Square Roots of One and the Idempotents of the Biquaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the square roots of the central value $+1$ in the general plain bilinear product of two biquaternions $\tilde P\tilde Q$, the multiplication of the algebra $\mathbb{B}=\mathbb{C}\otimes_\mathbb{R}\mathbb{H}$, the one of the four general products that is associative and two-sidedly unital; the problem and its reduction by the vector–scalar decomposition, $2\Xi_0\boldsymbol\Xi=0$ forcing $\Xi_0=0$ or $\boldsymbol\Xi=0$ since $\mathbb{C}$ is a field; the classification of the roots of $+1$ as the two central scalars $\pm e_0$, the two-real-parameter family $\pm i\boldsymbol\mu$ over the pure real quaternions $\boldsymbol\mu$ of square $-e_0$, and the four-real-parameter family $\boldsymbol\xi+i\boldsymbol\xi'$ with $\boldsymbol\xi\neq0$ and the two real conditions, the squared sums written out, the case $\boldsymbol\xi'=0$ shown impossible; the roots of $+1$ as units and the nonzero roots of $0$ as zero divisors; the free real parameters of the root families; the roots read in the general plain bilinear product, the other three products having different squares and different roots; the roots of $-1$ as one short paragraph closing the part, deduced from the roots of $+1$ by multiplication by the central imaginary $i$, the centrality and the bilaterality the deduction needs, and the products that have other roots of $-1$ or none; the relation to the idempotents through the halving map $\tilde\Xi\mapsto\tfrac12(e_0+\tilde\Xi)$, a bijection from the roots of $+1$ onto the idempotents with inverse $\tilde\Xi=2\tilde\Pi-e_0$, so that every idempotent is read on the roots of $+1$ alone; the two idempotents a root carries, $\tilde\Pi_+(\tilde\Xi)=\tfrac12(e_0+\tilde\Xi)$ and $\tilde\Pi_-(\tilde\Xi)=\tfrac12(e_0-\tilde\Xi)=e_0-\tilde\Pi_+(\tilde\Xi)$, a complete orthogonal pair summing to $e_0$, multiplying to $0$ and differing by the root, with multiplication by the root acting by $+1$ on the first and $-1$ on the second, the pair splitting the algebra into the eigenspaces, and the pair map a bijection from the roots onto the ordered complete orthogonal pairs; the idempotents of the general plain bilinear product, the equation $\tilde\Pi^2=\tilde\Pi$ being relative to the product: idempotents and the direct sum decompositions they carry; orthogonal, complete and primitive idempotents and the primitivity criterion; the standard idempotents $\tilde\Pi_+(ie_3)$ and $\tilde\Pi_-(ie_3)$ as the diagonal matrix units; the families of idempotents through the halving map, the trivial $0$ and $e_0$ from the central roots, the Hermitian idempotents from the family $\pm i\boldsymbol\mu$, and a four-real-parameter family from the non-trivial roots; the complementary pair carried by $\{\tilde\Xi,-\tilde\Xi\}$; idempotents as projections and the Hermitian idempotents as orthogonal projections; the non-pure zero divisors as complex multiples of idempotents; the complex-dimension reading of the idempotent set; the other three products carrying idempotents of their own. The companion articles are *Square Roots of Zero and the Nilpotents of the Biquaternion Algebra* and *Square Roots of a General Element in the Biquaternion Algebra*; the four general products and their idempotents are *Comparison Between the Four General Products*; the zero-divisor set is *Zero Divisors of the Biquaternion Algebra*; and the minimal left ideals are *Ideals and Peirce Decomposition of the Biquaternion Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/square-roots-of-zero-and-the-nilpotents-of-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">Square Roots of Zero and the Nilpotents of the Biquaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the square roots of the central value $0$ in the general plain bilinear product of two biquaternions $\tilde P\tilde Q$, the multiplication of the algebra $\mathbb{B}=\mathbb{C}\otimes_\mathbb{R}\mathbb{H}$; the problem and its reduction by the same vector–scalar decomposition, giving $\Xi_0=0$ or $\boldsymbol\Xi=0$; the roots of $0$ as the element $0$ together with the pure elements of vanishing complex square $\Xi_1^2+\Xi_2^2+\Xi_3^2=0$, a four-real-parameter family written in the two real parts $\boldsymbol\xi+i\boldsymbol\xi'$, with $e_1+ie_2$ as the worked instance; the nonzero roots of $0$ as the nilpotents of the algebra; the roots of $+1$, the roots of $-1$ and the idempotents as the companion article *Square Roots of One and the Idempotents of the Biquaternion Algebra*; the nilpotents: the definition $\tilde\Upsilon^2=0$, with $0$ the trivial one and the nonzero ones the subject; the criterion, $\tilde P^2=[P_0^2-(\mathbf P,\mathbf P)]e_0+2P_0\mathbf P$, so that a nilpotent is pure with isotropic vector part, $P_0=0$ and $(\mathbf P,\mathbf P)=0$; the nilpotent cone, a complex cone of complex dimension two and real dimension four, the two real equations $\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf p=\mathbf p'\cdot\mathbf p'$ and $\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf p'=0$ on the two real vector parts $P_k=p_k+ip'_k$, parametrised as $r(\hat{\mathbf p}+i\hat{\mathbf p}')$ over orthogonal real unit pairs; index two, $\tilde P^3=0$ exactly when $\tilde P^2=0$, with the cube $\tilde P^3=P_0[P_0^2-3(\mathbf P,\mathbf P)]e_0+[3P_0^2-(\mathbf P,\mathbf P)]\mathbf P$; the self-annihilation $\tilde\Upsilon\tilde\Upsilon=0$, so that a nonzero nilpotent is a two-sided zero divisor and its own annihilating partner, and the nilpotents are the pure family of the zero-divisor set; the disjointness of the nilpotents and the idempotents, meeting only at $0$; the action of the conjugations, the star pairing the class and fixing none of it; the model $M_2(\mathbb{C})$, where a nilpotent is a nonzero trace-free singular matrix, $\mathrm{tr}\,\Phi(\tilde P)=2P_0$ and $\det\Phi(\tilde P)=C(\tilde P)$, with the off-diagonal Peirce units $\hat\Upsilon_1,\hat\Upsilon_2$; the coincidence $\mathbb{B}\tilde\Upsilon=I_{\tilde\Upsilon}$ of the ideal generated and the annihilator; the position in the remarkable subspaces, the vector subspace being the only one containing a nilpotent; and the free real parameters of the root family. The zero-divisor set and the two families are *Zero Divisors of the Biquaternion Algebra*; the roots of the general quadratic are *Square Roots of a General Element in the Biquaternion Algebra*; the minimal ideals are *Ideals and Peirce Decomposition of the Biquaternion Algebra*; and the same class read against the four products is the zero-divisor article of the derived-structures category. -->

<a href="articles_maths/square-roots-of-a-general-element-in-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">Square Roots of a General Element in the Biquaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the problem $\tilde P^2=\tilde Q$ for an arbitrary $\tilde Q$; the method free of Clifford algebras, norms and forms, by the same vector–scalar split that solves the central values; the two equations $2P_0\boldsymbol{P}=\boldsymbol{Q}$ and $P_0^2-(\boldsymbol{P},\boldsymbol{P})=Q_0$; the two cases according to whether the vector part $\boldsymbol{Q}$ vanishes; the reduced quadratic $4x^2-4Q_0x-(\boldsymbol{Q},\boldsymbol{Q})=0$ for $x=P_0^2$, of discriminant $16n$ with the conjugate scalar $n=Q_0^2+Q_1^2+Q_2^2+Q_3^2$, the scalar of $\tilde Q\tilde Q^{\natural}=ne_0$, and the pair $\pm(\sqrt{x}\,e_0+\boldsymbol{Q}/(2\sqrt{x}))$ from each nonzero solution; the complex-scalar case, with the elements $\pm\sqrt{Q_0}e_0$ and the four-real-parameter family of pure $\boldsymbol{P}$ of complex square $-Q_0$, the nilpotent cone at $\tilde Q=0$; the classification of no root, two roots, four roots and continuum, with the roots stated in each case; the specialisation to the three central values, cited to the two companion articles, the roots of $+1$ and of $-1$ in the first and the roots of $0$ in the second and used as a consistency check; the worked examples, verified by squaring. This article owns the classification of $\tilde P^2=\tilde Q$. -->

##### Advanced Properties

<a href="articles_maths/the-specificities-of-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">The Specificities of the Biquaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the specificities of the block read in the block's own terms: the criterion, **left alternativity**, $\tilde X(\tilde X\tilde Y)=(\tilde X\tilde X)\tilde Y$ at every pair, equivalently the operator identity $L_{\tilde X}L_{\tilde X}=L_{\tilde X\tilde X}$, and the theory it unlocks — the projector calculus of the idempotents, the square-zero operators of the nilpotents, the quadratic Peirce decomposition into two corner subalgebras and two one-dimensional mixed spaces with matrix units $E_{ij}E_{kl}=\delta_{jk}E_{il}$; the algebra $\mathbb{B}\cong M_2(\mathbb{C})$, central simple, centre $\mathbb{C}e_0$; the ideal generated by a square-zero element equal to its annihilator; the ideal lattice, the enveloping operator algebra $\mathbb{B}^{\mathrm e}\cong M_4(\mathbb{C})$ and the semisimple module category; and the isolation of the block among the twelve with the three generating operations and the boundary of the criterion at the general quaternionic product. The companions are *Ideals and Peirce Decomposition of the Biquaternion Algebra* and *Modules over the Biquaternion Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/ideals-and-peirce-decomposition-of-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">Ideals and Peirce Decomposition of the Biquaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- ideals in an algebra; the two-sided ideals and the simplicity of $\mathbb{B}$; Artinian, semisimple and length two; idempotents and orthogonal idempotents, the nontrivial ones being the primitive ones; the pair of a root of $+1$, the two idempotents $\tilde\Pi_+$ and $\tilde\Pi_-$ attached to $+1$ and to $-1$, with $ie_3$ the standard root; the off-diagonal elements and the matrix units, with the normalisation $uw=\lambda e$ and its reciprocal $\mathbb{C}^\times$; the Peirce decomposition, attached to a root of $+1$ and forced by a single idempotent, with as many decompositions as roots of $+1$ modulo the sign change; the decomposition into minimal left and right ideals, with the bases and dimensions of the two minimal left ideals and $\mathbb{C}^2$ as a left module; the lattice of left ideals as a projective line; the radical; the real structure. -->

<a href="articles_maths/eigenvalue-decomposition-of-a-biquaternion.html">Eigenvalue Decomposition of a Biquaternion</a>
<!-- the eigenvalue decomposition of a biquaternion with distinct eigenvalues: the pure unit $\vec U=\vec Q/B$ and the pure root of $+1$ $\vec\Xi=-i\vec Q/B$, the eigenvalues $Q_t\pm iB$ and the characteristic polynomial $(X-Q_t)^2+B^2$; the eigenprojections $\tilde\Pi_\pm=\frac12(e_t\pm\vec\Xi)$, primitive, orthogonal and complete; the decomposition $\tilde Q=\lambda_+\tilde\Pi_++\lambda_-\tilde\Pi_-$, unique up to the swap $B\to-B$; the Peirce decomposition $\mathbb{B}=\mathbb{B}_{++}\oplus\mathbb{B}_{+-}\oplus\mathbb{B}_{-+}\oplus\mathbb{B}_{--}$ relative to $\tilde\Pi_+$ and the centraliser $\mathbb{C}[\tilde Q]=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{C}}\{e_t,\tilde Q\}$; the polynomial calculus, the inverse and the parity-matched lattice $\{\pi i m\,e_t+\pi n\,\vec U:m\equiv n\pmod2\}$; the algebraic fibre and the coordinate change to the scalar part and the complex angle; the zero-divisor regime $B\neq0$, $\langle\tilde Q\rangle_{\natural}=0$, with one eigenvalue zero and the decomposition $\tilde Q=2Q_t\tilde\Pi_\sigma$; the nilpotent regime $B=0$, $\vec Q\neq0$, a single Jordan block with no nontrivial idempotent in its centraliser; the scalar regime $\vec Q=0$, semisimple with a repeated eigenvalue and non-unique two-projector decompositions; and the Hermitian case, where $\vec U$ is real, the idempotents are Hermitian and the decomposition is the spectral theorem. -->

<a href="articles_maths/modules-over-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">Modules over the Biquaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the modules over $\mathbb{B}\cong M_2(\mathbb{C})$, the algebra acting on its own additive group and the category of all its modules: the left regular module ${}_\mathbb{B}\mathbb{B}$, the right regular module $\mathbb{B}_\mathbb{B}$ and the regular bimodule ${}_\mathbb{B}\mathbb{B}_\mathbb{B}$; the submodules are the left, the right and the two-sided ideals, so the ideal theory of *Ideals and Peirce Decomposition of the Biquaternion Algebra* is the submodule theory of the regular object; cyclic on the unit, faithful, free of rank one on $\{e_0\}$, a generator and the identity of the tensor product, $M\otimes_\mathbb{B}{}_\mathbb{B}\mathbb{B}\cong M$ and ${}_\mathbb{B}\mathbb{B}\otimes_\mathbb{B}N\cong N$; the endomorphism rings $\operatorname{End}_\mathbb{B}(\mathbb{B}_\mathbb{B})\cong\mathbb{B}$, $\operatorname{End}_\mathbb{B}({}_\mathbb{B}\mathbb{B})\cong\mathbb{B}^{\mathrm{op}}$ and $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{B}\text{-}\mathbb{B}}(\mathbb{B})\cong Z(\mathbb{B})=\mathbb{C}e_0$; the defining module $S=\mathbb{B}\tilde\Pi_1=\mathbb{C}\{\tilde\Pi_1,\tilde T\}$ as the unique simple left module, with the left action in the idempotent basis and the isomorphism $\mathsf{M}_2(e_k)=-i\sigma_k$; the classification, every left module a direct sum $S^{\oplus k}$ and every module projective; ${}_\mathbb{B}\mathbb{B}\cong S\oplus S$, so that $S\cong\mathbb{C}^2$ and the minimal left ideals $L_\ell$ are indexed by the lines of $\mathbb{C}^2$; the parity criterion for freeness, $S^{\oplus k}$ free iff $k$ is even, so that $S$ is projective and not free; the endomorphism algebras $\operatorname{End}_\mathbb{B}(S)=\mathbb{C}$, $\operatorname{Hom}_\mathbb{B}(S^{\oplus m},S^{\oplus n})\cong M_{n\times m}(\mathbb{C})$, $\operatorname{End}_\mathbb{B}(S^{\oplus k})\cong M_k(\mathbb{C})$ with automorphism group $\mathrm{GL}_k(\mathbb{C})$, and the double centralizer $\operatorname{End}_\mathbb{C}(S)=\mathbb{B}$; the standard bimodule ${}_\mathbb{B}S_\mathbb{C}$ with its commuting actions, the dual $S^*\cong S$ and quaternion conjugation as the adjugate $\mathsf{M}_2(\tilde Q^{\natural})=\varepsilon\mathsf{M}_2(\tilde Q)^{\mathrm T}\varepsilon^{-1}$; the Morita equivalence $\operatorname{Mod}(\mathbb{B})\cong\operatorname{Mod}(\mathbb{C})$ and the doubling of every complex dimension; the degeneration of the naive torsion and the torsion-freeness of the category; the real structures of the modules obtained from $\mathbb{H}$ by extension of scalars, exactly the free ones; and $\mathbb{B}$ von Neumann regular and self-injective, so that ${}_\mathbb{B}\mathbb{B}$ is a projective generator and an injective cogenerator. The norm, its vanishing, the invertibility criterion and the group of units are in *Norm and Invertibility in the General Quaternionic Algebra*; the group-theoretic representations are in *Biquaternion Rotations and Lorentz Transformations*; the $4\times4$ regular matrices are in *Introduction to the 4×4 Matrix Element Representation $M_4(\mathbb{C})_L$ of Biquaternions*; and the involution, the twist and the canonical form are in *The Canonical Hermitian Form on the Regular Module of the Biquaternion Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-group-of-units-of-the-biquaternion-algebra-and-the-complement-of-the-zero-divisor-cone.html">The Group of Units of the Biquaternion Algebra and the Complement of the Zero-Divisor Cone</a>

the multiplicativity $\mathrm{Norm}(\tilde P\tilde Q)=\mathrm{Norm}(\tilde P)\mathrm{Norm}(\tilde Q)$ as the reason the complement is a group, with the cone absorbing, the units closed and $\mathrm{Norm}:\mathbb{B}^\times\to\mathbb{C}^\times$ a surjective homomorphism onto the nonzero scalars of kernel the norm-one group; the boundary of the group as the vanishing set of the general quaternionic norm and not the vanishing set of the plain product's own algebraic norm $B=\sum_\mu\varepsilon_\mu Q_\mu^{2}$, with the witnesses $e_0+e_1$ (a unit with $B=0$) and $e_0+ie_1$ (a zero divisor with $B=2$), so that the units of the plain product are read from the norm of a different product; the topology collected and cited, the group open, dense and connected of real dimension eight, of homotopy type $S^{1}\times S^{3}$ with $\pi_1\cong\mathbb{Z}$, with $\partial\mathbb{B}^\times=\partial\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{C}$; the cone slice and the units on the remarkable subspaces, empty on the centre and the two quaternionic subspaces and the complex cone and the null cone on the vector subspace and the two sectors; the complement of the cone in the other eleven structures, the four general products selecting the same off-cone set through the inverse equations solved by $(\tilde P^{-1})^{\natural}$, $(\tilde P^{-1})^{*}$ and $(\tilde P^{-1})^{\natural*}$, the symmetrised plain algebra having the same invertible set with the Jordan inverse $(2P_0e_0-\tilde P)/\mathrm{Norm}(\tilde P)$ and no group, the witness $e_1\bullet e_2=0$, and the seven structures without a unit; and the isolation, that the biquaternion algebra is the only one of the twelve whose invertible elements form a group. The article states the criterion that *Norm and Invertibility in the Biquaternion Algebra* declines to read from the product's own algebraic norm, and the topology of the group is *The Biquaternion Unit Group as a Topological Group*. -->

#### Remarkable Subspaces

<a href="articles_maths/the-group-of-involutions.html">The Group of Involutions</a>
<!-- the two commuting involutive anti-automorphisms of the algebra, the Hermitian conjugation ${}^{*}$ and the quaternion conjugation ${}^{\natural}$, the first the C*-involution and the second the extra involution, linear where ${}^{*}$ is conjugate-linear, both reversing the order of the product; their composition rules and the order-two property; the Klein four-group $G=\{\mathrm{id},{}^{*},{}^{\natural},\bar{\cdot}\}\cong V_4$ they generate with the identity and their composite the complex conjugation, its Cayley table and its abelian character; the subgroup structure, the three order-two subgroups, any two non-identity elements generating the group, the two presentations by generators, and the direct-product form $G=\{\mathrm{id},{}^{*}\}\times\{\mathrm{id},{}^{\natural}\}$; and the exclusion of the reversal $\flat=-{}^{*}$, an anti-automorphism only up to the central sign; the composition table with the reversal, whose entries are the maps of the group and their negatives; and the orbits of the group on the algebra, of size one, two or four by the orbit–stabilizer count, with worked elements of each size. The formulas of the conjugations are *The Biquaternion Algebra as a Vector Space over $\mathbb{C}$ and $\mathbb{R}$* and the lattice of the fixed spaces is *Comparison of the Remarkable Subspaces*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/introduction-to-the-remarkable-subspaces.html">Introduction to the Remarkable Subspaces</a>
<!-- the entry point of the group that treats the remarkable subspaces of $\mathbb{B}$, one to a section: the centre $\mathbb{C}_{\mathbb{B}}$, defined as the fixed space of quaternion conjugation, the set of elements with vanishing vector part, real basis $e_0, ie_0$, dimension $2$, the centre of the algebra and a field; the vector subspace $\mathrm{Vect}(\mathbb{B})$, the anti-fixed space of quaternion conjugation and the kernel of the scalar part, real basis $e_1,e_2,e_3,ie_1,ie_2,ie_3$, dimension $6$, a Lie algebra and not a subalgebra; the quaternion subspace $\mathbb{H}_{\mathbb{B}}$, the fixed space of complex conjugation, the elements with real coefficients, real basis $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$, dimension $4$, a division subalgebra; the anti-quaternion subspace $i\mathbb{H}_{\mathbb{B}}$, the anti-fixed space of complex conjugation, the elements with purely imaginary coefficients, real basis $ie_0,ie_1,ie_2,ie_3$, dimension $4$, a module over $\mathbb{H}_{\mathbb{B}}$; the Hermitian subspace $\mathbb{M}_+$, the fixed space of Hermitian conjugation, real scalar part with purely imaginary vector part, real basis $e_0,ie_1,ie_2,ie_3$, dimension $4$, a Jordan algebra under the symmetrized product; and the anti-Hermitian subspace $\mathbb{M}_-$, the anti-fixed space of Hermitian conjugation and the fixed space of the reversal $\flat=-{}^{*}$, purely imaginary scalar part with real vector part, real basis $ie_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$, dimension $4$, a real Lie algebra; each section giving the defining condition, the coordinate condition, the real basis, the dimension and the role, and the remarkable subspaces also tabulated at a glance in the introduction. The four conjugations themselves, the group they form and the two spaces each defines are *The Biquaternion Algebra as a Vector Space over $\mathbb{C}$ and $\mathbb{R}$*, *The Group of Involutions* and *Comparison of the Remarkable Subspaces*; the coordinate blocks, the pairwise intersections, the sums, the action of the conjugations as sign patterns and the action of the central imaginary unit are *Comparison of the Remarkable Subspaces*; the product and its two halves, the Jordan and Lie algebras, the units, the zero divisors, the idempotents and projections, the ideals and the Peirce decomposition, the roots of minus one, the two matrix representations, the forms and the analysis are the thematic articles of the group. This article replaces the articles that treated the subspaces one at a time; it also carries the elements of the remarkable subspaces, with the criterion table of units and zero divisors, and their structure, with the idempotents confined to the Hermitian subspace and the minimal ideals of a Hermitian idempotent. -->

<a href="articles_maths/decompositions-along-the-remarkable-subspaces.html">Decompositions Along the Remarkable Subspaces</a>
<!-- the three direct-sum decompositions of $\mathbb{B}$ cut out by the conjugations, each a fixed space paired with an anti-fixed space of the remarkable subspaces; the quaternion decomposition $\mathbb{B}=\mathbb{H}_{\mathbb{B}}\oplus i\mathbb{H}_{\mathbb{B}}$ from complex conjugation, of dimensions $4+4$, expressing $\tilde{Q}=\tilde{Q}_r+i\tilde{Q}_i$ as a real quaternion plus the scalar imaginary times another, the real and imaginary parts of the complexification, with $\tilde{Q}_r=\frac12(\tilde{Q}+\bar{\tilde{Q}})$ and $\tilde{Q}_i=\frac{1}{2i}(\tilde{Q}-\bar{\tilde{Q}})$; the Hermitian decomposition $\mathbb{B}=\mathbb{M}_+\oplus\mathbb{M}_-$ from the Hermitian conjugation, of dimensions $4+4$, with $\tilde{Q}_\pm=\frac12(\tilde{Q}\pm\tilde{Q}^{*})$, the algebraic analogue of real and imaginary parts, whose halves are not subalgebras; the centre–vector decomposition $\mathbb{B}=\mathbb{C}_{\mathbb{B}}\oplus\mathrm{Vect}(\mathbb{B})$ from quaternion conjugation, of dimensions $2+6$, with $\tilde{Q}_{\mathrm{c}}=\frac12(\tilde{Q}+\tilde{Q}^{\natural})$ and $\tilde{Q}_{\mathrm{v}}=\frac12(\tilde{Q}-\tilde{Q}^{\natural})$, the splitting into scalar and pure vector parts and the one whose halves have unequal dimension; and the proof that there are exactly three, the reversal $\flat=-{}^{*}$ reproducing the eigenspaces of ${}^{*}$ with the signs exchanged. <a href="articles_maths/comparison-of-the-remarkable-subspaces.html">Comparison of the Remarkable Subspaces</a>

#### The Krein Form

<a href="articles_maths/the-fundamental-symmetry-of-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">The Fundamental Symmetry of the Biquaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the fundamental symmetry $J=\natural$: $\mathbb{C}$-linear, $J^2=\mathrm{id}$, self-adjoint for the Krein form, with the bridge $[\tilde Q,\tilde Q']=\langle J\tilde Q,\tilde Q'\rangle$ to the Hermitian form and $[J\tilde Q,\tilde Q]=\lVert\tilde Q\rVert_E^2$; the eigenspaces, the centre and the vector subspace, as the fundamental decomposition, so the decomposition is the splitting of an Algebra involution; $\natural$ as the $\mathbb{C}$-algebra anti-automorphism exchanging the sides of the left and right multiplications and the uniqueness of $\natural$ among the fundamental symmetries that respect the algebra; the whole family of fundamental symmetries as the open unit ball of the vector subspace, $\ell_{\tilde V}=\mathbb{C}(e_0+\tilde V)$ with $\lVert\tilde V\rVert_E<1$; the $J$-adjoint and the dictionary; the $J$-positive cone containing $J$; and the Pontryagin data — signature $(2,6)$ over $\mathbb R$ and $(1,3)$ over $\mathbb{C}$, negative index $6$ and $3$, Pontryagin index $\min(p,q)=2$ and $1$, so the algebra is $\Pi_6$ over $\mathbb R$ and $\Pi_3$ over $\mathbb{C}$. General theory: *The Fundamental Symmetry*, *Krein Spaces*, *Pontryagin Spaces*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-krein-gram-matrix-and-the-restrictions-of-the-form.html">The Krein Gram Matrix and the Restrictions of the Form</a>
<!-- the matrix side of the Krein form: the Gram matrix in the coefficient basis, the sign matrix $E=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$ of determinant $-1$, and in the real basis $\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1,1,-1,-1,-1)$ of signature $(2,6)$; the form as the Hilbert–Schmidt pairing $\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{adj}\mathsf{M}_2(\tilde Q)^{\dagger}\mathsf{M}_2(\tilde Q'))$ in the $2\times2$ model; Sylvester's law, the inertia $(1,3)$ over $\mathbb{C}$ and $(2,6)$ over $\mathbb R$, and the maximal positive definite subspaces; the restrictions to the remarkable subspaces — centre $(2,0)$, vector $(0,6)$, and the quaternion, anti-quaternion, Hermitian and anti-Hermitian subspaces each $(1,3)$ — set against the restrictions of the norm; the centre and the vector subspace as mutual Krein-orthogonal complements; the discriminant, of class $-1$ over $\mathbb R$ for the form and for each restriction. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-isotropic-structure-of-the-general-quaternionic-sesqualgebra.html">The Isotropic Structure of the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the isotropic structure of the Krein form: the null set $[\tilde Q,\tilde Q]=0$ as $\lVert c\rVert_E=\lVert v\rVert_E$, a real cone of dimension $7$, non-singular off the apex; the comparison with the norm cone of the zero divisors, of real dimension $6$, meeting it in the union of the doubly null lines $\mathbb{C}(e_0\pm i\hat\mu)$, a cone of real dimension $4$; the totally isotropic subspaces, the Witt index $\min(p,q)=1$ over $\mathbb{C}$ and $2$ over $\mathbb R$, the maximal isotropic complex line $\mathbb{C}(e_0+e_1)$ and the maximal isotropic real plane $\mathrm{span}_\mathbb R\{e_0+e_1,i(e_0+e_1)\}$; the Peirce lines generated by the rank-one Hermitian idempotents $\tilde\Pi_{1,2}(\hat\mu)=\tfrac12(e_0\pm i\hat\mu)$, exactly the doubly null lines, with the minimal left and right ideals they generate; the isotropic lines and the minimal ideals they carry. -->

<a href="articles_maths/krein-orthogonality-and-the-fundamental-decomposition.html">Krein Orthogonality and the Fundamental Decomposition</a>
<!-- the indefinite structure of the Krein form: the Krein-orthogonal complement with $\dim W+\dim W^{\perp_K}=4$ over $\mathbb{C}$ and the non-degeneracy criterion $W\cap W^{\perp_K}=\{0\}$; the classification of subspaces into definite, neutral, degenerate and totally isotropic, with the neutral plane $\mathrm{span}_\mathbb R\{e_0+e_1,e_0-e_1\}$ and the dimension bounds $1$ and $3$; the maximal positive definite subspaces as the lines $\mathbb{C}(e_0+\tilde V)$ with $\lVert\tilde V\rVert_E<1$; the fundamental decomposition $W\perp_K W^{\perp_K}$ and its fundamental symmetry $J_W=\pm\mathrm{id}$, with the bridge $[\tilde Q,\tilde Q']=\langle J_W\tilde Q,\tilde Q'\rangle$ and the canonical case $J=\natural$; the $J$-self-adjoint idempotents as exactly the Krein-orthogonal projections onto the non-degenerate subspaces, a class strictly larger than the definite-orthogonal projections commuting with $J$; the Krein Gram–Schmidt process. -->

<a href="articles_maths/indefinite-positivity-and-the-krein-cone-of-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">Indefinite Positivity and the Krein Cone of the Biquaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the Krein cone $P_K=\{\tilde Q:[\tilde Q,\tilde Q]\ge0\}=\{\lVert c\rVert_E\ge\lVert v\rVert_E\}$, closed but neither convex nor pointed, with boundary the Krein null set; the intersection with the Hermitian subspace as the full null cone of the interval form, whose future nappe is the Hermitian cone $P$, so $P\subseteq P_K$; the operator $J$-positive cone $\mathcal{P}_J=J\cdot\{S\ge0\}$, convex, larger than the Hilbert cone and containing $J$; the $J$-projections as exactly the Krein-orthogonal projections onto the non-degenerate subspaces, of which the definite-orthogonal projections commuting with $J$ and the spectral projections $\pi_{1,2}$ are the special case, with the rank-one counterexample on the isotropic line; the $J$-Cartan involution $\theta_J(T)=(T^{\dagger})^{-1}$ with fixed group $U_J(\mathbb{B})\cong U(1,3)$, contrasted with the Cartan involution of $U(1,3)$, whose fixed group is $U(1)\times U(3)$. General theory: *Krein Algebras*. -->

### Topology

#### Introduction to Topology on the Biquaternions

<a href="articles_maths/topology-in-the-space-of-biquaternions.html">Topology in the Space of Biquaternions</a>
<!-- the topology of the space of biquaternions, built from the linear structure alone and with no form and no algebraic norm entering: a **norm** defined by the three axioms (real-valued, non-negative, definite, homogeneous, subadditive) and the norm $\lVert\tilde Q\rVert=(\sum_\mu\lvert Q_\mu\rvert^{2})^{1/2}$ of the real space $\mathbb{B}=\mathbb{R}\text{-span}\{e_\mu,ie_\mu\}\cong\mathbb{R}^{8}$; **the theorem of finite dimension** — every two norms on a finite-dimensional real space are equivalent, and such a space carries exactly one Hausdorff vector-space topology — whence **one topological norm** and one topology (Rudin 1.21–1.22, Bourbaki I, *Normed and Banach Spaces*, *Comparison of Norms and Invertibility*); **the construction** of the topology: the metric $d(\tilde P,\tilde Q)=\lVert\tilde P-\tilde Q\rVert$, the balls, the coordinate isomorphism and the arrival at the **Euclidean topology of $\mathbb{R}^{8}$**, with the usual properties (Hausdorff, second countable, locally compact, complete, path connected, Heine–Borel) and the subspace topology from the regular representation into $M_4(\mathbb{R})$; then the algebra structure in it — the product bound $\lVert\tilde P\tilde Q\rVert\leq\sqrt2\lVert\tilde P\rVert\lVert\tilde Q\rVert$, proved from $\lVert\mathsf{M}_2(\tilde Q)\rVert_F=\sqrt2\lVert\tilde Q\rVert$ and the Frobenius norm, so that $\mathbb{B}$ is a topological, normed and Banach algebra and its group of units is open. This is the only article of the introduction to topology: the topology does not depend on the forms. -->

#### Topology of the Biquaternion Algebra

<a href="articles_maths/the-euclidean-topology-of-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">The Euclidean Topology of the Biquaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the Euclidean structure of the ambient space, independent of the forms: the real inner product and the Euclidean norm, which is the topological norm, the linear isometry onto $\mathbb{R}^8$; the sharp normed-algebra inequality $\lVert\tilde Q\tilde R\rVert\le\sqrt2\lVert\tilde Q\rVert\lVert\tilde R\rVert$; the contractibility with $\pi_n(\mathbb{B})=0$ and the contractibility of the remarkable subspaces; the Euclidean unit sphere $S^7$, not a group and meeting the singular cone in the compact $5$-manifold link; the Riesz duality and the flat Riemannian metric. Moved into this region out of the former parked region, where it sat under a heading that named a topology for a form. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-biquaternion-unit-group-as-a-topological-group.html">The Biquaternion Unit Group as a Topological Group</a>
<!-- $\mathbb{B}^\times$ with its group structure and its topology, open and dense as the complement of the singular cone; the determinant and the matrix model $GL_2(\mathbb{C})$; the retraction of $\mathbb{B}^\times$ onto its maximal compact subgroup; the retraction of the determinant-one group; the structure of the maximal compact subgroup; the homotopy groups, the generators and the universal cover; the connected components. This is the topological part of the Lie-theoretic block, which the boundary places in three parts: the Lie algebra in *The 12 Products of the Biquaternion Complex Space*, the topology here, the Lie-group theory in *Biquaternion Lie Group and Exponential Structure*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/biquaternion-orders-and-finite-groups-of-units.html">Biquaternion Orders and Finite Groups of Units</a>
<!-- the integral structures of the algebra and their groups of units: the Lipschitz and Hurwitz orders, the index two of the second over the first and its maximality; the groups of units $Q_8$ and the binary tetrahedral $2T$; the finite subgroups of the unit sphere $Sp(1)$ — the twofold preimages of the finite rotation groups of the plane and the three Platonic figures, cyclic, binary dihedral and the binary polyhedral $2T$, $2O$, $2I$ of orders $24$, $48$, $120$; the regular $24$-cell with the Hurwitz units as vertices and its symmetry groups $B_4$ and $F_4$; the twelve distinct rotations $\rho_v$ that the twenty-four units define; the McKay correspondence between the five families and the simply laced Dynkin types; the integral biquaternions over the Gaussian integers and their infinite group of units, generated by a nilpotent direction. The unit criterion is invertibility, the discrete side of the same topology, which places this article in Topology. The quotient $Sp(1)/\{\pm e_0\}\cong SO(3)$ and the rotation $\rho_v$ are *Biquaternion Rotations and Lorentz Transformations*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-topology-of-the-zero-divisor-cone.html">The Topology of the Zero-Divisor Cone</a>
<!-- the singular set of the algebra as a topological object, built with no form entering: the zero-divisor cone $\mathcal{Z}$ with its apex adjoined, closed with empty interior, a real algebraic cone of real dimension $6$, with the group of units as its open and dense complement; the punctured cone $\mathcal{Z}$ as a smooth complex $3$-manifold of which the apex is the only singular point; the contractibility of the cone by $\tilde Q\mapsto(1-s)\tilde Q$; the link $L=\mathcal{N}\cap S^7_E$ as a closed connected real $5$-manifold, an $S^1$-bundle over the projectivised cone $S^2\times S^2$, simply connected with $\pi_2(L)\cong\mathbb{Z}$ and so not $S^5$, which certifies the apex as genuinely singular; and the two pure real slices, which the cone meets only at the apex and whose unit sphere is the sphere of real roots of $-1$, $S^2$, compact, connected, simply connected and not a group. The equation $N=0$ and the algebraic norm itself are quoted from *The 4 Forms over the Biquaternion $\mathbb{C}$ Space*; the ambient Euclidean structure and the unit sphere are *The Euclidean Topology of the Biquaternion Algebra*; the projective geometry of the cone's complex lines is *The Null Quadric and Its Projective Geometry*. Carries the form-free half of the former *Biquaternion Topology*, which the corpus has since split between this article and *The Null Quadric and Its Projective Geometry*. -->

#### Metrics of the Biquaternion Algebra

<a href="articles_maths/topology-and-metric-for-each-of-the-twelve-operations.html">Topology and Metric for Each of the Twelve Operations</a>
<!-- the walk of the twelve names defined in *The 12 Products of the Biquaternion Complex Space* with respect to the two questions the region separates: the topology, one for all twelve since the space is a finite-dimensional real space and all its norms are equivalent, and the metric, which differs from operation to operation and is read from the scalar part. The two facts that distribute the twelve: the scalar part of a bilinear product is symmetric in its two arguments, so the symmetric half keeps it and the antisymmetric half loses it, which is why $\mathrm{APA}$ and $\mathrm{AQA}$ carry no form and why the general plain bilinear form is carried by the algebra and $\mathrm{SPA}$ and the general quaternionic bilinear form by $\mathrm{GQA}$ and $\mathrm{SQA}$; and the scalar part of a sesquilinear product is Hermitian, so the symmetric half takes the real form of the Hermitian form and the antisymmetric half the alternating form, which is why the four sesquilinear-row operations carry four forms and not two. The table of the eight non-vanishing forms with the operations that carry each, the kind of each, its inertia and its definiteness; the twelve read one by one in a fixed order — the operation and its scalar part, the inertia and the definiteness, the level set and the isometry group it owns, and its metric verdict in the two routes of *The 4 Forms over the Biquaternion $\mathbb{C}$ Space* — with the indefinite metrics of the algebra, $\mathrm{SPA}$, $\mathrm{GQA}$, $\mathrm{SQA}$, $\mathrm{GQS}$, $\mathrm{SQS}$, the positive definite metric of $\mathrm{GPS}$ and $\mathrm{SPS}$ by the diagonal route, the two alternating forms of $\mathrm{APS}$ and $\mathrm{AQS}$ with $Sp(8,\mathbb{R})$, the zero scalar parts of $\mathrm{APA}$ and $\mathrm{AQA}$ and the Killing form of the bracket of $\mathrm{APA}$, of inertia $(3,3)$ with the centre as radical; the summary table of the twelve; the one topology and the two objects the forms distinguish, the level sets and the isometry groups; and the sector $\mathbb{M}_{-}$ with the four restrictions $(3,1)$, $(1,3)$, $(4,0)$ and $(0,4)$, the three-dimensional compact part that preserves the definite restrictions against the six dimensions that preserve the indefinite ones, and the uniqueness up to scale of the indefinite form invariant under the whole algebra, which is why an indefinite metric is a metric and not a norm and why a group of motions of the indefinite kind cannot fix a positive definite form. The physics reading of the sector is *Biquaternion Lorentzian and Conformal Geometry* and *Biquaternion Automorphisms and Derivations*. -->

#### Exponential Polar Decomposition of Biquaternions

<a href="articles_maths/exponential-polar-decomposition-of-biquaternions.html">Exponential Polar Decomposition of Biquaternions</a>
<!-- the exponential member of the polar decompositions: the four exponentials $r=\exp(\ln r)$, $\zeta=\exp(i\alpha)$, $\tilde U_{\mathrm b}=\exp(i\frac{\psi}{2}\vec u_{\mathrm b})$ and $\tilde u_{\mathrm r}=\exp(\frac{\theta}{2}\vec u_{\mathrm r})$, with their ranges, closed forms and characters; the eigenvalues $Q_t\pm iB$ and the eigenprojections $\tilde\Pi_\pm$ are those of *Eigenvalue Decomposition of a Biquaternion*; the amalgamation into one exponential exactly when the axes are parallel, with the complex angle $(\theta+i\psi)/2$; the theorem of existence and uniqueness, with the parameter count $1+1+(1+2)+(1+2)=8$ from the Cartan decomposition $SL(2,\mathbb{C})=P\cdot K$ and the degeneracies at $\psi=0$ and $\theta\in\{0,2\pi\}$; the two logarithms, the Cartan pair $(\tilde H,\tilde K)$ in $\mathfrak{p}\times\mathfrak{k}$ and the single logarithm, and the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff defect of the formal exponent, whose first term $\frac{i\psi\theta}{4}\vec u_{\mathrm b}\times\vec u_{\mathrm r}$ is again a boost; the kernel of the exponential, its failure to be a subgroup and the fibre, which is not a coset; the group law as the bracket of the symmetric pair, the Thomas–Wigner rotor and the boost set; the matrix picture with $\mathfrak{gl}_2(\mathbb{C})=\mathfrak{u}(2)\oplus\mathfrak{p}$; the exponential coordinates, the homotopy type $S^{1}\times S^{3}$ and the conformal factor $r^{4}$; and two worked examples, one in the interior where the formal exponent misses the element by $0.54$ while the single logarithm reproduces it to $2.2\times10^{-16}$, and one at the boundary; the boundary theory: the null cone and its two strata; the minimal idempotents $\frac12(e_t+\vec\Xi)$ with $\vec\Xi^{2}=e_t$ and the Hermitian ones $\frac12(e_t+i\vec u)$, which form the Bloch sphere and the celestial sphere; the Peirce decomposition; the boundary limits $\frac{R\zeta}{2}(e_t+i\vec u_{\mathrm b})\tilde u_{\mathrm r}$ at infinite rapidity with the scale collapsing as $\exp(-\psi/2)$; and the projective action of the group on the sphere -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-quaternion-pairing-of-the-polar-decomposition-of-biquaternions.html">The Quaternion Pairing of the Polar Decomposition of Biquaternions</a>
<!-- the second partial two-factor grouping of the four factors, $\tilde Q = \tilde q\exp(i\tilde\Psi)$ with $\tilde q = r\tilde u_{\mathrm r}$ the quaternion modulus and $\tilde\Psi = \alpha+\theta_{\mathrm b}\vec u_{\mathrm b}'$ the quaternion angle, both factors real quaternions, the split being made by the real quaternion part $\tilde q_r$; the construction $\tan\tilde\Psi = \tilde q_r^{-1}\tilde q_i$ and $\tilde q = \tilde q_r(\cos\tilde\Psi)^{-1}$ and the identity that ties it to the polar grouping; its domain, on which the real quaternion part is invertible, and the distinction between the factorisation, which the four factors provide off the null cone, and the construction; the comparison with the Hamilton pairing, the two domains not nested, and the complement of the null cone their union together with the nonzero purely imaginary complex scalars; the degenerate limits, the non-scalar real quaternion, where the Hamilton pairing is the quaternion polar form, and the complex scalar with nonzero real part, where this pairing is the complex polar form; behaviour under the quaternion, complex and Hermitian conjugations, the quaternion and Hermitian ones exchanging the order of the two factors; and the worked examples. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-hamilton-root-pairing-of-the-polar-decomposition-of-biquaternions.html">The Hamilton Root Pairing of the Polar Decomposition of Biquaternions</a>
<!-- the first partial two-factor grouping of the four factors, $\tilde Q = \Rho\exp(\vec U\Theta)$ with $\Rho = re^{i\alpha}$ the complex modulus and $\vec U = \vec Q/B$ the non-central root of $-1$ parallel to the vector part; the price of its complex modulus, undefined when the vector part is null, and its domain as the complement of the null cone and the quadric cone; the exponential of the element, whose Hamilton parameters are generally not those of the element; the correlated non-uniqueness of the axis, angle and modulus and its role in the multivaluedness of the logarithm; behaviour under the quaternion, complex and Hermitian conjugations; the roots of one in the two exponential forms, the polar word at a root, the direct derivation from $\tilde\Xi^2 = e_t$, the idempotent exponential form $\tilde\Xi = \exp(i\pi\tilde\Pi_-)$, the bridge $-i\tilde\Xi = \tilde U_{\mathrm b}\tilde u_{\mathrm r}$, the Hermitian roots and the two pure elements as the source of the word, of the idempotents and of the Peirce decomposition; and the worked examples. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-cartan-hermitian-pairing-of-the-polar-decomposition-of-biquaternions.html">The Cartan Hermitian Pairing of the Polar Decomposition of Biquaternions</a>
<!-- the third pairing of the four factors, $\tilde Q=HU$ with $H=r\tilde U_{\mathrm b}$ Hermitian positive and $U=e^{i\alpha}\tilde u_{\mathrm r}$ unitary; the single equation $\tilde Q\tilde Q^{*}=H^2$, whence $H=\sqrt{\tilde Q\tilde Q^{*}}$ and $U=H^{-1}\tilde Q$; the Hermitian positive factor, its norm $\langle H\rangle_{\natural}=r^2$ and its matrix image the positive definite polar factor; the unitary factor and $U(\mathbb{B})\cong U(2)$; the Hermitian and anti-Hermitian exponent split, $\ln H$ in $\mathbb{M}_+$ and $\ln U$ in $\mathbb{M}_-$, and the Cartan decomposition $\mathfrak{gl}(2,\mathbb{C})=\mathfrak{u}(2)\oplus\mathfrak{p}$; the theorem with existence, uniqueness and the full domain, the complement of the null cone; the relation to the polar decomposition and to the two partial regroupings, and the sense in which this pairing is not partial; behaviour under the three conjugations; the Cartan decomposition of the unit group and the physical interpretation as a Lorentz boost times a rotation; the published form and its three differences. -->

#### Operators Representations

### Geometry

<a href="articles_maths/biquaternion-rotations-and-lorentz-transformations.html">Biquaternion Rotations and Lorentz Transformations</a>
<!-- the isometric motions of the form and the action that carries them: the unit sphere $Sp(1)$ and its complexification $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$; the double covers $SL(2,\mathbb{C})\to SO^+(1,3)$ and $SU(2)\to SO(3)$, with the dimension count that excludes a six-dimensional group from the four-dimensional quaternions and places the double cover in the eight-dimensional algebra, the group itself in the projective complement of the null quadric; the rotor and the sandwich action, the half-angle and the doubling of the angle; the dagger sandwich $\mathrm{H}_{\tilde{Q}}(x)=\tilde{Q}x\tilde{Q}^{*}$ on the whole algebra, its preservation of the two Hermitian sectors and of no other pair of the remarkable subspaces, the scaling $N(\mathrm{H}_{\tilde{Q}}x)=\lvert N(\tilde{Q})\rvert^2N(x)$, its kernel the central circle $U(1)$ reducing to $\{\pm e_0\}$ on the unit-norm slice, and the theorem that the operators preserving the whole subspace structure are exactly the central multiples of the real unit quaternions; the infinitesimal operator $Xx+xX^{*}$, the commutator along the anti-Hermitian directions and the anticommutator along the Hermitian ones; the orbits and the invariants, the rank and the norm scaled by $\lvert N(\tilde{Q})\rvert^2$; the two-sided action and $SO(4)$; the boosts, or hyperbolic rotations, as the isometries of the indefinite form and the rotations as those of the definite one. The reflection $\rho_v(x)=-vxv^{-1}$ with $N(v)=1$ on the Clifford vector subspace, the anticommutation criterion and the Cartan–Dieudonné generation are stated here; the general statement is *Versors, Rotors and the Sandwich Action with Signed Inner Conjugation* and *The Clifford, Pin and Spin Groups with Signed Inner Conjugation* of Part II, cited and not restated. The article also owns the representation theory of the groups that carry the motions: the group of units $\mathbb{B}^{\times}\cong GL_2(\mathbb{C})$ with its two ground fields, its dimension, its centre and its maximal compact subgroup $U(2)$, and its finite-dimensional algebraic representations by highest weight $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)$; the unit-norm subgroup $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$; the finite-dimensional representations of the Lorentz group, the outer products $(m,n)=V_m\boxtimes V_n$ of dimension $(2m+1)(2n+1)$ and the polynomial representations $V_j=\operatorname{Sym}^{2j}(\mathbb{C}^2)$; the unitary trick relating them to the unitary representations of $SU(2)$; the defining representation $V_{1/2}=\mathbb{C}^2$ as the unique simple module of $M_2(\mathbb{C})$, the two Weyl spinors $(\tfrac12,0)$ and $(0,\tfrac12)$, the Dirac spinor, the four-vector representation $(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ and the adjoint $(1,0)\oplus(0,1)$; the self-duality of the defining module against the non-isomorphism of its conjugate; the Clebsch–Gordan rule for the $V_j$ and for the $(m,n)$, with the ballot-number multiplicities of the tensor powers of the spinor; and the unitary representations, the non-unitarity of every nontrivial finite-dimensional representation of $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ and the principal and complementary series. -->

<a href="articles_maths/biquaternion-automorphisms-and-derivations.html">Biquaternion Automorphisms and Derivations</a>

<a href="articles_maths/biquaternion-lorentzian-and-conformal-geometry.html">Biquaternion Lorentzian and Conformal Geometry</a>

<a href="articles_maths/biquaternion-versors-and-the-orthogonal-group.html">Biquaternion Versors and the Orthogonal Group</a>

#### Fractal Geometry

<a href="articles_maths/the-biquaternion-quadratic-map-and-its-julia-sets.html">The Biquaternion Quadratic Map and Its Julia Sets</a>

<a href="articles_maths/the-slices-of-the-biquaternion-julia-sets.html">The Slices of the Biquaternion Julia Sets</a>

<a href="articles_maths/the-escape-radius-and-the-greens-function-for-the-biquaternions.html">The Escape Radius and the Green's Function for the Biquaternions</a>
<!-- the escape radius of the biquaternion quadratic map and the difficulty it meets, since the norm is not multiplicative on a non-division algebra and the zero divisors allow a product to collapse; the Green's function as the limit of the normalised logarithmic potential of the iterates, together with the domain on which the limit exists; the comparison with the complex and the quaternion cases, where the radius is controlled by the multiplicative norm; the point at which the escape theory of this category genuinely departs from the classical one. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-zero-divisors-and-the-singular-julia-sets.html">The Zero Divisors and the Singular Julia Sets</a>

#### The Twelve Products and Their Tables

<a href="articles_maths/the-12-multiplication-tables-of-the-biquaternion-complex-space.html">The 12 Multiplication Tables of the Biquaternion Complex Space</a>

the remark that the table alone does not determine the product, since the two readings of one table are in general different products; the proposition that every entry of every table is $0$ or $\pm e_\mu$ and that the central imaginary occurs in none, because the basis is real and closed under the two conjugations up to sign $\overline{e_\mu}=e_\mu$, $e_\mu^{\natural}=e_\mu^{*}=\varepsilon_\mu e_\mu$, and the plain product of real quaternions is a real quaternion;
