### The General Plain Sesqualgebra (GPS) over $\mathbb{C}$

#### Basic Properties

<a href="articles_maths/introduction-to-the-general-plain-sesqualgebra.html">Introduction to the General Plain Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the general plain sesquilinear product $\tilde P\tilde Q^{*}$ read as a multiplication, and the sesqualgebra it defines: the rule on the four coordinates, the two scalar rules, $\mathbb{C}$-linear in the first slot and conjugate-linear in the second, the base involution being the complex conjugation; the sixteen products of the basis, with diagonal $e_0$ throughout and the first row the negation of the identity row; the reading of the product as the derived operation of the algebra with its conjugate-linear Hermitian involution; the right unit $e_0$ and the absence of a left one, the left action by $e_0$ being the involution; the collapse of *Sesqualgebras*, the algebra being of full type with a nontrivial involution, so that the product is neither associative nor commutative, with the witnesses $(e_0,e_1,e_1)$ and $(e_1,e_2)$; the associator; the involution exchanging the two slots, $(\tilde P\star\tilde Q)^{*}=\tilde Q\star\tilde P$; the Hermitian and skew-Hermitian elements as the two remarkable subspaces $\mathbb{M}_+$ and $\mathbb{M}_-$; the ternary product $\tilde P\tilde Q^{*}\tilde R$, the algebraic $J^{*}$-algebra it defines and the recovery of the multiplication and the involution by inserting the unit; the Hermitian square $\tilde Q\star\tilde Q=\tilde Q\tilde Q^{*}$ and the algebraic positive cone it generates, with the caution that the square is not the norm; the simplicity of the sesqualgebra, whose two-sided ideals are $0$ and $\mathbb{B}$; the idempotents of the multiplication as the Hermitian idempotents of the algebra; and the comparison that makes the general plain sesquilinear product the only derived operation among the four, with the caution that the $\mathbb{C}$-linear ${}^{\natural}$ yields the bilinear structures and requires the star for the sesquilinear one. The product is *The Four General Products of the Biquaternion $\mathbb{C}$ Space*, the algebra is *Introduction to the General Plain Algebra of Biquaternions*, the form is *The 4 Forms over the Biquaternion $\mathbb{C}$ Space* and the general theory is the sesquilinear block. -->

<a href="articles_maths/norm-and-invertibility-in-the-general-plain-sesqualgebra.html">Norm and Invertibility in the General Plain Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- The general plain sesqualgebra $\tilde P\star\tilde Q=\tilde P\tilde Q^{*}$ has a right unit $e_0$, because $\tilde Q\star e_0=\tilde Q e_0^{*}=\tilde Q$, and no left unit, because the left action of $e_0$ is the involution, $e_0\star\tilde Q=\tilde Q^{*}$; consequently it has no two-sided unit and no group of units in the ordinary sense. What replaces the inverse is the one-sided inverse, and its two equations, $\tilde Q\star\tilde R=e_0$ and $\tilde R\star\tilde Q=e_0$, have a solution for exactly the elements of non-vanishing biquaternion norm $N(\tilde Q)=\tilde Q\tilde Q^{\natural}=\sum_\mu Q_\mu^{2}$, the solution is unique, it is the same for the two equations, and it is $\tilde Q^{-1\star}=(\tilde Q^{-1})^{*}=\overline{\tilde Q}/\overline{N(\tilde Q)}$, the star-conjugate of the parent inverse. The criterion is therefore the criterion of the parent, $N(\tilde Q)\neq0$, but the inverse is the star-conjugated one and the invertible set is a group only as a set, the product being non-associative and the unit only right. The norm is conjugate-multiplicative on the block, $N(\tilde P\star\tilde Q)=N(\tilde P)\overline{N(\tilde Q)}$, so that $N(\tilde Q\star\tilde Q)=\lvert N(\tilde Q)\rvert^{2}$. The block-square $\tilde Q\star\tilde Q=\tilde Q\tilde Q^{*}$ is Hermitian, its scalar part is the definite Euclidean norm $\sum_\mu\lvert Q_\mu\rvert^{2}$, and it is not the plain square, its vector part being generally non-zero; the two quadratic forms, the complex indefinite $N$ that decides the invertibility and the real definite scalar form that the product uses, must be kept apart. -->

<a href="articles_maths/zero-divisors-of-the-general-plain-sesqualgebra.html">Zero Divisors of the General Plain Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- The zero divisors of the general plain sesqualgebra are decided by one equation in the element alone, and the equation is the parent's: because $\tilde P\star\tilde R=\tilde P\tilde R^{*}$ and ${}^{*}$ is a bijection, an element is a zero divisor of the block exactly when it is a zero divisor of the plain product, that is exactly when its biquaternion norm vanishes, $N(\tilde Q)=Q_0^{2}+(\mathbf Q,\mathbf Q)=0$ with $\tilde Q\neq0$. The set is the nonzero zero-divisor cone, of complex dimension three, which is the common set of the four general products, and every member is two-sided. The annihilators are equal on the two sides and are the image under the involution of the plain annihilator $K(\tilde Q)=\{\tilde Z:\tilde Q\tilde Z=0\}$, a complex plane of dimension two for every nonzero zero divisor and the origin otherwise; the two-sided annihilator is $\{0\}$. The two families of the parent are inherited as a partition of the elements, since the partition is read on the scalar coordinate: the pure family has $Q_0=0$ and isotropic vector part, and the non-pure family consists of the nonzero complex multiples of the nontrivial idempotents. What changes is the square-theoretic reading: a pure zero divisor is a nilpotent of index two for the parent and a nilpotent of index three for the block, its block-square being the nonzero Hermitian element $\tilde Q\tilde Q^{*}$ with positive scalar part; the non-pure zero divisors are nilpotent for neither; and of the non-pure multiples, exactly the Hermitian idempotents $\tfrac12(e_0+i\hat\mu)$ are idempotents of the block. The block keeps the set, keeps the criterion, the partition and the annihilators, and changes the index. -->

<a href="articles_maths/annihilators-of-the-general-plain-sesqualgebra.html">Annihilators of the General Plain Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the annihilators of the general plain sesquilinear product $\tilde P\star\tilde X=\tilde P\tilde X^{*}$; the coincidence of the two sides, which follows from ${}^{*}$ being a conjugate-linear anti-automorphism of order two, and the reading of the common annihilator as the conjugate of the plain annihilator $K(\tilde Q)=\{\tilde Z:\tilde Q\tilde Z=0\}$; the $\{0\}$ off the cone and the complex plane on it; the rank table of the conjugate-linear operator; and the example at $e_0+ie_1$. The block is the parent with the star added; the zero-divisor set is *Zero Divisors of the General Plain Sesqualgebra*, the parent is *Annihilators of the General Plain Algebra*, and the sibling is *Annihilators of the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/square-roots-of-one-and-the-idempotents-of-the-general-plain-sesqualgebra.html">Square Roots of One and the Idempotents of the General Plain Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- The square of an element of the general plain sesqualgebra is the Hermitian element $\tilde Q\star\tilde Q=\tilde Q\tilde Q^{*}=(\lvert q_r\rvert^{2}+\lvert q_i\rvert^{2})e_0+2i(q_{r0}\mathbf v-q_{i0}\mathbf u+\mathbf u\times\mathbf v)$ in the real halves $\tilde Q=q_r+iq_i$, whose scalar part is the definite quantity $\sum_\mu\lvert Q_\mu\rvert^{2}$. The root set of $+1$ is exactly the family $Aw$ over the unit complex scalars $A$ and the real unit quaternions $w$, that is $U(1)\cdot S^{3}$, a single real four-dimensional family containing $e_0$, $-e_0$ and the pure imaginary unit vectors $i\hat\mu$; it is a single family and not the parent's several families together with the isolated elements $\pm i$. The Hermitian roots of $+1$ are $\pm e_0$ and the $i\hat\mu$. An element is idempotent for the sesquilinear multiplication exactly when it is a Hermitian idempotent of the algebra, because applying the involution ${}^{*}$ to the equation $\tilde Q\tilde Q^{*}=\tilde Q$ forces $\tilde Q^{*}=\tilde Q$, and a Hermitian element has the same square in the two products; the idempotents of the multiplication are the trivial pair $0,e_0$ and the projections $\tilde\Pi_1(\hat\mu)=\tfrac12(e_0+i\hat\mu)$ over the real unit vectors $\hat\mu\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$, a family whose scalar part is the sum of the modulus squares of its coordinates and whose complement is the projection $\tilde\Pi_2(\hat\mu)=e_0-\tilde\Pi_1(\hat\mu)=\tilde\Pi_1(-\hat\mu)$ at the antipodal direction. The halving map $\tilde Q\mapsto\tfrac12(e_0+\tilde Q)$ is a bijection from the Hermitian roots of $+1$ onto the idempotents, with inverse $\tilde Q=2\tilde\Pi-e_0$, and each Hermitian root carries the two idempotents of the halved pair $\tilde\Pi_+(\tilde Q)=\tfrac12(e_0+\tilde Q)$ and $\tilde\Pi_-(\tilde Q)=\tfrac12(e_0-\tilde Q)$: a complete pair, orthogonal in the two products at once, their sum the unit, their difference the root, the root fixing $\tilde\Pi_+$ and negating $\tilde\Pi_-$ so that the two subscripts are the two eigenvalues of multiplication by the root, and the two roots $\pm\tilde Q$ carrying the same pair with the members exchanged; against the idempotents of the associative multiplication, which are the halved roots of $+1$ of the algebra and form a real four-dimensional family, the $\star$-idempotents are the Hermitian half, so every non-Hermitian idempotent of the algebra is not idempotent for the multiplication. The two sets agree exactly on the trivial pair and the projections, which is the sense in which the multiplication picks out the half of the algebra's idempotent set that the algebra itself calls the projections. The value $-1$ has no root: in a sesquilinear product the scalar multiplication cannot flip the sign, the second slot conjugating, so the roots of $-1$ are not read off the roots of $+1$ by multiplication by the central imaginary, and the root set of $-1$ is empty. -->

<a href="articles_maths/square-roots-of-zero-and-the-nilpotents-of-the-general-plain-sesqualgebra.html">Square Roots of Zero and the Nilpotents of the General Plain Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- The value $0$ has no root: the scalar part of the square vanishes only at the origin and the origin is excluded, so the root set of $0$ is empty, although the block has plenty of nilpotents at the next index. The powers of the general plain sesqualgebra are the left-nested iterations $\tilde X^{\star k}=\tilde X(\tilde X^{*})^{k-1}$, so the index is a property of the pair $(\mathsf{M}_2(\tilde X),\mathsf{M}_2(\tilde X)^{\dagger})$ and can exceed two. The block has **no nonzero square-zero element**: the Hermitian square $\tilde X\star\tilde X=\tilde X\tilde X^{*}$ has scalar part $\sum_\mu\lvert X_\mu\rvert^{2}$, which vanishes only at the origin, so no nilpotent has index two. The block does have nilpotents, written $\tilde\Upsilon$ (a general element whose powers are at stake keeps the letter $\tilde X$), and they are exactly the parent's pure zero divisors: $\tilde\Upsilon$ is a nilpotent of the block if and only if it is nonzero, has vanishing scalar coordinate $\Upsilon_0=0$, and has vanishing central square $C(\tilde\Upsilon)=(\boldsymbol\Upsilon,\boldsymbol\Upsilon)=0$, that is, if and only if it lies in the pure isotropic cone $\{\Upsilon_0=0,\ (\boldsymbol\Upsilon,\boldsymbol\Upsilon)=0\}$, of complex dimension two. The index is exactly three: $\tilde\Upsilon^{\star2}=\tilde\Upsilon\tilde\Upsilon^{*}\neq0$ and $\tilde\Upsilon^{\star3}=0$, proved directly for the pure elements and proved in the $2\times2$ matrix model, where the nilpotents are the rank-one traceless matrices and the condition is $\operatorname{Tr}=0$, that is $\Upsilon_0=0$. The non-pure zero divisors of the parent are zero divisors of the block and not nilpotents of it; the nilpotent set, the zero-divisor partition and the criterion $\Upsilon_0=0$ are inherited, and the index is changed from two to three. -->

<a href="articles_maths/square-roots-of-a-general-element-in-the-general-plain-sesqualgebra.html">Square Roots of a General Element in the General Plain Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- The square of an element of the general plain sesqualgebra is the Hermitian element $\tilde X\star\tilde X=\tilde X\tilde X^{*}$, whose scalar part $s=\lvert q_r\rvert^{2}+\lvert q_i\rvert^{2}$ and vector part $\mathbf w=2(q_{r0}\mathbf v-q_{i0}\mathbf u+\mathbf u\times\mathbf v)$ satisfy $\lvert\mathbf w\rvert\leq s$ in the real halves $\tilde X=q_r+iq_i$. The equation $\tilde X\star\tilde X=\tilde a$ has a solution exactly for $\tilde a\in\mathcal{C}$, and on the interior the root set is the orbit $\{e^{i\theta}\tilde X_0u\}$ of any one root under the action $\tilde X\mapsto e^{i\theta}\tilde Xu$ of $U(1)\times S^{3}$, whose kernel is $\mathbb{Z}/2$: a single real four-parameter family. #### Advanced Properties

<a href="articles_maths/the-specificities-of-the-general-plain-sesqualgebra.html">The Specificities of the General Plain Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- The general plain sesqualgebra satisfies the right-composition law $R^{\star}_{\tilde P}R^{\star}_{\tilde Q}=R^{\star}_{\tilde P\tilde Q}$ in the forward order, and it is the only one of the twelve structures that does. The law is the operator form of the isotope identity $R^{\star}_{\tilde P}=R_{\tilde P^{*}}$, the right multiplication of the block being the plain right multiplication at the conjugated index; because the conjugation is an anti-automorphism, the reversal it introduces cancels the reversal of the plain composition law, and the right multiplications of the block form a monoid isomorphic (not anti-isomorphic) to the multiplicative monoid of the algebra. Exactly three of the twelve structures carry a one-sided law: the plain product (forward on the left, reversed on the right), the general quaternionic product (reversed, on the left), and the block (forward, on the right); the general quaternionic sesquilinear product and the eight derived parts satisfy none. The consequences are the operator face of the block: the projector criterion is that $R^{\star}_{\tilde P}$ is a projector exactly when $\tilde P$ is a plain idempotent, a family of complex dimension two, while the block's own idempotents are only the Hermitian ones, of real dimension two; the left multiplications are conjugate-linear with no projector but the zero operator; the right ideals of the block are exactly the plain right ideals, and the left ideals collapse to the two trivial ones, $0$ and $\mathbb{B}$, so the block is right-faithful and left-blind; and the involution exchanges the two families, $\eta R^{\star}_{\tilde P}\eta=L_{\tilde P}$, with $(R^{\star}_{\tilde P})^{-1}=R^{\star}_{\tilde P^{-1}}$ on the units. The block is the right-handed mirror of the general quaternionic product, and the pair of criteria is the element-level statement that the twist of the two sesquilinear products sits in the two different slots. -->

the scalar shadow $\mathrm{Sc}\,G(\omega)=\int\cos(2\pi\langle\omega,x\rangle)d\mu$ positive definite for every root, which is why the loss appears only in the full $\mathbb{B}$-valued form; the answer to the eighth open question of *Biquaternion Continuous Harmonic Analysis*, the pairing it looks for being the plain sesquilinear form itself and the Euclidean form its diagonal; ### The Biquaternion General Quaternionic Algebra (GQA) over $\mathbb{C}$

#### Basic Properties

<a href="articles_maths/introduction-to-the-general-quaternionic-algebra.html">Introduction to the General Quaternionic Algebra</a>
<!-- the general quaternionic bilinear product $\tilde P^{\natural}\tilde Q$ read as a multiplication, and the $\mathbb{C}$-algebra it defines: the rule on the four coordinates and its well-definedness; the sixteen products of the basis, first row the identity row and first column the negation of the basis, the three-by-three block the negated quaternion table; the four quaternionic scalar laws and the failure of three of them, so that the product is quaternionic in name and complex in base ring, the whole difference with the plain product being carried by the vector part of the first factor; the reading as the isotope of the general plain bilinear product by the $\mathbb{C}$-linear natural conjugation, and the associator $(\tilde Q^{\natural}\tilde P-\tilde P^{\natural}\tilde Q^{\natural})\tilde R$; non-associativity, the left unit $e_0$ and the absence of a right one, non-commutativity and the trivial centre, with the complex scalars still acting by left multiplication by $Ae_0$; the failure of the alternative, flexible and degree-three identities and the monoid of left multiplications anti-isomorphic to the multiplicative monoid of the algebra; the square as the norm $\tilde Q\star\tilde Q=N(\tilde Q)e_0$, so that the idempotents are $0$ and $e_0$ alone and the nilpotents are the zero divisors; the symmetrisation as the general quaternionic bilinear form and the antisymmetrisation as the corresponding vector form; the behaviour on the scalar line, on the vector part and on the real quaternion subspace, where the product is the plain product with the quaternionic conjugate inserted in the first slot and the splitting $\mathbb{B}=\mathbb{H}_{\mathbb{B}}\oplus i\mathbb{H}_{\mathbb{B}}$ is a $\mathbb{Z}/2$-grading; and the two conditions of the derived-operation test, both failing. The product is *The Four General Products of the Biquaternion $\mathbb{C}$ Space*, the table is *Comparison Between the Four General Products*, the sibling readings are *Introduction to the General Plain Algebra of Biquaternions* and *Introduction to the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra of Biquaternions*, and the general theory of the weak algebra is *Algebras: A General Introduction* and *Non-Associative Algebras and the Property Ladder*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/zero-divisors-of-the-general-quaternionic-algebra.html">Zero Divisors of the General Quaternionic Algebra</a>
<!-- For the general quaternionic bilinear product $\tilde P\star\tilde Q=\tilde P^{\natural}\tilde Q$, a nonzero element is a zero divisor exactly when its norm vanishes, $N(\tilde Q)=\sum_\mu Q_\mu^2=0$, and the zero divisors are the nonzero points of the zero-divisor cone, a real cone of dimension six that is not a subspace and is closed under the product. The cone is the union of the pure family, the plain nilpotents $\boldsymbol\rho+i\boldsymbol\rho'$ with $\boldsymbol\rho\perp\boldsymbol\rho'$ and equal lengths, on which the quaternionic and the plain squares vanish together, and the non-pure family, the complex multiples of the nontrivial plain idempotents, on which the quaternionic square vanishes while the plain square is the nonzero multiple $2Q_0\tilde Q$. The left and the right annihilator of a zero divisor are each a complex plane containing the element, and both are $0$ for a unit; the two annihilators coincide for every element, because the natural conjugation is a $\mathbb{C}$-linear anti-automorphism of order two that turns the one equation into the other. The zero-divisor set is the same set as for the plain product, a coincidence of the algebra proved in *Zero Divisors in the Algebraic Structures over the Biquaternion $\mathbb{C}$ Space*; what this product changes is the equation, the cone-shaped square, and the annihilator, which is symmetric here where the sesquilinear products make it conjugate-symmetric. -->

<a href="articles_maths/annihilators-of-the-general-quaternionic-algebra.html">Annihilators of the General Quaternionic Algebra</a>
<!-- the annihilators of the general quaternionic bilinear product $\tilde P\star\tilde X=\tilde P^{\natural}\tilde X$; the coincidence of the two sides, which follows from ${}^{\natural}$ being a $\mathbb{C}$-linear anti-automorphism of order two; the operator of determinant $C(\tilde P)^2$ and trace $4P_0$, of rank four off the cone and rank two on it; the annihilator $\{0\}$ off the cone and a complex plane on it, containing the element; and the examples at $e_1+ie_2$ and $e_0+ie_1$. The block shares the cone and the plane with *Annihilators of the General Plain Algebra* and the coincidence with *Annihilators of the Symmetric Quaternionic Algebra*; the zero-divisor set is *Zero Divisors of the General Quaternionic Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/square-roots-of-one-and-the-idempotents-of-the-general-quaternionic-algebra.html">Square Roots of One and the Idempotents of the General Quaternionic Algebra</a>
<!-- In the general quaternionic bilinear product $\tilde P\star\tilde Q=\tilde P^{\natural}\tilde Q$ the square is always central, $\tilde P\star\tilde P=N(\tilde P)e_0$, so the roots of a central value are the level sets of the norm and the roots of $+1$ are the solutions of $N=1$, a nondegenerate complex quadric of real dimension six containing the central pair $\pm e_0$, the real vector roots $\hat\mu$ over the real unit vectors and a mixed family; the roots of $\pm1$ are units of the algebra. The idempotent equation forces centrality and reduces to $A^2=A$ on the scalar line, so the idempotents of the product are $0$ and $e_0$ alone and the product has no nontrivial idempotent. The halving map from the roots of $+1$ to the idempotents, which is a bijection for the plain product, yields an idempotent of this product only at $\pm e_0$; the plain idempotents satisfy $\tilde\Pi\star\tilde\Pi=0$ and are roots of $0$ of the product. On the operator side the plain idempotents recover their role: $L_{\tilde P}$ is a projector exactly when $\tilde P$ is a plain idempotent, so the product has a family of projectors of complex dimension two indexed by elements that are not its idempotents, and each of them is a square-zero element whose operator is a projector. The non-pure zero divisors of the product are exactly the complex multiples of the nontrivial plain idempotents, so a nontrivial plain idempotent is an idempotent of the plain product and a nilpotent of this one. Read on the remarkable subspaces, the idempotent equation leaves the two trivial idempotents in the centre, the quaternion subspace and the Hermitian subspace, and only $0$ in the vector, anti-quaternion and anti-Hermitian subspaces. The roots of $-1$ are the images of the roots of $+1$ under multiplication by the central imaginary $i$, the solutions of $N=-1$ containing the central pair $\pm i$ and the imaginary vector roots $i\hat\mu$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/square-roots-of-zero-and-the-nilpotents-of-the-general-quaternionic-algebra.html">Square Roots of Zero and the Nilpotents of the General Quaternionic Algebra</a>
<!-- The roots of $0$ in the general quaternionic product are the level set $N=0$, the whole zero-divisor cone, of real dimension six, the union of the pure isotropic elements $\boldsymbol\rho+i\boldsymbol\rho'$ with $\boldsymbol\rho\perp\boldsymbol\rho'$ and $|\boldsymbol\rho|=|\boldsymbol\rho'|$ and the complex multiples $2\Xi_0\tilde\Pi$ of the nontrivial plain idempotents; the plain idempotents are roots of $0$ of the product, and the roots of $0$ are its zero divisors. A nonzero element is nilpotent exactly when its norm vanishes, so the nilpotent set is that whole cone: a real cone of dimension six that is not a subspace and is stable under the product. The index of nilpotency is two and only two, the powers running $\tilde\Upsilon,\tilde\Upsilon^{\star2}=Ne_0,\tilde\Upsilon^{\star3}=N\tilde\Upsilon,\dots$ with $N=N(\tilde\Upsilon)$, so a vanishing cube already forces a vanishing square. Every nilpotent annihilates itself, and, in contrast to the plain product, every zero divisor is a nilpotent; the plain idempotents are nilpotents of this product, and the only element that is both an idempotent of the product and a nilpotent is the origin. The natural, the coefficientwise and the Hermitian conjugations preserve the cone, and the complex structure does too, multiplying the norm by $-1$; in the matrix model the nilpotents are the singular matrices, of which the plain nilpotents are the trace-free ones; in the ideal theory the pure nilpotents have their ideal equal to their annihilator and the non-pure ones do not; and among the remarkable subspaces the vector, the Hermitian and the anti-Hermitian carry nilpotents while the centre, the quaternion and the anti-quaternion carry none, with the element $e_0+ie_1+e_2+ie_3$ lying outside all six. -->

<a href="articles_maths/square-roots-of-a-general-element-in-the-general-quaternionic-algebra.html">Square Roots of a General Element in the General Quaternionic Algebra</a>
<!-- The square-root equation $\tilde P\star\tilde P=\tilde Q$ of the general quaternionic product has a solution exactly when $\tilde Q$ is a central value; an element with non-zero vector part has no root, because the quaternionic square is always central. For a central radicand the equation reduces to the single complex equation $N(\tilde P)=\lambda$, the square of the equation being the norm, and the root set is the nondegenerate complex quadric $N=\lambda$ of real dimension six when $\lambda\neq0$, and the zero-divisor cone of real dimension six when $\lambda=0$. Every central value has roots, among them the central root $\sqrt\lambda\,e_0$, and the root set of $\lambda$ is the root set of $1$, or of $-1$, scaled by a square root of the value. The three special values generate the classification: $R(-1)$ contains the imaginary vector roots $i\hat\mu$, $R(+1)$ the real vector roots $\hat\mu$, and $R(0)$ the whole nilpotent cone of the product. The roots of a non-zero value are units of the algebra, the non-zero roots of $0$ are its zero divisors, and the absence of a root for a non-central radicand is stated and not filled. -->

#### Advanced Properties

<a href="articles_maths/the-specificities-of-the-general-quaternionic-algebra.html">The Specificities of the General Quaternionic Algebra</a>
<!-- the operator theory of the general quaternionic product, whose left multiplication is the plain one with a conjugated index, $L_{\tilde P}(\tilde X)=\tilde P^{\natural}\tilde X=L^{\mathrm{plain}}_{\tilde P^{\natural}}(\tilde X)$; the projector criterion $L_{\tilde P}^{2}=L_{\tilde P}$ exactly when $\tilde P$ is a plain idempotent, so that the elements which project form a family of complex dimension two while the idempotents of the product are $0$ and $e_0$ alone, and the plain idempotents are $\star$-nilpotents, $\tilde\Pi\star\tilde\Pi=N(\tilde\Pi)e_0=0$, whose left multiplication is a projector; the orthogonal projector pairs $L_{\tilde\Pi}+L_{\tilde\Pi'}=\mathrm{Id}$ and $L_{\tilde\Pi}L_{\tilde\Pi'}=0$ with the decomposition $\mathbb{B}=\tilde\Pi\star\mathbb{B}\oplus\tilde\Pi'\star\mathbb{B}$ into two minimal ideals of complex dimension two; the theorem that the left ideals of the product are exactly the left ideals of the plain product, the right and the two-sided theory being absent and the Peirce corner bracket-dependent; the square-zero criterion, $L_{\tilde Q}^{2}=0$ exactly for the pure isotropic elements, strictly smaller than the zero-divisor cone of complex dimension three where the nilpotents of the product live; and the resolution of the paradox, the non-associativity of the product being carried by the elements and not by the operators, which are plain and faithful. The twin article is *The Specificities of the General Plain Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-associator-and-the-ternary-product-of-the-quaternionic-product.html">The Associator and the Ternary Product of the Quaternionic Product</a>

<a href="articles_maths/the-general-quaternionic-algebra-in-the-2x2-matrix-element-representation.html">The General Quaternionic Algebra in the $2\times2$ Matrix Element Representation $M_2(\mathbb{C})$</a>

### The General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra (GQS) over $\mathbb{C}$

#### Basic Properties

<a href="articles_maths/introduction-to-the-general-quaternionic-sesqualgebra.html">Introduction to the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the general quaternionic sesquilinear product $\tilde P^{\natural}\tilde Q^{*}$ read as a multiplication, and the sesqualgebra over $\mathbb{C}$ with the conjugation that it defines: the rule on the four coordinates and its scalar–vector form, the two scalar rules, and the admission into the sesquilinear row of the comparison; the sixteen products of the basis, first row and first column the negation of the basis and the three-by-three block the quaternion table; the failure of the derived-operation test, the first row $\sigma(\tilde Y)=e_0\star\tilde Y$ being the star, which satisfies condition (i) alone and fails condition (ii); the two one-sided actions of $e_0$, the star on the left and the natural conjugation on the right, and the absence of a unit on either side; non-associativity, non-commutativity, the non-flexibility and the failure of the degree-three identity, with the associator $\overline{\tilde Q}\tilde P\tilde R^{*}-\tilde P^{\natural}\tilde R\overline{\tilde Q}$ and the left multiplications whose composition is the sandwich $\tilde A^{\natural}(\cdot)\overline{\tilde B}$, linear where each is conjugate-linear; the star of a product as the plain product in the reversed order, $(\tilde P\star\tilde Q)^{*}=\tilde Q\overline{\tilde P}$, so that the involution does not exchange the two slots, and the reading of the two halves $\mathbb{M}_+,\mathbb{M}_-$ by the multiplication, with the scalar square $N(\tilde P)e_0$ on $\mathbb{M}_+$ and $-N(\tilde P)e_0$ on $\mathbb{M}_-$; the square $(\overline{\tilde Q}\tilde Q)^{\natural}$, its scalar part the Krein form of signature $(2,2)$, and the idempotents $0$, $e_0$ and the sphere $-\tfrac12e_0+\mu$ with $(\mu,\mu)=\tfrac34$ in the real vector subspace, which are not the Hermitian idempotents and for which the Hermitian idempotents of the algebra are isotropic; the ternary product $\overline{\tilde Q}\tilde P\tilde R$ as the left model $\tilde X^{*}\tilde Y\tilde Z$, with the parity of an algebraic $J^{*}$-algebra and the failure of the Jordan triple identity at $(e_0,e_1,e_0,e_2,e_0)$; the simplicity of the sesqualgebra; and the scalar part as the Krein form; the associator witnesses $(e_0,e_0,e_1)$ and $(e_0,e_1,e_1)$ with the values $-2e_1$ and $2e_0$ and its non-vanishing on $256$ of the $512$ basis triples, so that the defect of composition carries both a central and a vector part; and the synthesis that the metric, the absence of a unit and the failure of the Jordan triple identity are the first slot's work, while non-commutativity, non-associativity, non-flexibility, the degree-three failure and the non-closure of the antisymmetric half are shared with the sibling product that conjugates a single slot (the same counts on the eight-element basis). The product is *The Four General Products of the Biquaternion $\mathbb{C}$ Space*, the comparison is *Comparison Between the Four General Products*, the sibling readings are *Introduction to the General Plain Sesqualgebra of Biquaternions* and *Introduction to the General Quaternionic Algebra of Biquaternions*, and the general theory is the sesquilinear block, among it *Sesqualgebras*, *The Sesquilinear Associator and the Ternary Product* and *Algebraic J\*-Algebras*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/norm-and-invertibility-in-the-general-quaternionic-sesqualgebra.html">Norm and Invertibility in the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- The general quaternionic sesquilinear product $\tilde P\star\tilde Q = \tilde P^{\natural}\tilde Q^{*}$ has no unit, no inverse and no invertible element: the left action of $e_0$ is the star, $e_0\star\tilde Q = \tilde Q^{*}$, and the right action is the natural conjugation, $\tilde Q\star e_0 = \tilde Q^{\natural}$, so no element is a two-sided unit. The two quadratic objects of the space are the central square $C(\tilde Q) = \sum_\mu Q_\mu^2$, the norm of the plain algebra, vanishing exactly on the zero-divisor cone, and the Krein form $K(\tilde P,\tilde Q) = \sum_\mu\varepsilon_\mu P_\mu\overline{Q_\mu}$, of signature $(2,6)$. The central square obeys the twisted law $C(\tilde P\star\tilde Q) = C(\tilde P)\overline{C(\tilde Q)}$ and is not multiplicative, and the Krein form is not multiplicative. The invertibility available to the block is the plain criterion $c\neq0$, and it separates the classes: the idempotents of the block, the roots of $-1$ and the roots of $+1$ are units of the plain algebra, the square-zero elements are the plain zero divisors, and the plain unit $e_0$ is an idempotent of the block but a unit of no sesquilinear product of the twelve. The block therefore carries an element theory but no division theory. -->

<a href="articles_maths/zero-divisors-of-the-general-quaternionic-sesqualgebra.html">Zero Divisors of the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- The zero divisors of the general quaternionic sesquilinear product $\tilde P\star\tilde Q = \tilde P^{\natural}\tilde Q^{*}$ are defined relative to the product, and they are the nonzero elements with $C(\tilde Q) = \sum_\mu Q_\mu^2 = 0$, equivalently $\tilde Q\tilde Q^{\natural} = 0$; the left and the right reading give the same condition. The set is the complex cone $c = 0$ of complex dimension three and real dimension six, the same subset of the space that the plain product, the natural product and the general plain sesquilinear product cut out, a coincidence that is a theorem of *Zero Divisors in the Algebraic Structures over the Biquaternion $\mathbb{C}$ Space* because the criterion is the vanishing of the central square and the four products differ only by the two slot involutions. The set splits by the scalar part into the pure family $Q_0 = 0$, with $\sum_k Q_k^2 = 0$, and the non-pure family $Q_0 \neq 0$, with $\sum_k Q_k^2 = -Q_0^2$; the square-zero elements, which are a real four-dimensional proper subfamily, lie in the non-pure family, so the split by the square and the split by the scalar part cut across each other and the analogy with the plain product stops at the criterion. The element $e_1 + ie_2$ is a pure zero divisor whose square is $-2e_0 - 2ie_3$, and the element $e_0 + ie_1$ is a non-pure zero divisor whose square vanishes. -->

<a href="articles_maths/annihilators-of-the-general-quaternionic-sesqualgebra.html">Annihilators of the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the annihilators of the general quaternionic sesquilinear product $\tilde P\star\tilde X=\tilde P^{\natural}\tilde X^{*}$, which carries both involution signs and whose two sides are therefore **distinct**; the left annihilator read as the star of the plain annihilator of $\tilde P^{\natural}$; the $\{0\}$ off the cone and the two distinct complex planes on it; the rank table; and the example at $e_0+ie_1$, where the planes are spanned by $\tilde Q$ and $e_2\mp ie_3$. The block is the meeting point of the two general families; the zero-divisor set is *Zero Divisors of the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra*, and the siblings are *Annihilators of the General Plain Sesqualgebra* and *Annihilators of the General Quaternionic Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/square-roots-of-one-and-the-idempotents-of-the-general-quaternionic-sesqualgebra.html">Square Roots of One and the Idempotents of the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the roots of the central value $+1$ of the general quaternionic sesquilinear product $\tilde P\star\tilde Q=\tilde P^{\natural}\tilde Q^{*}$ and the idempotents of the product; a root of $\lambda$ a nonzero $\tilde P$ with $\tilde P\star\tilde P=\lambda e_0$, the reduction $\tilde P\star\tilde P=(\overline{\tilde P}\tilde P)^{\natural}$, the scalar part the Krein form $\sum_\mu\varepsilon_\mu\lvert P_\mu\rvert^2$ with $\varepsilon=(1,-1,-1,-1)$, so no root unless $\lambda$ is real, the coordinate system $\xi_0^2+\xi'^2_0-\lvert\boldsymbol{\xi}\rvert^2-\lvert\boldsymbol{\xi}'\rvert^2=\lambda$, $\xi_0\boldsymbol{\xi}+\xi'_0\boldsymbol{\xi}'=0$, $\boldsymbol{\xi}\times\boldsymbol{\xi}'=0$, the family $\tilde P=c(\hat\mu+it)$ with $(t^2-1)\lvert c\rvert^2=\lambda$ of real dimension four and the central circle $\lvert a\rvert^2=\lambda$ when $\lambda>0$, the central square $C(\tilde P)=c^2(1-t^2)$, the value $+1$ taking the slopes $\lvert t\rvert>1$ with $\lvert c\rvert^2=1/(t^2-1)$ beside the central circle and containing $e_0$ and $i$, so that every root of one is a unit of the plain algebra and none is square-zero; the value $-1$ quoted in a short paragraph, taking the slopes $\lvert t\rvert<1$ with $\lvert c\rvert^2=1/(1-t^2)$, containing $e_1,e_2,e_3$, non-empty, every one of them a unit of the plain algebra and not obtained by multiplying the roots of one by the central imaginary, the three central classes not being the plain classes of the same name; the idempotents, the solutions of $\tilde Q^{\natural}\tilde Q^{*}=\tilde Q$, equivalently of $\overline{\tilde Q}\tilde Q=\tilde Q^{\natural}$, whose coordinate equations are $Q_0=u\in\mathbb{R}$, $u=u^2-\lvert\mathbf Q\rvert^2$, $(2u+1)\mathbf a=0$ and $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b=-\tfrac12\mathbf b$, classified over the whole algebra as $0$, $e_0$ and the family $\tilde\Pi(\mu)=-\tfrac12e_0+\mu$ with $\mu$ in the real vector subspace and $(\mu,\mu)=\tfrac34$, every nontrivial idempotent of central square $1$ and hence a unit of the plain algebra with inverse $-\tfrac12e_0-\mu$; the family as a single class under the action of the unit quaternions by conjugation, outside the Hermitian subspace because a nontrivial idempotent is neither Hermitian nor skew-Hermitian, the absence of complementation, and the failure of the halving map $\tilde\Pi=\tfrac12(e_0+\tilde\Xi)$, $\tilde\Xi=2\tilde\Pi-e_0$ of the products with a unit, which here carries the roots of one to idempotents only at the two trivial roots $\pm e_0$; the contrast of the four idempotent sets, the plain product and the sibling sesquilinear product having infinite families of zero divisors, the sibling bilinear product only $0$ and $e_0$, and this product alone a family of units of the plain algebra, with the sibling sesquilinear idempotents isotropic here. The roots of $0$ and the nilpotents are *Square Roots of Zero and the Nilpotents of the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra*; the general element is *Square Roots of a General Element in the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra*; the plain reading is *Square Roots of Minus One, Zero and Plus One in the General Plain Algebra* and *Idempotents of the General Plain Algebra*; the zero divisors and the invertibility are *Zero Divisors of the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra* and *Norm and Invertibility in the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra*; and the square and the four idempotent sets are *The Square of the General Quaternionic Sesquilinear Product and the Two Halves* and *Comparison Between the Four General Products*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/square-roots-of-zero-and-the-nilpotents-of-the-general-quaternionic-sesqualgebra.html">Square Roots of Zero and the Nilpotents of the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- The roots of the central value $0$ of the general quaternionic sesquilinear product $\tilde P\star\tilde Q=\tilde P^{\natural}\tilde Q^{*}$ and the nilpotents of the product; a root of $\lambda$ a nonzero $\tilde P$ with $\tilde P\star\tilde P=\lambda e_0$ and a root of zero a nonzero $\tilde P$ with $\tilde P\star\tilde P=0$, the reduction $\tilde P\star\tilde P=(\overline{\tilde P}\tilde P)^{\natural}$ quoted from *Square Roots of One and the Idempotents of the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra*, so the square-zero equation is $\overline{\tilde P}\tilde P=0$, whose coordinates are $x_0^2+y_0^2=\lvert\mathbf p\rvert^2+\lvert\mathbf p'\rvert^2$, $x_0\mathbf p+y_0\mathbf p'=0$ and $\mathbf p\times\mathbf p'=0$ for $\tilde P=x_0+iy_0+\mathbf p+i\mathbf p'$; the value $0$ taking the slopes $t=\pm1$, the square-zero elements exactly the family $c(\hat\mu+i)$ over the complex numbers $c$ and the real unit vectors $\hat\mu$, equivalently $c(1+i\hat\nu)$, of real dimension four, the union of the complex lines based at the real unit directions, every nonzero member non-pure with scalar part $ic$, so the family lies in the non-pure part of the zero-divisor cone and is incomparable with the plain nilpotent cone, the two square-zero sets sharing only the origin; the nilpotent, its left-nested power, its index and the square-zero element quoted from *Definitions for the Study of the Algebraic Structures over the Biquaternion $\mathbb{C}$ Space*, the nonzero roots of zero being exactly the nilpotents of index two, the cube of a square-zero element vanishing so that its index is two and the question of a nilpotent of index three left unsettled; every root of zero a two-sided zero divisor with itself as partner, on the cone $C(\tilde P)=0$, a proper real four-dimensional subfamily of the real six-dimensional cone witnessed by the pure zero divisor $e_1+ie_2$ whose square is $-2e_0-2ie_3$, against the pure nilpotent cone of the plain product. The roots of one and the idempotents are *Square Roots of One and the Idempotents of the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra*; the general element is *Square Roots of a General Element in the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra*; the four square-zero sets, the chain and the cone are *Zero Divisors in the Algebraic Structures over the Biquaternion $\mathbb{C}$ Space*, *Nilpotents of the General Plain Algebra* and *Zero Divisors of the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/square-roots-of-a-general-element-in-the-general-quaternionic-sesqualgebra.html">Square Roots of a General Element in the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- A square root of $\tilde A$ in the general quaternionic sesquilinear product $\tilde P\star\tilde Q = \tilde P^{\natural}\tilde Q^{*}$ is an element with $\tilde P\star\tilde P = \tilde A$, and the square reduces to $\tilde P\star\tilde P = (\overline{\tilde P}\tilde P)^{\natural}$, so the equation is the plain equation $\overline{\tilde P}\tilde P = \tilde A^{\natural}$. On coordinates $\tilde P = x_0+iy_0+\mathbf p+i\mathbf q$ and $\tilde A$ with scalar part $A_0$ and vector part $\mathbf R+i\mathbf S$ the equation is the system $x_0^2+y_0^2-\lvert\mathbf p\rvert^2-\lvert\mathbf q\rvert^2 = A_0$, $2(x_0\mathbf p+y_0\mathbf q) = -\mathbf R$, $2\mathbf p\times\mathbf q = -\mathbf S$. The element $\tilde A$ is a square if and only if $A_0$ is real, $\mathbf R$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf S$, and the scalar part satisfies the bound $A_0<0$ with $A_0^2\ge\lvert\mathbf S\rvert^2-\lvert\mathbf R\rvert^2$ when $0<\lvert\mathbf R\rvert\le\lvert\mathbf S\rvert$, with no further restriction when $\lvert\mathbf R\rvert>\lvert\mathbf S\rvert$ and in the central case $\mathbf R = \mathbf S = 0$ where the roots are the roots of the central value. The image of the square map is a real six-dimensional set, so a non-empty set of elements has no square root; the solution family is of real dimension two in the interior of the image, and the nonzero nilpotents, in particular $e_0+ie_1$, are never squares. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-square-of-the-quaternionic-sesquilinear-product-and-the-two-halves.html">The Square of the General Quaternionic Sesquilinear Product and the Two Halves</a>
<!-- the square $\tilde Q\star\tilde Q=\tilde Q^{\natural}\tilde Q^{*}$, equivalently the ${}^{\natural}$-image of $\overline{\tilde Q}\tilde Q$, and its scalar part $\sum_{\mu=0}^{3}\varepsilon_\mu Q_\mu\overline{Q_\mu}$; the two halves of the square and the elements whose square vanishes, a proper subfamily of the zero divisors, against the two bilinear quaternionic multiplications, whose square-zero elements are the whole zero-divisor cone; the worked elements of the two-sphere of idempotents. -->

#### Advanced Properties

<a href="articles_maths/the-specificities-of-the-general-quaternionic-sesqualgebra.html">The Specificities of the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- The general quaternionic sesquilinear product $\tilde P\star\tilde Q = \tilde P^{\natural}\tilde Q^{*}$ is the unique one of the twelve structures on the biquaternion space whose two actions of $e_0$ are the natural conjugation on the right and the star on the left, $\tilde P\star e_0 = \tilde P^{\natural}$, $e_0\star\tilde Q = \tilde Q^{*}$; equivalently the unique one satisfying the star identity $(\tilde P\star\tilde Q)^{*} = \tilde Q\overline{\tilde P}$ and the factorization $\tilde P\star\tilde Q = (\overline{\tilde Q}\tilde P)^{\natural}$. The other eleven fail at least one of the two actions or the identity itself, and the four general products are excluded structurally by the parity of the two slots. The consequences are the specificities of the block. The product is linear in the first slot and conjugate-linear in the second, the left multiplication is $L_{\tilde P}(\tilde X) = \tilde P^{\natural}\tilde X^{*}$ with composite the linear sandwich $L_{\tilde P}L_{\tilde R}(\tilde X) = \tilde P^{\natural}\tilde X\overline{\tilde R}$, the right multiplication $R_{\tilde P}(\tilde X) = \tilde X^{\natural}\tilde P^{*}$ is linear, and the parity obstruction removes every projector and every square-zero operator, in contrast to the plain and the natural products. The square is the natural conjugate of the plain product, its scalar part is the Krein form of signature $(2,6)$, and its vanishing defines the non-pure family $c(\hat\mu+i)$. The idempotents are the family $-\tfrac12e_0+\mu$ with $\sum_k\mu_k^2 = \tfrac34$, and they are units of the plain algebra while the block has no unit. The ternary product fails the Jordan triple identity at a basis quintuple, and the first-slot conjugation is the common source of the criterion, the sign vector of the scalar form, the absence of a unit and the failure of the identity. The block has the element theory of the sesquilinear structures and none of their operator theory. -->

### The Biquaternion Symmetric Plain Sesqualgebra (SPS) over $\mathbb{C}$

<a href="articles_maths/introduction-to-the-symmetric-plain-sesqualgebra.html">Introduction to the Symmetric Plain Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the symmetric part of the sesquilinear product under the conjugate transpose read as a multiplication, $\tfrac12\bigl(\tilde P\tilde Q^{*}+\overline{\tilde Q\tilde P^{*}}\bigr)=\mathrm{Sc}\bigl(\tilde P\tilde Q^{*}\bigr)e_0=H(\tilde P,\tilde Q)e_0$ with $H(\tilde P,\tilde Q)=P_0\overline{Q_0}+(\mathbf{P},\overline{\mathbf{Q}})$, which is the Hermitian form read as a product; the class, which is sesquilinear over $(\mathbb{C},\bar{\cdot}\,)$, $\mathbb{C}$-linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second; conjugate-commutativity, $\tilde P\star\tilde Q=\overline{\tilde Q\star\tilde P}$; the central image and the absence of a unit; the diagonal $H(\tilde Q,\tilde Q)=|Q_0|^2+(\mathbf{Q},\overline{\mathbf{Q}})$, real and positive off the origin; the failure of the Jordan identity with the witness $x=y=e_1$, where the two sides are $0$ and $e_0$; the reconstruction $\mathrm{GPS}=\mathrm{SPS}+\mathrm{APS}$; and the placement of the block among the twelve. The general construction of the sesqualgebra parts is *The Symmetric and Antisymmetric Parts of a Sesqualgebra Product*; the form $H$ is *The 4 Forms over the Biquaternion $\mathbb{C}$ Space*; the product it splits is *Introduction to the General Plain Sesqualgebra of Biquaternions*; and the two matrix element representations of the block, the realization $\mathsf{M}_2$ in $M_2(\mathbb{C})$ and the left regular model $\mathsf{M}_4$ in $M_4(\mathbb{C})_L$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/norm-and-invertibility-in-the-symmetric-plain-sesqualgebra.html">Norm and Invertibility in the Symmetric Plain Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- The symmetric plain sesqualgebra $\tilde P\star\tilde Q = H(\tilde P,\tilde Q)e_0$ has no unit, because every value of the product is central and $\mathbb{B}$ has non-central elements; consequently it has no inverse, no group of units and no division structure, and the relative definitions are empty. Its norm is the diagonal of the Hermitian form, $N(\tilde{Q}) = H(\tilde{Q},\tilde{Q}) = \sum_\mu\lvert Q_\mu\rvert^{2} = $ the coefficient of $\tilde{Q}\star\tilde{Q}$, a real non-negative definite quadratic form of signature $(8,0)$, invariant under the three conjugations. The norm is not multiplicative: $N(\tilde P\star\tilde Q) = \lvert H(\tilde P,\tilde Q)\rvert^{2}$, the defect is the discriminant $N(\tilde P)N(\tilde Q) - \lvert H(\tilde P,\tilde Q)\rvert^{2}\geq 0$, vanishing exactly on linearly dependent pairs, and the norm is multiplicative on the centre alone. What replaces multiplicativity is the exact identity $H(\tilde P\star\tilde Q,\tilde R) = H(\tilde P,\tilde Q)H(e_0,\tilde R)$. The norm polarises to the Hermitian form, $\Re H$ at the symmetric step and $H$ at the four-term display. What replaces the invertibility criterion is the definiteness, $N(\tilde{Q}) = 0\Leftrightarrow\tilde{Q} = 0$: the block has no nonzero isotropic vector and no invertible element, its element classification is two-way, and the complement of the origin is the zero-divisor set. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-specificities-of-the-symmetric-plain-sesqualgebra.html">The Specificities of the Symmetric Plain Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- The symmetric plain sesqualgebra is the only one of the twelve structures that is Hermitian: it is conjugate-commutative, $\tilde P\star\tilde Q = \overline{\tilde Q\star\tilde P}$, and it has central image, $\tilde P\star\tilde Q\in\mathbb{C}e_0$, and the two clauses together are equivalent to the product being a Hermitian form read as a multiplication. The other eleven fail at least one clause: the four general products fail the centrality; the four antisymmetric parts fail both, being alternating ($\mathrm{APA}$, $\mathrm{AQA}$) or conjugate-alternating ($\mathrm{APS}$, $\mathrm{AQS}$) with image in the vector subspace; and among the symmetric parts the plain one fails both, the quaternionic one fails the centrality, and the quaternionic sesquilinear one fails the centrality after satisfying conjugate-commutativity. The operator face of the criterion is the composition law $L^{\star}_{\tilde A}L^{\star}_{\tilde B} = A_0R^{\star}_{\tilde B}$ with $R^{\star}_{\tilde B} = \overline{L^{\star}_{\tilde B}}$, the second identity being conjugate-commutativity read on the operators, and the projectors collapse to the zero operator because a conjugate-linear idempotent operator is zero. Everything peculiar to the block, the definite norm, the absence of unit and of isotropic vectors, the ray image of the square map and the linear subspace of the index-three nilpotents, follows from the one Hermitian clause. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-conjugate-commutative-law-and-the-idempotents-of-the-symmetric-plain-sesqualgebra.html">The Conjugate-Commutative Law and the Idempotents of the Symmetric Plain Sesqualgebra</a>

The positivity and the cone of the Hermitian form are *Positivity and the Hermitian Cone of the Biquaternion Algebra with Hermitian Adjoint*; the projections of the sesqualgebra are *Projections of the Biquaternion Sesqualgebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-hermitian-form-as-a-product-on-the-symmetric-plain-sesqualgebra.html">The Hermitian Form as a Product on the Symmetric Plain Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the identification of the block with the Hermitian form $H$ read as a product and the rank-one structure that follows: the image the centre, the Gram matrix of $H$ on the algebra basis, which is the identity, and its positivity on the real basis; the positivity $H(\tilde Q,\tilde Q)=|Q_0|^2+(\mathbf{Q},\overline{\mathbf{Q}})$ and the absence of an isotropic vector; the Cauchy and Schwarz inequality for $H$, with its equality case; the trace functional and the trace form of the block, computed; the invariance of $H$ under the block, computed, and its comparison with the invariance of the trace form of $\mathrm{SPA}$; the restriction of $H$ to the remarkable subspaces with its rank and its positivity; the coincidence with the quaternion form $N$ of $\mathrm{SQA}$ on the real part. The form $H$, its cone and its positivity theory are *The 4 Forms over the Biquaternion $\mathbb{C}$ Space*, *Positivity and the Hermitian Cone of the Biquaternion Algebra with Hermitian Adjoint* and *The Canonical Hermitian Form on the Regular Module of the Biquaternion Algebra*; here it is read as the multiplication of the block. -->

The pattern is the one of *Remarkable Subspaces under the General Plain Sesqualgebra of Biquaternions*; the subspaces themselves are *Introduction to the Remarkable Subspaces*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-multiplication-operators-of-the-symmetric-plain-sesqualgebra.html">The Multiplication Operators of the Symmetric Plain Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the operators of the block, $L^{\star}_{\tilde A}\tilde R=H(\tilde A,\tilde R)e_0$ and $R^{\star}_{\tilde A}\tilde R=H(\tilde R,\tilde A)e_0$, their conjugate-linearity in the second argument and their relation through the coefficientwise conjugation; the rank one of every nonzero operator, its image the centre and its kernel the hyperplane $H(\tilde A,\cdot\,)=0$; the trace of the operator, computed; the adjoint of $L^{\star}_{\tilde A}$ with respect to $H$, computed, and the verification of whether it is $R^{\star}_{\tilde A}$; the composition and the failure of multiplicativity; the group of linear maps preserving $H$ and its Lie algebra, taken as groups of linear maps; the structure group of the block. ### The Biquaternion Symmetric Quaternionic Algebra (SQA) over $\mathbb{C}$

<a href="articles_maths/introduction-to-the-symmetric-quaternionic-algebra.html">Introduction to the Symmetric Quaternionic Algebra</a>
<!-- the symmetric part of the quaternionic product read as a multiplication, $\tfrac12(\tilde P^{\natural}\tilde Q+\tilde Q^{\natural}\tilde P)=N(\tilde P,\tilde Q)e_0$ with $N(\tilde P,\tilde Q)=P_0Q_0+(\mathbf{P},\mathbf{Q})$, which is the quaternion form of *Comparison Between the Four General Products* read as a product; the class, which is $\mathbb{C}$-bilinear; commutativity; the image in the centre $\mathbb{C}_{\mathbb{B}}$ and the absence of a unit; the failure of the Jordan identity with the witness $x=y=e_1$, where the two sides are $0$ and $e_0$; the sixteen products of the basis, all central; the reconstruction $\mathrm{GQA}=\mathrm{SQA}+\mathrm{AQA}$; and the placement of the block among the twelve; the realisation in $M_2(\mathbb{C})$, where the product becomes the symmetrisation of a matrix product with the adjugate, the matrix of the quaternion conjugation, acting on it, and the value is the scalar matrix $N(\tilde P,\tilde Q)I_2$, with the trace and the rank of the resulting endomorphism and the trace pairing of the form; and the left regular realisation in $M_4(\mathbb{C})_L$, where the product becomes the symmetrisation of a product of left multiplications, the transpose carrying the quaternion conjugation, and the value is the scalar matrix $N(\tilde P,\tilde Q)I_4$, with the trace $4N(\tilde P,\tilde Q)$, the rank and the trace pairing of the form. The general construction of the parts is *The Symmetric and Antisymmetric Parts of an Algebra Product*; the product it splits is *Introduction to the General Quaternionic Algebra of Biquaternions*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/norm-and-invertibility-in-the-symmetric-quaternionic-algebra.html">Norm and Invertibility in the Symmetric Quaternionic Algebra</a>
<!-- The symmetric quaternionic product has no unit and no one-sided unit, hence no inverse and no group of units: the definitions of the unit and the inverse are those of *Definitions for the Study of the Algebraic Structures over the Biquaternion $\mathbb{C}$ Space*, and the block answers them with an absence, the element $e_0$ being a unit of the central line alone. The substitute the block uses is the single quadratic form $N(\tilde Q)=N(\tilde Q,\tilde Q)=\sum_\mu Q_\mu^2$, the diagonal of the pairing, which is exactly the multiplicative norm $\tilde Q\tilde Q^{\natural}$ of the parent plain product; the block's product is its polarisation placed in the centre, the conjugate square $\tilde Q\star\tilde Q^{\natural}$ is the different form $Q_0^2-(\mathbf Q,\mathbf Q)$, and $N$ is not multiplicative for the block, $N(\tilde P\star\tilde Q)=N(\tilde P,\tilde Q)^2$. The non-isotropic class $N\neq0$ is precisely the group of units of the parent, with the inverse $\tilde Q^{-1}=\tilde Q^{\natural}/N(\tilde Q)$, so the invertibility theory of the parent is read on the diagonal of the block; the isotropic class $N=0$ consists of $0$ together with the square-zero elements. The group-theoretic substitute inside the block is the group of linear maps preserving $N$, which is treated in the Operators entry and not here. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-specificities-of-the-symmetric-quaternionic-algebra.html">The Specificities of the Symmetric Quaternionic Algebra</a>
<!-- the operator theory of the rank-one pairing $\tilde P\bullet\tilde Q=N(\tilde P,\tilde Q)e_0$ of the block, whose single identity is $L_{\tilde X}^{2}=X_0L_{\tilde X}$ with $X_0$ the scalar coordinate, read from the composition law $L^{\bullet}_{\tilde A}L^{\bullet}_{\tilde B}=N(\tilde A,e_0)L^{\bullet}_{\tilde B}$; the rank one of every nonzero left multiplication, its image the central line $\mathbb{C}e_0$ and its kernel the hyperplane $N(\tilde X,\cdot\,)=0$, and its faithfulness in $\tilde X$ because the form is non-degenerate; the classification of the idempotent endomorphisms, exactly the elements of scalar coordinate $1$ together with the origin, a family of complex dimension three of pairwise distinct rank-one projections onto the central line, indexed by the affine hyperplane and not by the idempotents of the algebra, which are $0$ and $e_0$ alone, so that even the unit gives the projection $E:\tilde Y\mapsto Y_0e_0$ and not the identity, the algebra having no unit; the classification of the square-zero endomorphisms, exactly the elements of scalar coordinate $0$, that is the vector subspace, distinct from the isotropic cone of the square-zero elements; the failure of the criterion at $e_1$, where $e_1\bullet(e_1\bullet e_0)=0$ and $(e_1\bullet e_1)\bullet e_0=e_0$; and the scalar law — commutative with central values, equivalently $\tilde X\circ\tilde Y=\beta(\tilde X,\tilde Y)e_0$ — with the isolation of the block among the twelve by a compact table, and the remark on the four symmetric structures. The companions are *The Specificities of the General Quaternionic Algebra* and *The Multiplication Operators of the Symmetric Quaternionic Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-radical-and-the-isotropic-elements-of-the-symmetric-quaternionic-algebra.html">The Radical and the Isotropic Elements of the Symmetric Quaternionic Algebra</a>

### The Biquaternion Symmetric Quaternionic Sesqualgebra (SQS) over $\mathbb{C}$

#### Basic Properties

<a href="articles_maths/introduction-to-the-symmetric-quaternionic-sesqualgebra.html">Introduction to the Symmetric Quaternionic Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the symmetric part of the quaternionic sesquilinear product under the conjugate transpose read as a multiplication, $\tfrac12\bigl(\tilde P^{\natural}\tilde Q^{*}+\tilde Q^{*}\tilde P^{\natural}\bigr)=\bigl[P_0\overline{Q_0}-(\mathbf{P},\overline{\mathbf{Q}})\bigr]-P_0\overline{\mathbf{Q}}-\overline{Q_0}\mathbf{P}$, with scalar part the form $K$ and vector part the mixed term, the cross product cancelling between the two orders; the class, which is sesquilinear over $(\mathbb{C},\bar{\cdot}\,)$; conjugate-commutativity; the absence of a unit and the values in no one of the remarkable subspaces; the diagonal $\tilde Q\star\tilde Q=K(\tilde Q,\tilde Q)e_0-Q_0\overline{\mathbf{Q}}-\overline{Q_0}\mathbf{Q}$, central at $e_1$ ($-e_0$) and at $e_1+ie_2$ ($-2e_0$) and non-central at $e_0+e_1$ ($-2e_1$); the failure of the Jordan identity with the witness $x=y=e_1$, where the two sides are $-e_0$ and $e_0$; the two-halves relation to the two orders of the plain product $\overline{\tilde Q}\tilde P$; the reconstruction $\mathrm{GQS}=\mathrm{SQS}+\mathrm{AQS}$; and the placement of the block among the twelve. The general construction of the sesqualgebra parts is *The Symmetric and Antisymmetric Parts of a Sesqualgebra Product*; the form $K$ is *Introduction to the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra of Biquaternions* and its Gram matrix *The Krein Gram Matrix and the Restrictions of the Form*; the product it splits is *Introduction to the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra of Biquaternions*. The two matrix element representations of the block are merged into this article: the isomorphism model $\mathsf{M}_2(\tilde Q)=Q_0I-i(Q_1\sigma_1+Q_2\sigma_2+Q_3\sigma_3)$ with $\mathsf{M}_2(\tilde P\star\tilde Q)=\tfrac12(\operatorname{adj}\mathsf{M}_2(\tilde P)\mathsf{M}_2(\tilde Q)^{\dagger}+\mathsf{M}_2(\tilde Q)^{\dagger}\operatorname{adj}\mathsf{M}_2(\tilde P))$, trace $2K$, determinant $N$ and form $K=\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{adj}\mathsf{M}_2(\tilde P)\mathsf{M}_2(\tilde Q)^{\dagger})$, and the left regular model with $\mathsf{M}_4(\tilde P\star\tilde Q)=\tfrac12(\mathsf{M}_4(\tilde P)^{\mathsf T}\mathsf{M}_4(\tilde Q)^{\dagger}+\mathsf{M}_4(\tilde Q)^{\dagger}\mathsf{M}_4(\tilde P)^{\mathsf T})$, trace $4K$ and determinant $N^{2}$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/norm-and-invertibility-in-the-symmetric-quaternionic-sesqualgebra.html">Norm and Invertibility in the Symmetric Quaternionic Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the unit and the inverse of the block, defined relative to a general product and cited to *Definitions for the Study of the Algebraic Structures over the Biquaternion $\mathbb{C}$ Space*; the absence of a unit proved afresh, hence no inverse and an empty group of units; the two quadratic objects, the square map with scalar part $K$ and the plain norm $N=\tilde Q\tilde Q^{\natural}=C(\tilde Q)$, both non-multiplicative, with the pair $e_3,e_2$ as the common witness; regularity in the place of invertibility, $L^{\star}_{\tilde Q}$ injective iff $Q_0\neq0$ and $C(\tilde Q)\neq0$, with the ranks $8,6,4$ and rank $0$ at the origin; and the dissociation of the Krein form from the divisor class, $K(e_0+e_1,e_0+e_1)=0$ for a regular element and $K(e_1,e_1)=-1$ for a divisor. The norm of the plain product is *Norm and Invertibility in the General Plain Algebra*; the divisors are *Zero Divisors of the Symmetric Quaternionic Sesqualgebra*; the operators are *The Multiplication Operators of the Symmetric Quaternionic Sesqualgebra*. -->

### The Biquaternion Antisymmetric Plain Algebra (APA) over $\mathbb{C}$

<a href="articles_maths/introduction-to-the-antisymmetric-plain-algebra.html">Introduction to the Antisymmetric Plain Algebra</a>
<!-- the antisymmetric part of the plain product read as a multiplication, $\tfrac12(\tilde P\tilde Q-\tilde Q\tilde P)=\mathbf{P}\times\mathbf{Q}$, scalar part zero and vector part the cross product of the two vector parts; the class, which is $\mathbb{C}$-bilinear; alternation and the vanishing of the diagonal; the image in the vector subspace $\mathrm{Vect}(\mathbb{B})$ and the absence of a unit; the Jacobi identity, which this operation alone of the twelve satisfies, so that it is a Lie product; the identity of the operation with half the commutator of the algebra; the sixteen brackets of the basis; the reconstruction $\mathrm{GPA}=\mathrm{SPA}+\mathrm{APA}$; and the placement of the block among the twelve. The general construction of the parts is *The Symmetric and Antisymmetric Parts of an Algebra Product*; the Lie structure it carries is *The Unitary Lie Algebra*. The block in the $2\times2$ matrix element representation $M_2(\mathbb{C})$ is the halved commutator $\tfrac12(XY-YX)$, of image the trace-free matrices identified with $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{C})$ and kernel the scalar matrices identified with the centre, and the trace form of that model is the Killing form of the block; in the $4\times4$ regular model $M_4(\mathbb{C})_L$ the bracket is the halved commutator of the left multiplication operators, and its adjoint representation gives the six-dimensional real matrices of vanishing trace and determinant, rank four and the characteristic polynomial $\lambda^2(\lambda^2+4)^2$ at the real units. -->

<a href="articles_maths/norm-and-invertibility-in-the-antisymmetric-plain-algebra.html">Norm and Invertibility in the Antisymmetric Plain Algebra</a>
<!-- the norm and the inverse of the block, and the absence of both: no unit on either side, hence no invertible element, an empty group of units and no solution of $\tilde X\wedge\tilde Y=e_0$, and no norm, the square and the conjugated square vanishing identically by alternation ($\tilde X\wedge\tilde X^{\natural}=\mathbf X\times(-\mathbf X)=0$); the two quadratic objects that survive, the operator trace form $K(\tilde A,\tilde B)=\operatorname{Tr}(L_{\tilde A}L_{\tilde B})=-2\,\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf B$, of Gram matrix $\operatorname{diag}(0,-2,-2,-2)$, rank three and radical the centre, which is the invariant form of the block, and the rank-one scalar-part form $\varphi(\tilde P,\tilde Q)=P_0Q_0$, whose radical and isotropic cone are the vector subspace; the independence of the two, their spanning of the invariant symmetric forms, and the failure of multiplicativity at the pairs $(e_1,e_2)$ and $(e_0,e_0)$. The twin is *Norm and Invertibility in the General Plain Algebra*; the invariant form is *The Killing Form of the Antisymmetric Plain Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-specificities-of-the-antisymmetric-plain-algebra.html">The Specificities of the Antisymmetric Plain Algebra</a>

### The Biquaternion Antisymmetric Plain Sesqualgebra (APS) over $\mathbb{C}$

<a href="articles_maths/introduction-to-the-antisymmetric-plain-sesqualgebra.html">Introduction to the Antisymmetric Plain Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the antisymmetric part of the sesquilinear product under the conjugate transpose read as a multiplication, $\tfrac12\bigl(\tilde P\tilde Q^{*}-\overline{\tilde Q\tilde P^{*}}\bigr)=\mathrm{Vect}\bigl(\tilde P\tilde Q^{*}\bigr)=-P_0\overline{\mathbf{Q}}+\overline{Q_0}\mathbf{P}-\mathbf{P}\times\overline{\mathbf{Q}}$, the vector part of the general plain sesquilinear product; the class, which is sesquilinear over $(\mathbb{C},\bar{\cdot}\,)$; conjugate-alternation, $\tilde P\diamond\tilde Q=-\overline{\tilde Q\diamond\tilde P}$; the pure-vector image $\mathrm{Vect}(\mathbb{B})$ and the absence of a unit; the non-vanishing diagonal $\tilde Q\diamond\tilde Q=\mathrm{Vect}(\tilde Q\tilde Q^{*})$, which is $2ie_3$ at the element $e_1+ie_2$; the failure of the Jacobi identity with the witness $(e_0,e_1,e_2)$, whose cyclic sum is $e_3$; the reconstruction $\mathrm{GPS}=\mathrm{SPS}+\mathrm{APS}$; the placement of the block among the twelve; and the two matrix element representations, in which the block is the traceless part of the conjugate-transposed product, $\mathsf{M}_2(\tilde P\diamond\tilde Q)=M-\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}(M)I=\tfrac12(M-\operatorname{adj}M)$ with determinant $N$, and $\mathsf{M}_4(\tilde P\diamond\tilde Q)=\mathsf{M}_4(\tilde P)\mathsf{M}_4(\tilde Q)^{\dagger}-\tfrac14\operatorname{Tr}(\cdot)I=\tfrac12(M-M^{\mathsf T})$ with determinant $N^{2}$. The general construction of the sesqualgebra parts is *The Symmetric and Antisymmetric Parts of a Sesqualgebra Product*; the sesquilinear bracket is *The Sesquilinear Commutator*; the product it splits is *Introduction to the General Plain Sesqualgebra of Biquaternions*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/norm-and-invertibility-in-the-antisymmetric-plain-sesqualgebra.html">Norm and Invertibility in the Antisymmetric Plain Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the two notions the block does not carry and the functional that survives: **no unit** on either side, by the parity of the scalar part, the one-sided actions being $\tilde u\diamond e_0=\mathbf{u}$ and $e_0\diamond\tilde u=-\overline{\mathbf{u}}$ against the central $e_0$, hence **no inverse**, an empty group of units and no solution of the one-sided equations $\tilde Q\diamond\tilde R=e_0$, $\tilde R\diamond\tilde Q=e_0$, the left member being a pure vector and the right member central; the right unit $e_0$ of the parent product destroyed by the projection, which leaves $\tilde P\diamond e_0=\tilde P$ holding on the pure vectors alone and at no element with a non-zero scalar part; the algebraic norm $N(\tilde Q)=\tilde Q\tilde Q^{\natural}$ not descending, its multiplicativity failing on the diagonal, $e_0\diamond e_0=e_1\diamond e_1=0$ against $N(e_0)N(e_0)=N(e_1)N(e_1)=e_0$; and the form that survives, the positive definite Hermitian form $H(\tilde P,\tilde Q)=\operatorname{Sc}(\tilde P\tilde Q^{*})$, nondegenerate, of signature $(3,0)$ on the image. The twin is *Norm and Invertibility in the General Plain Algebra*; the pairing of the surviving form is *The Sesquilinear Pairing of the Antisymmetric Plain Sesqualgebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-specificities-of-the-antisymmetric-plain-sesqualgebra.html">The Specificities of the Antisymmetric Plain Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the operator criterion of the block: the right multiplication by the ambient unit is the **projection onto the vector subspace**, $R^{\diamond}_{e_0}\tilde X=\tilde X\diamond e_0=\operatorname{Vect}\tilde X$, while the left one is its conjugate, $L^{\diamond}_{e_0}=-\overline{\cdot}\circ P_{\operatorname{Vect}}$; the block is the **only** one of the twelve structures in which the splitting $\mathbb{B}=\operatorname{Vect}(\mathbb{B})\oplus\mathbb{C}_{\mathbb{B}}$ is realised on the right by a single element, and no other structure has any element whose right multiplication is $P_{\operatorname{Vect}}$, the splitting being realised on the left by $\mathrm{AQA}$ instead; the projector classification $R^{\diamond}_{\tilde X}{}^{2}=R^{\diamond}_{\tilde X}\iff\tilde X\in\{0,e_0\}$, with $R^{\diamond}_{e_0}=P_{\operatorname{Vect}}$ and $R^{\diamond}_{0}=0$; the compact isolation of the block among the twelve by the table of $R^{\star}_{e_0}$ over the six families; the companion law of conjugate-alternation, shared with $\mathrm{AQS}$ alone and separated from it by the non-vanishing of the diagonal; and the reading of the whole element theory of the block, the absence of the unit and of the inverse, the unique idempotent, the absent roots of $\pm1$, the thin nilpotents and the total zero-divisor set, as consequences of the one identity. The model is *The Specificities of the General Plain Algebra*; the twins are *The Specificities of the General Quaternionic Algebra*, *The Specificities of the Symmetric Quaternionic Algebra* and *The Specificities of the Symmetric Plain Algebra*; the left twin is *Introduction to the Antisymmetric Quaternionic Algebra of Biquaternions*. -->

### The Biquaternion Antisymmetric Quaternionic Algebra (AQA) over $\mathbb{C}$

<a href="articles_maths/introduction-to-the-antisymmetric-quaternionic-algebra.html">Introduction to the Antisymmetric Quaternionic Algebra</a>
<!-- the antisymmetric part of the quaternionic product read as a multiplication, $\tfrac12(\tilde P^{\natural}\tilde Q-\tilde Q^{\natural}\tilde P)=P_0\mathbf{Q}-Q_0\mathbf{P}-\mathbf{P}\times\mathbf{Q}$, scalar part zero and vector part the mixed term with the cross term subtracted; the class, which is $\mathbb{C}$-bilinear; alternation and the vanishing of the diagonal; the pure-vector image $\mathrm{Vect}(\mathbb{B})$ and the absence of a unit; the failure of the Jacobi identity, with the witness $(e_0,e_1,e_2)$ whose cyclic sum is $-e_3$; the identity of the operation with half the quaternionic commutator; the sixteen brackets of the basis; the reconstruction $\mathrm{GQA}=\mathrm{SQA}+\mathrm{AQA}$; and the placement of the block among the twelve. The general construction of the parts is *The Symmetric and Antisymmetric Parts of an Algebra Product*; the product it splits is *Introduction to the General Quaternionic Algebra of Biquaternions*; the two operators of the quaternionic product are *The Left Multiplications of the Quaternionic Product and the Opposite Monoid*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/norm-and-invertibility-in-the-antisymmetric-quaternionic-algebra.html">Norm and Invertibility in the Antisymmetric Quaternionic Algebra</a>
<!-- The antisymmetric quaternionic multiplication $\tilde P\diamond\tilde Q=P_0\mathbf Q-Q_0\mathbf P-\mathbf P\times\mathbf Q$ has no unit on either side, hence no invertible element and an empty group of units, and the inverse equation $\tilde X\diamond\tilde Y=e_0$ has no solution because every value of the block is a pure vector. The block has no norm: its square vanishes identically by alternation, and its conjugated square is the pure vector $-2X_0\mathbf X$, never central for a general element, so the central-valued norm of the parent product is lost with the scalar part of the parent. The two quadratic maps that survive are the invariant form $\varphi(\tilde P,\tilde Q)=P_0Q_0$, of rank one, radical and isotropic cone the vector subspace, the unique invariant form of the block, and the operator trace form $K(\tilde A,\tilde B)=3A_0B_0-2\sum_kA_kB_k$, non-degenerate and not invariant; none of the three is multiplicative, the pair $(e_0,e_0)$ separating the two sides of the multiplicativity equation in every case. The substitute the block uses is $\varphi$; the invertibility criterion of the general plain algebra is not transferred, and its place is taken by the absence of a unit and of an inverse. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-specificities-of-the-antisymmetric-quaternionic-algebra.html">The Specificities of the Antisymmetric Quaternionic Algebra</a>
<!-- The antisymmetric quaternionic multiplication is the alternating structure whose left multiplication by the algebra unit is the projection onto the vector subspace, $L_{e_0}\tilde X=\mathbf X$, $L_{e_0}^{2}=L_{e_0}$, with $R_{e_0}=-L_{e_0}$; the projector classification of the block is the pair $L_{\tilde X}^{2}=L_{\tilde X}\Leftrightarrow\tilde X\in\{0,e_0\}$, so the projector class is the smallest a structure with a nonzero projector can have. The projection is the canonical splitting $\mathbb{B}=\mathrm{Vect}(\mathbb{B})\oplus \mathbb{C}_{\mathbb{B}}$ realised by the multiplication of one element, the vector subspace being the image of the block and a left ideal and the centre its kernel. The block is the only one of the twelve in which the algebra unit multiplies as the projection onto the vector subspace, and the only one admitting an element $\tilde E$ with $\tilde E\star\tilde X=\mathbf X$ for every $\tilde X$, the element being $e_0$ uniquely; the other eleven give the identity, the projection onto the centre, the zero operator or a conjugate-linear map at the unit, and none of them gives this projection. The alternativity criterion of the plain algebra and the rank-one criterion of the symmetric quaternionic algebra both fail for the block, and the criterion stated here is its own. What the block delivers is two projectors, one splitting and one left ideal, and no Peirce calculus. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-jacobi-failure-and-the-associator-defect-of-the-antisymmetric-quaternionic-algebra.html">The Jacobi Failure and the Associator Defect of the Antisymmetric Quaternionic Algebra</a>
<!-- the cyclic sum of the bracket of the block, its failure to vanish, the witness $(e_0,e_1,e_2)$ with cyclic sum $-e_3$, and the minimal witnesses; the expression of the cyclic sum through the associator of the quaternionic product, which is the Lie-admissibility defect, computed on the witness; the comparison with the three Jacobi failures of the twelve, of which $\mathrm{AQA}$ is the one whose defect comes from non-associativity alone; the derived bracket and the algebra it generates; the alternating centre and the annihilator of the block; the elements whose adjoint operators commute; the failure read on the basis, on the real part and on the remarkable subspaces. The general construction of the parts is *The Symmetric and Antisymmetric Parts of an Algebra Product*; the associator of the quaternionic product is *The Associator and the Ternary Product of the Quaternionic Product*; the failure caused by a sesquilinear slot is *Lie Algebras of Sesqualgebras*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-invariant-bilinear-forms-of-the-antisymmetric-quaternionic-algebra.html">The Invariant Bilinear Forms of the Antisymmetric Quaternionic Algebra</a>
<!-- the bilinear forms invariant under the block, those $\beta$ with $\beta(\tilde P\star\tilde Q,\tilde R)+\beta(\tilde Q,\tilde P\star\tilde R)=0$, their space, their basis and their dimension, computed on the basis pairs; the vanishing of the trace form, the block being of scalar part zero; the symmetric invariant forms and the alternating ones, separated; the radical of each; the adjoint of the operator $L^{\star}_{\tilde A}$ with respect to a form; the comparison with the Lie case $\mathrm{APA}$, which carries a Killing form, and the substitute computed in the absence of a Jacobi identity; the restriction of each form to the remarkable subspaces. The forms of the general quaternionic algebra are *Comparison Between the Four General Products*; the invariant forms of the algebra are *The 4 Forms over the Biquaternion $\mathbb{C}$ Space*. -->
