<!-- the bracket of the block read on the remarkable subspaces, one to a section: the vanishing on the centre, the pure-vector image and the failure of closure of the Hermitian and anti-Hermitian subspaces, the elements whose bracket vanishes, the isotropic elements, and the table of the remarkable subspaces. The pattern is the one of *Remarkable Subspaces under the General Quaternionic Algebra of Biquaternions*; the subspaces themselves are *Introduction to the Remarkable Subspaces*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-adjoint-operators-of-the-antisymmetric-quaternionic-algebra.html">The Adjoint Operators of the Antisymmetric Quaternionic Algebra</a>
<!-- the operator $L^{\star}_{\tilde A}$ of the block, $\tilde R\mapsto\tilde A\star\tilde R=P_0(\tilde A)\mathbf{R}-R_0\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{R}$, its matrix in the real basis, its trace, zero, and its characteristic polynomial; its rank for a general element and the elements for which it drops; the commutator of two such operators and its deviation from $L^{\star}_{\tilde A\star\tilde B}$, which is the operator form of the Jacobi failure; the derivations that the block admits and the inner ones, computed; the structure group and the automorphism group of the bracket as groups of linear maps; the comparison with the Lie case $\mathrm{APA}$. The operators of the general quaternionic algebra are *The Left Multiplications of the Quaternionic Product and the Opposite Monoid*. -->

### The Biquaternion Antisymmetric Quaternionic Sesqualgebra (AQS) over $\mathbb{C}$

<a href="articles_maths/introduction-to-the-antisymmetric-quaternionic-sesqualgebra.html">Introduction to the Antisymmetric Quaternionic Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the antisymmetric part of the quaternionic sesquilinear product under the conjugate transpose read as a multiplication, $\tfrac12\bigl(\tilde P^{\natural}\tilde Q^{*}-\tilde Q^{*}\tilde P^{\natural}\bigr)=\mathbf{P}\times\overline{\mathbf{Q}}$, scalar part zero and vector part the cross product of the vector part of the first argument with the conjugate of the vector part of the second; the class, which is sesquilinear over $(\mathbb{C},\bar{\cdot}\,)$; conjugate-alternation; the pure-vector image $\mathrm{Vect}(\mathbb{B})$ and the absence of a unit; the non-vanishing diagonal, the cross product of the vector part with its conjugate, which is $-2ie_3$ at $e_1+ie_2$ and is $-2i\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}$ at $\mathbf{a}+i\mathbf{b}$ with $\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}$ real; the failure of the Jacobi identity with the witness $(e_1,e_1,ie_2)$, whose cyclic sum is $-2ie_2$, the only Jacobi failure of the twelve that needs a complex element off the real basis; the coincidence of the block with $\mathrm{APA}$ on the real part, so that the failure is invisible there; the reconstruction $\mathrm{GQS}=\mathrm{SQS}+\mathrm{AQS}$; and the placement of the block among the twelve; the count of its Jacobi failure on $72$ of the $512$ basis triples, and the closure of the block, whose values span the whole six-dimensional vector subspace so that the closure is a span and not a Lie algebra. The general construction of the sesqualgebra parts is *The Symmetric and Antisymmetric Parts of a Sesqualgebra Product*; the product it splits is *Introduction to the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra of Biquaternions*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/norm-and-invertibility-in-the-antisymmetric-quaternionic-sesqualgebra.html">Norm and Invertibility in the Antisymmetric Quaternionic Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- The block has no unit on either side, so no element of it is invertible and the group of units is empty; the notion of a regular element is unavailable, since it is defined only in a unital product; and the block has no algebraic norm, since the square of an element is never a nonzero central value and the norm of the algebra fails the multiplicativity at the block, the pair of the element $e_1$ with itself being the witness. The unit of the parent algebra is a square-zero element of the block, and the whole central line is annihilated by the block in both slots. The substitutes are three: the annihilators, which are complex planes of real dimension four for every non-central element and the whole space for the central ones; the relative inverse, in which the left multiplication by a non-central element is a $\mathbb{C}$-linear bijection of a quotient of the space onto the plane of the values orthogonal to its vector part, so that the equation $\tilde A\diamond\tilde R=\tilde W$ is solvable exactly on that plane and the solutions form a coset of the annihilator; and the pairing of the values with the Krein form, whose self-pairing is the negative of a non-negative real number. The comparison with the four general products is the table in which the block is the only row with no unit, no invertibility criterion and no norm. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-specificities-of-the-antisymmetric-quaternionic-sesqualgebra.html">The Specificities of the Antisymmetric Quaternionic Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- The block is the product of the twelve that is $K$-orthogonal to its own second argument: $K(\tilde X\diamond\tilde Y,\tilde Y)=0$ for all biquaternions, with $K$ the Krein form of the row. The law is equivalent to the alternating character of the induced form $K_{\tilde X}(\tilde Y,\tilde Z)=K(\tilde X\diamond\tilde Y,\tilde Z)$ and to the skew-adjointness of the conjugate-linear left multiplication, $L_{\tilde X}^{\dagger}=-L_{\tilde X}$; it is the classical perpendicularity of the cross product transferred to the sesquilinear class; and it is satisfied by no other of the twelve, each of the other eleven failing the law on a named witness. The law restricted to the pairs of pure vectors holds for eight of the twelve, so the criterion is the law on the whole space. The law delivers the element theory of the block: no unit, since a unit would make every element isotropic for a form that is positive at $e_0$; no root of a nonzero central value; no nontrivial idempotent, the isotropy together with the purity forcing the origin; and the index of the nilpotents at two and at four, through the recurrence of the left-nested powers. The zero-divisor set of the block is read from the rule and not from the law, and the criterion is form-theoretic, which is what separates the block from the symmetric half of its own row and makes the article the last of the block. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-conjugate-cross-product-and-the-jacobi-failure-of-the-antisymmetric-quaternionic-sesqualgebra.html">The Conjugate Cross Product and the Jacobi Failure of the Antisymmetric Quaternionic Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the block as the cross product with the conjugate of the second argument; the diagonal $\tilde Q\wedge\tilde Q=\mathbf{Q}\times\overline{\mathbf{Q}}$ and its vanishing exactly on the elements whose vector part is a complex multiple of a real vector, so that it is a genuine four-real-dimensional condition, with the quadric it cuts; the conjugating of the value; the failure of the Jacobi identity and the witness $(e_1,e_1,ie_2)$, the smallest witness, with the reason it needs a complex element and the reason the failure is invisible on the real forms where the block coincides with $\mathrm{APA}$; the comparison with the two other failing brackets $\mathrm{AQA}$ and $\mathrm{APS}$; the elements of square zero; the obstruction of *Lie Algebras of Sesqualgebras*. The general construction of the sesqualgebra parts is *The Symmetric and Antisymmetric Parts of a Sesqualgebra Product*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-sesquilinear-pairing-of-the-antisymmetric-quaternionic-sesqualgebra.html">The Sesquilinear Pairing of the Antisymmetric Quaternionic Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the pairing of the block with the Krein form, $K(\tilde P\wedge\tilde Q,\tilde R)$ and $K(\tilde P\wedge\tilde Q,\tilde P\wedge\tilde Q)$, with the Gram matrix of the block computed on the basis pairs, its rank and its radical; the invariance forms $\beta$ with $\beta(\tilde P\wedge\tilde Q,\tilde R)=-\overline{\beta(\tilde P,\tilde Q\wedge\tilde R)}$, their space and its dimension, computed; the vanishing of the trace form, checked and not assumed; the relation of the pairing to the norm of the value and to the quadric of the diagonal; the restriction to the remarkable subspaces with the signs of $K$ on each; the comparison with the pairing of $\mathrm{APS}$, where the form is $H$. The form $K$ is *The Krein Gram Matrix and the Restrictions of the Form* and *The Isotropic Structure of the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra*. -->

The pattern is the one of *Remarkable Subspaces under the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra of Biquaternions*; the subspaces themselves are *Introduction to the Remarkable Subspaces*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-adjoint-operators-of-the-antisymmetric-quaternionic-sesqualgebra.html">The Adjoint Operators of the Antisymmetric Quaternionic Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the operator $L^{\wedge}_{\tilde A}$ of the block, $\tilde R\mapsto\mathbf{A}\times\overline{\mathbf{R}}$, its conjugate-linearity in the second argument and the conjugate-linear operator theory it forces; its matrix in the real basis, its rank for a general element and its trace, zero; its composition with its conjugate and the conjugate-linear invariants; the adjoint with respect to $K$, computed; the derivations and the structure group of the block; the coincidence of the operator with the operator of $\mathrm{APA}$ on the real elements and the divergence off them. The operators of the general quaternionic sesquilinear product are *The Left and Right Multiplications of the General Quaternionic Sesquilinear Product*; the operators with the conjugate transpose are *J-Self-Adjoint and J-Unitary Operators on the General Quaternionic Sesqualgebra of Biquaternions*. -->

### Comparisons with $\mathbb{B}$

<a href="articles_maths/zero-divisors-in-the-algebraic-structures-over-the-biquaternion-c-space.html">Zero Divisors in the Algebraic Structures over the Biquaternion $\mathbb{C}$ Space</a>
